div.head: HUMAN HAM MUSTRI
div.p: THE HUMAN HAM MUSTRI

Few are aware what a large trac,e is tone in human hair. Italy is one of the , argest coiltetors and the value of her exports of this article amount to £BOO,OOO per annum. Human hair varies consiverably in value according to its quality ranging from 2s. per lb. to about 40s per lb. Naples is a great centre fer collec- tion, and the women of Italy save their combings and sell them regularly to the collectors. Many Italian women have a plan by which they can produce an annual supply yet not • appear to have, been clipped at all. This is dune by having half of the hair at the back of the head cut if, then twisting the remaining half over the exposed part and dressing it in such a manner that the clipped part is quite unexposed. By this means an annual crop is harvested, and their own hair is a source of income td,the women who live in the impoverished , districts. The Italians do not appear to convert thel hair into its permament uses but rather act as collectors, sorters, and exporters to the different countries in Europe and America where it is employed for many purposes. A considerable quantity goes to Paris where it is cleaned, bleaChed, and dyed the various colours and shades which the market demands. Human hairis largely used for the making of hair- nets, and the hair required for this passes born Paris to Germany, especially to Strassberg, which is a great centre for the hair-net industry. It is estimated that Strassberg sells annually about 12,000,000 hair nets, which are made almost wholly in the homes of Alsatian peasants. Weaving the nets is a work requiring, manual dexterity which can only he acquired successfully in youth when the fingers are supple and the eyesight good. This industry and the peculiar skill required to net hair, has become in part hereditary. The children begin first to tie the hairs together, end to end, to make one long hair. Then, without any implementi3, except a round piece of w ood about six inches long and half an inch in diameter, aud a needle, the older girls and women, and sometimes the men also, wease the nets. Each mesh is knotted,in much the same way that fish nets or hammocks are made, only, of course, tying a single hair is a more delicate and difficult task than tying a string. According to the American Consul at ISehl the work is poorly paid. The rate is =usually low at present, about ninepence halfpenny a dozen nets of ordinary colour. This means that a worker must tie about 12,000 knots to earn ninepenco half-penny, besides knotting the hair together, adjusting, counting, folding, and pack- ing the nets, To make a dozen nets is a day's work of ten or twelve hours. When the demand is greater, the pay increases more or less in proportion. The greater part of the human hair used for hair nets comes originally not from Italy but from China. No other hair possesses just the right degree ( f coarse- ness and resilience to give that p-culiar elastic spring to the mesh that a good hair-net rcquires. The hair of the northern races is too fine and soft and useless for this purpose. The black hair of the Italians and the Spanish is coarser and more suitable but the Chinese hair is the best.

div.head: TEMPTED TAXI-DRIVER.
div.p: THE TEMPTED TAXI-DRIVER.

Henry Stanle:f, the taxi-cab driver indicted at the Old 13ai1ey for complicity in stealing £1,350 worth of diamonds from Mr Myer Goldberg, a hackney diamoad merchant was sentenced on Tuesday to 18 months' hard labour. The Recorder endorsed the opinion of the jury that the prisoner was a man of good character who had been tempted by the offer of £lOO from a gang of skilful thieves.

div.head: NATURAL HISTORY PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: NATURAL HISTORY PHOTOGRAPHY.
Lecture to the Literary and Philosophical Society.

Expert advice on the subject of" Natural History Photo graphy " was given by Mr C C Champion, B.Sc., science master at Haileybury, on Monday evening, at a meet- ing of the Literary and Philosophical Society held in the Patten Hall. There was a fair attendance,includiog a number of ladies and members of the Photo- graphic' Society and Field Club. Mr Oswald Lotthouse presided. The lecture was illustrated with many beautiful lantern slides, taken by Mr Chattgon, aed as he explained, many of the photographs had been difficult to secure. The lecturer treated his subject in a masterly manner, always endeavouring to stimulate interest, while introducing diversions in the way of witty descriptions of the attitudes he had sometimes struck in search of good pictures. At the outset he said they would find that a natural history photographer took photographs of all kinds of subjects, except perhaps buildings and persons. (Laughter.) But he was not going to deal with the photographing of views and landscapes but rather devote more time to what was usually more difficult, namely, the photographing of animals, flowers and is sects themselves. Natural history photography included a great many subjects, but they would often find that a very good subject that could hardly be called a natural history one, would present itself when out on some natural history expedition. There was no reason, of course, why they should not take it, except the lark of plates, and that touched on one of the gleatest diffi- culties of natural history photography. The photo- graphs one took were such that one could never be sure that a good one had been obtained until they were developed, so that when possible, two were taken of the same subject. That soon used up plates, so they should be very cat eful in the choice of subject and not waste any plates in case they might want more than ot e exposure for a soorl subject. For instance, in the case of a bird going on to a nest, tea or a dozen ;sere often taken in the hope that some would be good. He exhibited some robin photographs and stated that they were the best of about 50,although the robin was the easiest of all birds to photograph. A great deal depended on the oice of camera and the lecturer advised sharp focussing as the best possible way to secure good natural history and scientific photographs. The so-called artistic smudges favoured in photogrephio exhibitions, of course, were useless. He even hat: seen this carried so far that at a Cambridge examination an architectural prize was awarded to one of those blurs, although there was a beautiful sharp photograph of an equally beautiful stone-stairway being shown. For that reason he thought slides were the best kind of positive, all the detail being more clearly shots n than in the best paper print. The best all-round cameo, he thought, for nsture p'natography was a quarter pla'.o with triple extension and a tripsd. In the case of living subjects, such as birds, it was essential to have a lens with a long focus, because otherwise such a small picture was secured. He then gave illustrations dealing with the various sizes of plates. All the slides he used be had printed himself, and the chief necessaries were time and patience which, unfortunately, were not to be bad for the asking, in the case of " etill life " photography such as flowers, trees, &c„ the greatest difficulty was the wind. In " moving life" photography the chief difficulty was the light. Altogether it was generally a matter of compromise, and one had to make the best of a bad job. In conclission, after many slides had been shown, the Lecturer announced that he would be glad to tell any- one anything he knew on the subject, though he was afraid that was not much, as he had only picked up photegraphy, so to speak, as he went along, and he bad used it more as a means than an end. He hoped they would do so too. He then gave much useful informa- tion on development, focussing and background. Discussifon followed, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded as lecturer on the proposition of Mr L GREENING, seconded by Mr A J JOLLEY.

div.head: PROSPECTIVE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WHINES.
div.p: PROSPECTIVE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WHINES.
MR. J. B. MARTINDALE, OF MANCHESTER.

Mr J B Martindale, of Manchester, on Tuesday night addressed a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Widnes Division Liberal Association. Be had been invited to become the prospective Liberal candidate for the civision in oppositi:in to the sitting member, Colonel Hall Walker. He accepted the invitation. In the coarse of his address Mr Martindale gave his support to all the great proposals of the Government. Touching upon the taxation of land values, he said he believed in such a reform but knew that it alone could not cure all social ills. An inquiry was being made into the land problem, and when it had concluded the Government would produce a scheme as well con- sidered in all its details as the Insuranci- Act. Mr Martindale, who is 25 years of age, is 'junior partner in the firm of John Bell and Co., woollen merchants, of Manchester. Mr Martindale for some time has acted as secretary to Sir W P Byles in North Salford. He is a member of the Executive Committee of the Knutsford Liberal Association, and has a seat on the Committee of the '95 Club, Manchester. Mr lvlartindale was born at Chorlton-cum-Hardy, his n.other being a daughter of the late Mr Robert Wright, of Sale, who was managing director of Messrs Barlow and Jones, of Manchester. ,Ife was educated at Kilgriggan School and at Manchester University. wh-re he came under the influence of Professor S J Chapman.

div.head: Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Militarism. A Justifiable Strike.
div.p: Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Militarism. A Justifiable Strike.

The Rev A M Mitchell, vicar of Burtonwood, writes as follows in his Parish Magazit.e :—There is a strike we long to see,—net the strike of traders and workets but of natiens and peoples. 'Forte tk ill not be much difference of opieion as 10 the justifiability of strike against war, except among those whose it terest it is to promote and foster the spirit of militarism. If it he said, " No strike is justifiable," we beg respectfully th coffer, one strike, at least, can justify itscli,—the strike against teilirteistu' its expansion, its growth, the evils, the horrors which follow la its tram. It is idle, worse than idle, it is wickeO,it is blaspht mous, to assert, that huge armies and navies, and all the abominable cievides of modern " arilihraente," preserve the peters of Europe. Swollen arrays ited ..navies must find an outlet for their energies; that outlet is in war, by hind and sea. Peace, natioual and internatioeal, like the peace betweeu man and man, rests in the evolution of toe sense of justice, the recognition of human rights , and the brotherhood of nations. Enorrueus taxation for the maiuteliaece of opposing eimies and navies will never ensure peace to the world, nor is "diplomatic secrecy" built that way. A European Armageddon is no remote coniingeecy ; if War promoters and the apostles of militarism have their way it will very soon come to pass. A European blaze wi a mean more than War, more then N fllltl3 expenditure of the people's money, more than horrible, euruan .carnage, it will, it must result in European suicide. The voice of the War charmer must not be listened to; we must turn to him the deaf ear, charm be never so wisely. We strike against • militarism with its inevit- able issues—taxation, war coMeliption, carnage, the destruction of the flower of 11P,nhood. We are not Without hope. What more hopeful sign could there be than this,—" the party of Labour in every country is pledged against War and devoted to the cause of Peace." Militarism and all its works is the enemy of Peac3, of the entente cordiale, of commerce, of home prosperity. The cry of destitution is heard on every ride in our own and foreign landso, hilst hundreds, even thousands of millions if money are forced out of the taxpayers' pockets to be freely squandered in maintaining Europe as an armed Camp. lu tifty yeers the sum of 2,137,553,253, or an average of £42,751,065, per annum, throuehote, has been expended in this country alone. We are weary of war scares, disgusted with unjust, unfounded suspicions" engendered by the , self-interested, saddened and angered by the never ceasing demand for more battalions more dreadnoughts and super-dreadniaights. Let us make an end of the "idolatry of militarism," let us insist, es is the duty of overy Christina that law shail be suostituted for force in the ,e:ations of nations, as it has been already substituted within the nations. History 'witnesses to the decline and final passing of great and powerful notions in consequence of the insatiable toll of militarism. That history repeats itself is no fiction.

div.head: Free Church United Service.
div.p: Free Church United Service.

Th 9 annual interchange of pulpits in connection with the INarrington Free Churcti Council took place on Sunday. It was notable for the fact that fot the first time in the history of the Council the Cairo-street Unitarian Church took part in the exchange, Dr Mellor preaching at the Independent Methodieat Church, Stockton Fleatb, and Mr A Mounfield at Cairo-street. The United Communion service was held at Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church at eight o'clock. The Rev W T Jae presided and the address was given by the Rev W Cooper. Others taking part were the Revs W A Beckett, W Reid, GI Curtis and Parry Jones and Mr A Mounfleld. Notwithstanding the wretched weather, there was a good congregation—in fact, the service was one of the most successful ever held in connection with the Council.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S A. Society:
div.p: Wycliffe P.S A. Society:

Ihere was a fair attendance on Stmday-.The ureAodent (Mr B Farrar) presided, and Mr W Street gave the address on "Digging deep, or a good foundation,' These were the thoughts suggested by the words of Christ who said that to build upon the rock was good and wise, because storms and winds could not destroy, but to neglect a good foundation was very unwise and ruinous. The building would not resist the fury of the storms. o.lr 2piritual foundation must be with being born again, and building upon the rock of ages of Christ. Then we could build up a true manly character, the effect of our lives upon others would be good and the Church of Christ would benefit by our building. Miss E Tanner sang sweetly "I need Thee every hour" and" Lead kindly light," Mr Payton, Mug. Bac. pre- sided At the organ Mr Yearsley read the lesson. The Prcsicieilt led the prayer. St. John's Presbyterian Guild.

At the usual weekly meeting of the Guild at St. John's on Monday evening the minister, Rev W Reid, in speaking of hymn writers, referred to several instances in which the author's name had become popular through the writing of one hymn which had outlived all his other work. He instanced Canon Twells, and his "At even ere the sun was set," a hymn foundee on one of the most gracious events in the life of Jesus Christ. A few details of the author's history ware given, and the members joined in singing the hymn. Mr Byron's "Christians awake" was next treated, and the circum- stances under which the hymn was written were given. An impressive story was told reminiscent, of the France-Russian war when one of the French soldiers, midway between the walls of beseiged Paris and the Russian trenches, sang on Christmas Eve, the first four lines of " Hark ! the herald angels sing." Miss Clephane's "Ninety and nine," together wita the circumstances under which Mr Sankey first saw and made use of it, and Dr Matheson's" 0 Love that will not let me go" to St. Margaret, by Dr Peace, were next dealt witb, and effectively rendered as solos by Miss Snallham and Mr Cannon respectively. Rev. Dr. Burford Hooke at Wycliffe Church. The Rev Dr Burford Hooke, D.D., of London' again occupied the pulpit at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday.. In au address to the children he told a story of a London boy, illustrating the truth of the words " Seek early and ye shall end." The sermon was based on the woids " Take ye away the stone " (John xi., 39). Referring to Christ's command to the grumblers who 'stood around the tomb of Lazarus to take away the stone, he said Christ might easily have removed the stone himself but this was not God's way. rom the very dawn of history God had never done for the race that which the race could do for itself. The same thing was true in relation to spiritual things. God never did directly that which he could do through others. He did that which others could not do, but that which we could do was left to 113 to accomplish. The preacher proceeded to ref ,r to stones which were hindrances and which we could help to remove. Let them take away the stone from the doer of the Church and from the human heart. One of these stones was the coldness and half-heartedness of the Christian Church. Alnny men could be brought under the influence of the Christian Church if only this lack of reality could be removed. Other stones which needed removing were the stones of unbelief, bad habits,

div.head: LOCAL PARIJAMENT
div.p: LOCAL PARIJAMENT
PILDERPIIA.N BRI?IETT INTRCDUCES A TAIIiFF REFeliil BILL.

The subject of Tariff Reform can have but few attractions tor the members of the Warrington Perlia- meutary Debating Society if we are to judge them by the attendance at the meeting on Tburscay evening in Cairo-street schoolroom. One would have thought that the well-lenown eloquence of Alderman Bennett, who was announced to rntroduce a Bill on the eubjeet,would have had almoit sufficient influence alone, but even that failed-to charm an audience of more than 95,t0 30. This fact, however, old not discourage the Alderman, for be spoke with great enthusiasm for nearly an hour on what he descrited as a " Bill to Federate the Empire and impose au Imperial Tariff for Defence." The Bill proved to km a long ene, consisting of seven clauses. It proposed to set up an Imperial Cabinet, an Imperial tariff for defence, a Parliament of the United Kingdcm, an Imperial ' House of Commons, an Imperial House of Lords, a Referendum and, finally, an Imperial Court of Appeal. The Alderman's tariff proposals are, perhaps, most interesting. He advocated mat a special ad va!orent tax of five per cent, over mud above existing duties be levied in all the ports of the United Kingdom upon all foreign goods with the exception of such food sui plier or raw materials as c,nnot advantageously be proauced within the limits of the Empire; that every British Colony or Poesessien be invited to impose a similar tax, and that the proceeds of such tax, wherever levied, be administered by the Imperial Cabinet for purpoe3 of Imperial Defence ; that any dissentient State shall be entitled to repre- sentation in the Imperial Cabinet, Imt shall not paiticir ate in the preference afforded by the special tax; that the tax tney be increased provide:o that eacn increase is eccempanied by a proportionate decrease in the entries at present levied by the assenting States as between each other; end that similar fiscal privileges may be accorced to any foreign State which is willing to reciprocate. Alderman BENNETT, who is the secretary for the Colonies in the society, at the outset alluded to the tact that this was a subject in which he had been very .keeely interested lor many years. ‘Thether they agreed with the proposals or differed irom them, he added, he did not think they would disagree with their tremendous

importance. He Itoesidered -this Us most important question in politics. hi own political lite wan largely uonrim,ted by the points included n the Bill. The question had nem ma urgent. He thetight the attempt of Canada to negotiate reciprocity treatment with the United States ought to be a warning. There should be a mutual preferential arrangement between Great Britain and her Calorries if we were to keep the Empire together. The Alderman spoke of the menace of the German Fleet, and expressed the opinion that Germany intended eventually to contest with us for our world supremacy. 'rho offer of Colouial battle ships showed the importance of puffin.b our. Impurial relations on a businesslike toting. The Iniperito. Defence Committee was not a satisfactory body—it was purely advisory. He did not 'wish to belittle its importance, but he thoukht that if our relatioes with Canada and the other Colohie3 were to be maintained they should have some definite voice in deciding matters. We ought to put this ct.ntritiution of ships.for defence on a regular and automatic basis. Alderman BENNETT proceeded to advance arguments in tavour of his proposed special ad vato:cia tax of five percent. and the Prime Minister (Mr White) drew from him the admiss.ion that he included food taxes as well as on raw materials and manufactured goods. He was not afraid of this bogey of taxation. There should be an Imperial fund for Imperial defence, and it would only be incidentally p:otective to foster trade between every section of the Empire. Every part of the Empire would have its automatic protection of five per cent. Mr. WATSON (SOC.): Do you include diamonds? Alderman BENNETT : Yes, I include everything. Cape diamonds would come in five per cent cheaper than coSisers. The alderman advocated free trade within the Empire—that, he said, was the desired and ultimate ideal. There should be a ring fence round the Empire. He agreed that free trade was ideal if not one-sided. If foreign nations would give us equal privileges, we were prepared to give equal privileges as to our Colonies. (Applause). 111 r F %V IsHERwooD, president of the Board of Agriculture, formally seconded ,the adoption of the Bill. _ _ _

Jr Tommie; (L., Lincoln), criticised at some length Alderman Bennett's Bill. He said he would support this policy if he thought it meant greater prosperity to us as a nation and greater happiness to our people. But he challenged Alderman Bennett to prove that we should be a happier and more prosperous Empire if the whole of the £3,500,000 capital that we posser sed all over the world had been kept within the Empire. The cotton trade supplied a specific example that would perhaps be sufficiently striking to satisfy de hoc. members opposite. In 1908-9, according to the statistical tables relating to British poesessions, the British Empire imported £34,6C0,000 of cotton manu- factures from the United Kingdom and £4,200,000 from foreign countries. We exported to foreign countries in the same year something like £70,000,000 worth of cotton goods. In the face of such facts who was the greater patriot in Lancashire, the man who supported tbe policy that had made his trade one of the wonders of the world or the man who would penalise two- thirds of it? India would become a very different problem if this Bill became law, because they bought from us about 90. per cent, of their imports of manu- factnres and they would have to levy a five per cent. tariff on the remaining 10 per cent. that they exported from foreign countries. (Applause). Mr JARMAN, leader of the Opposition, contended that by the time they had got officials and collected the taxes, they would have epent more than the propose& taxes would bring in. The 13i11 was hopelessly muddled, a mixture of five or six which ought to have been brought in sPparately. Mr P W DAVENPORT (President of the Board of Trade) supported the Bill, and remarked that so far as Imperialist ideas were concerned the Opposition were past redemption. Mr CHAMBERLAIN (S., Gorton) characterised the Bill as a further attempt to exploit the workingolasses. Mr PARKER (L., Dundee), who arrived late, moved the adjournment of the House, and the motion was .greed to.

div.head: ARE THE CLERGY UNNATURAL?
div.p: ARE THE CLERGY UNNATURAL?

The Rev W Greswell, vicar of Marthall, Chelford, in his parish magazine, speaks of the failure of many clergymen to get into touch with their parishioners. "If only," he says, "the clergy would be their natural selves, and not that divine edition of themselves, which they seem to think necessary, the more they would 'catch men.' In all the years I have been a parson, so far as I know, I have only converted one man in my life, and I converted him not by my arts as a parson, but by my artlessness as a human being. That ruffianly man who used to sit during my mission service with his hat on to show his contempt at last turned to be my veriest guardian angel. We parsons are more attractive when we are natural and do not pretend to gifts and qualifications which we don't porsess."

div.head: WPaRRINGTII'N SHOW.
div.p: WPaRRINGTII'N SHOW.
ANOTHER ADVERSE BALANCE.
EFFECTS OF THE CATTLE PLAGUE.

The cattle plague which necessitated the abandon- ment of several classes at the last ‘Varring tort Show, greatly affected the finances of the Agri- cultural Society. the annual meeting of which organi- sation was held on Wednesday afternoon in the Mbsonic Hall, Bold-street. The President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., presided over a good attendance. The TREASURER, 11Ir Alfred Broome, presented the annual statement of accounts. It showed that the loss OD the year's working was £205 lOs 9d, but a donation of £2OO from Sir Gilbert Greenall, together with £4B 12s 6d balance in band 1911, and subscriptions paid in advance for 1913-14 £2, brought the balance in hand at the present time to £45 Is 9d. The total receipts were , £565 lls 9d, without special donation of £2OO and the total payments £771 2s 6d. The statement of accounts Nkfts I hen adopted.

The SECRETARY preaeuted the following report The twenty-third annual show was held on Thursday, 22nd August, in Walton Lea Park. Owing to the loot and mouth disease it was decided not to hold the Snow on the usual Show ground in Walton Park, but to transfer it to the Lea and to elute the Walton Hall grounds to the public. For the same reason there were no classes for cattle or pigs. There was a slight falling off in the number of entries es compared with 1911 owing to tilt ra being no classes for cattle and pigs and the amount for entries suffered accordingly. The figures of the balance sheet generally are not so good as last year. Subscriptions are a good deal less, owittg to a lot of resignations, and very few new members have joined the society. The Society are greatly ind-bted to Mr Coxon fur a silver cup given in the Shire Classes. The attendance is only about half what it was in 1911 and the grand stand receipts are less accordingly. The decrease in the gate receipts is probably due to the Walton Hall grounds not being thrown open to the public. The rents of private atands and receipts for bicycle storages and cloak room are about the same. The amount of prizes is reduced by about £7O in the cattle and pig sectiors. The show yard general expenses are slightly more than last year, but the cost of printing and advertising is a few pounds less. Postages are also slightly less. The remaining items of expenditure are about as usual. The whole of the catering was again errried out by Messrs. Agar and Son, of Nlanchester, and gave every tratis- fection. Owing to the very poor attendance Messrs Agar were not charged for the privilege of catering. The society are once again indebted to Sir Gilbert Greenall for the use of the show ground, the cost of erecting the rings, grand stand, stalls for the exhibits and other show yard expeeses, special prizes for some of the sections and a special donation to meet the deficit on the year's working. Lady Greenall's flower show was again a very popular attraction and there was an excellent exhibition. The council wish to thank her ladyship for tie very great interest she has taken in this and every other department of the show. The whole of the prizes in the horticultural section were given by Lady Greenall. The society had the honour of having Mr F Stapleton-Bretherton as its vice- presidentpfor the year and he very kindly gave a special prize in the shire section. Mr Nenworthy, Mr Gould, Messrs H and It Ainscough and Mr Massey also very kindly gave special prizes in the shire classes. There was a great falling off in the number of entries in this section and the council ask for the help of all breeders of shires in the district to make this section the success it should be. The Cheshire Hunt Covert Fund gave a premium in the hunter brood mare class, Messrs Henry Milling and Co. a special prize for cheese, and Mesers Day and Sons a special prize in the shire horse section. The three London Breed Societies offered their medals es usual. Had thegate amounted to the usual number the Society would have had a better balance sheet than for many years past. The hearty thanks of the Council are due to the stewards for the elating and efficient manner in which they carried out their duties en the show day." On the proposition of Mr WEST the report was adopted.

div.head: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.
div.p: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.

Mr A LISTER KATE proposed the re-election of Sir Gilbert Greenish as president, and iNdr T Warburton having secouded the puoposition was enthusiastically carried. Sir GILBERT GREENALL in responding remarked that although they had had some bad fortune with their show they always managed to get through. He thought the show as a snow improved each yer. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry to see a falling off in some of the classes especially shires, hut he hoped there would be more interest in that class this year and that they wculd have the numbers they had bad previously. Lust year the fact that there were no cattle and pigs at the show, was responsible for a failing off of interest, and another drawback was they had to transfer the show from the usual ground to Walton Lea. He hoped that this year they would ba able to hold t`le show in the old place as it was a very good one. They wanted to make the show an attraction for all. If they had only fine weather and a bit of luck—and they had never had both—they would see great changes. (Applause,)

div.head: LEATHER TRADE IN WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.
div.p: LEATHER TRADE IN WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.

The short pericd of holiday dulness has been replaced by the utmost animation, and the small stocks 'which had accumulated during the previous couple of weeks were speedily spent, and producers were putting ferth every effort to get goods forward. The week-end, however, saw many orders remaining to be dealt with, and customers were clamou • for deliveries. Buyers were very ring numerous through the week, and, where there was any inducement for business, were acting freely ; confined as it was by the size of available stocks, sales were necessarily of moderate dimensions, but totalled up to large aggregates. Fair enquiry was met with for forward parcels, and, at anything near late rates, the production might easily have been sold for the next six months. As mentioned last week, Prices have undergone some revilion, and it was the exception to find a tanner willing to sell anything beyond an odd prompt parcel at December rates. For several lines, even for prompt delivery, advances were demanded, and in feime cases paid ; rough strap butts seem to have taken the biggest jump, and I am credibly informed that a large parcel was sold a few days ago at id. advance on the price paid at the middle of last month by the same buyer. Following these, the most rapid progress was made by rough bellies arid ‘eelting goods in the order named, and bends are firmer all round. Fr-m all the signs present in the chief centres of the world, I venture to affirm the con- viction that we are just at the beginning of a record appreciation in values of leather of all kinds, and it will be difficult to get even then. SOLE LEATHER.'- Bends have been active all round; English in particular have had a good run, and weights of about 12 lbs. were very speedily cleared. Continental bends of heavy average were much enquired after, but the quantity tendering was small; foreign of all kinds were in strong demand and in all types the supply was short of the market. Bellies were steadily good, the busiest class being heavies, for which the demand still grows : shoulders were speedily as brisk as ever, and for special welting lines a substantial advance was paid. Roceit LEATHER.—An extensive call was made upon strap butts, and heavy orders were offered, some of which it has been impossible to accept ; light weights have been in such request that in a recent instance they made :Jd. over heavier averages. Rough bellies were exceedingly brisk, and sold in the neighbour- hood of 11d., and, owing to the scarcity of light butts, there was a very strong enquiry for rough strap , ranges.—" The Leather World."

div.head: CANINE SOCIETY'S SHOW.
div.p: CANINE SOCIETY'S SHOW.

A marked improvement in the quality' of the exhibits was the outstanding feature of the Warring- ton and District Canine Society's ninth members' show which was held at the Drill Hall, on Tuesday evening. The entries drawn from a radius of twenty miles, numbered over eighty and in nearly every section there was a great advance on last year's show. The prize for the best dog in the show was awarded to that well-known exhibitor, Mr V V Davies with his fine retriever Birchdale Barker,which was first in its class. This animal was only third at the aceiety's last show in July. Mr Davies also secured the special award for the best bitch in the show with Birchdale Madge,and Mr F W Waring was s-cond. Mr. H Milling carried off the prize for the best puppy with Windmill Topsy, and Mr F W White was second. The retrievers were undoubtedly the finest class in the show. As already stated, Mr V V Davies's Biracial° Barker gained the premier position, while the same exhibitor's Birchdale Madge was again second. Dark Night, owned by Mr F W White, came up from very highly commended to third place, while Birchdale Shadow, who won premier honours at the last show and carried off the challenge cup for the best dog in the show, could only secure the reserve ticket. Mr J Haywood again carried off the first prize in the class for wire fox terriers with Sankey Joke, and Badger Night, owned by Mr F W White, was second. In the class for smooth fox terriers Mr F W Warding, with Wytham Mystery, came up from the third nlace at the last show to premier honours in this class. div.head: MINERS' V.C. PRAISES ZAM-BUK.
div.p: MINERS' V.C. PRAISES ZAM-BUK.
The King Honours a Hero Who Saved 15 Lives.
WONDERFUL HEALING OF WOTJNDS DT ZANI DUE AVERTS
BLOOD-POISON.

There is no prouder man than Mr John Mitchell, of 132, Lily-lane, Platt Bridge, Wigan, who was recently decorated by King George with the Edward Medal for heroism in a mine, whereby thirteen lives were saved To a reporter Mr Mitchell paid a splendid tribute to the way Zam-Buk had cleansed and healed his injuries and saved him from dreaded blood-poison.

"On December 23rd, 1911," said Mr. Mitchell, who Is a colliery under-looker, " I received an urgent call to the Bamfurlong /Co 1. Pit, which had been flooded. In my hurry to save my comrades I slipped between two planks and scraped and bruised my right thigh. "The tremendous rush of water loosened stones, dirt, bushes and bramble, which came tumbling all over us. One big stone cut my head clean open, whilst the brambles tore and scratched my hands, arms, and body, as we worked through them to get at the plug to allow the water to escape. " Finally, all the thirteen imprisoned men were got out safely, but it was midnight before I got away. As soon as 1 reached home I washed all my wounds and sores and dressed them with Zam-I3uk, which we always keep handy. I soon got relief from pain, and my injuries were cleansed and all fear of blood-poison dispelled. On the Monday I was able to return to work. I persevered with ZArn-Buk and solely as a result of using this grand balm I never lost an bones work, for my bands, arms, leg and head healed up splendidly with new skin. "I felt glad I had used nothing lilt the genuine Zam-Buk (as sold in sealed boxes by chemists), when I heard that one man who helped me in the fl.,oded pit was off work six weeks with blood-poison. "At home my wife has found Zam-Buk a real treasure. Our little boy Jimmie had his face covered with blisters, which burst into running sores. His cheeks and chin were masses of scabs, which also spread to his neck. A week's use of Zam-Buk, how- ever, cleared Jimmie's face and neck of the nasty outbreak, and he now has a hien new skin. We have every reason to think well of Zam-Buk."

There is no first team match to-day and the "A " team will fill the bill at home with a Combination 'match, Leigh Shamrocks being the visitors. The Leigh "Irishmen" are a good side this season,and after their defeat of Rylands Recs there will be some .curiosity to- see them opposed _to the " A " team, especially as they beat the "A " team at Leigh by five points to nil.
Mclntye, full back; Clare, Dickenson, Joidan' and Davies, threhquarters ; Brown and Douglas, half- back"; Naylor, Harrison, Critchley, Bevan, Arnold and Gibbs forwards.

What is to be our Cup team ? The present thirteen? An answer m the affirmative seems the only one possible. All Cup-tie players have to be registered by February Ist, so that there is little time left for the Wirepullers to remedy the obvious deficiencies on the attack. The threequarter line is still leaden- footed, and the feebleness of the combination seems to be merely emphasised by the excellence of the forwards. The latter will, no doubt, play a big part in any cup contest, but they cannot be relied upon entirely for victory. Times are " hard "so we shall probably have to be content with the available players and hope for the best.
The League table up-to-date is as follows : For. _Aga._ Per-

The Warrington club officials are a patient and long suffering set of individuals. They have a just cause for a grumble at the capricious tricks played by the weather clerk. The loes of a big gate in the Wakefield match was keenly felt but another rebuff of fortune was experienced last Saturday when the usually popular fixture with St Helens was spoiled by the blizzard.

Snow and sleet fell continuously and a strong wind swept the stinging particles down the field, which was soon ploughed into a morass. The loss to the club will be nearly £ICO and bad the fixture been post- poned I don't think the club would have been any worse off. The wonder is that VVarrinoon possesses so many brave supporters who were willing to forsake a cornfortable fireside for the questionable pleasure of witnessing 26 players disport themselves in the mud.

The only satisfaction Warrington obtained was the fact that they retired victorious by the bare margin of one point. This result rather flatters the Saints and does not represent our own merits. Warrington were much the better side all round and adapted them- selves to the conditions with real-skill. A score of a dozen points to nil would not have over-estimated the Wirepullers' superiority. There were many lucky clearances by the St Helens backs and it was mar- vellous how the home forwards missed scoring. At least three certain tries were negatived by simple errors. Fearnley was the chief offender, and be will have to devote his attention to a study of the off-side iule. There were other causes which account for the lowness of the Warrington score. St Helens were prone to play the part of obstructionists whenever there was a possibility of a score from Warrington. We have in mind a glaring case when Tranter was going through with the ball at his toes. The penalty brought a goal from Thomas, but it is more than likely that a try would have accrued. Then again,the referee gave' some very curious and inconsistent decisions.

It was a decided advantage to the home team to play with the gale at their backs for tbe first forty minutes. The St. Helens line was, during this period, subjected to a severe bombardment. The bon:testers were assisted by the injudicious methods of the St. Helens backs, who persisted in trying to open out the game with passing movements. The policy was a bad one, for oftener than not, the ball never reached the wing man. Their kicking also lacked judgment and the frequent " ballooning " of the ball only put their defence in a worse tangle. It was from such a mistaken means of defending that Renwick opened our account with a dropped goal. On another occasion the ball was sent over the line and Renwick followed in hot pursuit, but the wind carried the leather against the railings. The Saints came very near scoring in the first half after Belshaw had removed hostilities to the Warrington end. The ball was taken over the line by the forwards but Renwick and Williams dropped on it in the nick of time.
The home forwards did _ not fully assert their

superiority until the second half when facing the elements. Previously the Saints had been gaining possession from the scrummage, but they bad evidently spent themselves in their efforts. Whenever danger threatened the Warrington line the forwards generally vune away with the ball at their toes, and neither Flanagan nor Belehaw relished the idea of checking the strong forward movements. George Thomas was irresistible, and I don't think he has ever played a better game. There was no mistake about the tackling whenever a St. Helens man had the misfor- tune to get into their clutches. The only time the defence wavqred was in the closing minutes of the game, when Renwick and Jolley were at sea in dealing with a St. Helens forward advance. Wilcox had nothing to do but drop on the ball over the line for a try. There was no time for St. Helens to to ake another .spurt, for the whistle sounded for time immediately after Barton had adaed the goal.

St Helens were outpointed both fore and aft and but for our lack of finish they would have been very badly beaten indeed. Whatever advantage the Saints held with regard to the speediness of their backs was negatived by the safe tackling and fielding of the home men. Their supporters are patiently awaiting Williams to reproduce some of his old Halifax form. lie has not yet obliged with any thrills but the condi- tions have not provided him with many opportunities of showing his Breed. One is pleased to note that Jolley has returned to the form which characterised his play at the end of last season. He was in great form on Saturday, some of his clearances bringing down the "house."

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE).

The general meeting at headquarters xas attended by a fair muster of members. The paying over of all the yearly awards was much appreciated, and the remarks in general were that so much prize money was seldom paid over in one season at any club house. Mr T Singleton came in for the lion's share and, strange to say, he won all his prizes from the Norton water. He quite put the competitors in the shade, even Mr C Ashton, who travelled as far as Yarmouth. The balance ,was more than antis actory, and the election of officers ck as gone through in quick style. The dates of the matches were selected, and they are as near as last year's as possible :—Opening match' July 27th; officials' match, August 17th ; annual match, September 14th. There is to be a rambling match this season, the date to be selected at the next general meeting, After all business bad been transacted, the members indulged in a sing-song that brought a pleasant evening to a close. The following are the officers for 1913 :—President Mr H Mather,; chairman, Mr J Osborne; vice- presidents, Messrs It Archer, W Bailey, A Bradley, W Brooks, B Bradbury, D Cooper, J Cox, J Haslem, G Eiamblett, E Hill, J Howard, lc Jolley, T Roberts, T Singleton, W Smith, 3 Sanson, J Sudlow, I F Smith, E Wales; treasurer, Mr E Brooks secretary, Mr A Stout; assistant secretary, Mr W Taylor; committee, Messrs J Bryere, W Ellison, W Bailey, P Fallon, W Henshall, T Dixon, H Moores, J Warburton W Walker. The Secretary's report was as follows :—I have great pleasure in announcing that the Northern Anglers of Warrington are in a better poaition this year than they have been for several years, and after hearing the reports of different societies up and down the country, I think we may congratulate ourselves on having had a successful season. We have done three great things this last season. First we have increased in members and this alone is something to be thankful for, con- sidering the decrease other societies have had to con- tend with. Secondly we have taken an additional water, namely the river Gowey. This again places members in a better position for specie hunting, and thirdly we are better in finance than we have been for several years. Although personally Ido not believe in making a savings bank of an Angling society, if a society has a substantial balance in hand, that I con- tend is all that is required, and by giving members the full benefit of the society's funds you will always have a fair amount to carry on until the following season ,as the members themselves are the clubs advertisement and are only too willing to introduce new 101 l iod. Take this last season for instance. We commenced the year with about 81 members and less than £2 in hand Now we can • turn to our books and count over 100 members and doable the balance we had, in spite of the fact that we have spent almost £8 more in prizes this year than the previous year. That goes to prove that the secret of our success is to give the full limit to all members. I here take the opportunity of thank- ing our patrons along with those members of the society who have given prizes. This item must have placed our society amongst the first fighters as regard prizes given in matches and specimen weighing, and I sin sure we are all extremely grateful to them for their kindness. We are about to lose one of our most energetic worters. I mean Mr Jack Potter, who is leaving us temporarily to fight fresh battles in another field. You will not lose him altogether, as he is still going to be a Northern Angler and wilt still be your representative at the Executive Council meet- ings of the Northern Anglers. This step has not been taken without a fair consideration, your assistant secretary and I think it will' be for the furthering of Northern Anglers in Warrington We are now about to open our centre in wider circles by affiliation of other Societies. That alone goes to show that we are making an impression in the town and if members will only expound their views to other anglers, I am sure we will still continue our march of progress and make the Northern analers a houtehold word in Warrington.

div.head: Warrington's single Point Win. Match In a Snowstorm at Wilderspool.
div.p: Warrington's single Point Win. Match In a Snowstorm at Wilderspool.

More wretched conditions for football than those which prevailed on Saturday could hardly have been imagined and there would certainly have been every justification for pestponing the match between Warrington and St Helens at Wilderspool. A blinding snowstorm raged throughout the afternoon and the players experienced a thorough gruelling. The loss on the gate was,of course, very considerable,the spectators numbering not more than 1,000. The Warrington team was at full strength:. Owing to injuries to Heaton and Browning, it was necessary for the Saints to make a couple of changes in their side, and Jim Webb, the Welsh international, and Fred Trenwith were intro- duced. MrEdmundson, of Bradford was tbe referee, and he had the following under his charge : St. Helens.—Molyneux ; Barton. Flanagan, Belshaw, H Kelly ; Trenwith, Richardson ; Parr, Webb, Wilcock, Waddell, Manchester, Prescott. Warrington.—Jolley ; Davies, Tranter, Renwick, Williams; Nicholas, Dainteth ; G Thomas, Cheaters, Skelhorne, Fearnley, R Thomas, Cox. Warrington won the toss and the visitors had to face the snowstorm. Prescott started for St. Helens. and a neat passing movement by the visitors' backs, resulted in Barton putting in a short kick. The wind blew the ball back in the direction of the St. Helens line. From succeeding play Renwick picked up in the loose and dropped a clever goal for Warrington. On resuming, the home forwards made a determined raid on the St Helens line, but - Flanagan raced across and saved the situation. Jolley was obstructed, and from the penalty Itt-nwick failed in front of the posts. St Helens put forth desperate efforts and Kelly was tackled by Williams near the half-way line. Although Sr. Helens were often in possession, their method of lofty kicking gave them no advantage. Maintaining the pressure, Nicholas served Tremor and the three- quarter was making good progress until he was badly hampered by Kelly, and the subsequent penalty was well taken by George Thomas, Warrington now being four points ahead. Daintith next got away. Williams failed to field thoroughly sad Kelly was enabled to get, up and Ea% e. The St Helens forwards, led by Man- chester, Waddell sad Wilcocks, reached the home quarters and Flanagan raced through, hut Tranter was safe in his tackling, and Warrington easily beat off the invaders. After Barton had tried to get his side out of a difficult position, he kicked wildly across the goal mouth, and Cox, marking PI a good position, George Thomas had little diffi- culty in placing Warrington further ahead. Another case of obstruction was followed by a penalty but this time Thomas was a few inches outside in his shot for goal. Jolley on one occasion tried to go through, but he was tacklea. Renwick was also held up a yard short of the line. St Helens were kept busily defending, and Belshaw on one occasion saved daringly from Tranter when the ball travelled over the line near tha posts. Flanagan brought relief with a strong run and kick, but Davies fell back anr saved the situation. Belshaw found touch near the Warrington line. Later Prescott got over, but the try was disallowed. Half- time, Warrington 6 points, Sr. Helens, nil. On resuming, the first dangerous move came from the home forwards, Skelhorne and It Thomas taking the ball to within a few yards of the line. Passing by the visitors' backs saw Tranter floor Flanagan when the latter was endeavouring to make an opening for Barton. The home forwards wheeled the scrimmage near mid-field and bore down on the Saints' line, Molyneanx making a clearance with a flying kick. Warrington were now pressing and Oaiutith, when trying to force his way through, fell a victim 41 Molyneux. A dead ball brought relief to the Saints. Tranter intercepted a passing movement by the Saints backs, and dribbled the ball past Molsneux. The St. Helens line was in danger until Barton dashed across and saved the situation. Hostilities were removed to the Warrington end, and eventually Flanagan got over. As the ball bad struck the referee when one of the half-backs was clearing, the try was disallowed. G Thomas brought relief to Warrington with a fine dribble which removed play to mid-fleld. Cox supplemented this with a fine run, but he was overhauled by Barton near the posts. St. Helens then had a splendid opportunity of tooriug, but Trenwith and Richardson bungled badly Barton secured and kicked away, but Daintith sent the ball out of plav:Just before the close the ball was taken over the Warrington line, and Wilcock dropped on it for a try. Barton took the I kick, and landed a fine goal from the touch line. Final: Warrinuton, 3 goals, G points; St Helens, 1 goal, I try, 5 points.

Almost immediately afterwards the Widnes full hack misfielded the ball, and Carmichael following up scored, and also added the goal, placing his side two points in front at half-time. HOCKEY.
LATCHFORD.

The first eleven renewed fixtures with South Man- chester, who were led by that excellent sportsman, F R Leroy, at centre-forward, and after being in arrears a long time brought off a sensational victory by 4-3 a few minutes off time after a gruelling but very interesting game under bad weather conditions. Leroy scored twice for the South early on, his second goal being the result of a magnificent shot such as could only come from a class player. Roberts improved the lead and then Pearson scored for Latchford and Wilkin- son reduced the lead. Following good forward play, Pearson equalized and immediately afterwards scored the winning goal. Pearson played finely. For South Manchester Leroy led his line like a true leader, and Smith and Watts at centre half and rieht hack played soundly. For Latchfor, Fletcher and Billington were a good pair of backs and Knight played a clever game against Pitt and Howard who are the South's stroegest wing. Minards did a lot of good work in the centre, and Dale and Pearson were a strong right wing. The Second Eleven were opposed to Stockport 'A " who leave not lost a match this season yet, end Were defeated 3-0. Latchford only had eight players on arrival at Heaton Moor, the three others hsving unfor- tunately surmised thet the match would be off on account of the snow. Two strbstitufes wire found but they were of no calibre, and all thing 3 considered the depleted visitors did quite well to lose by only threa goals Dixon for Latchford at left back was the best play er on the field, and hit the ball away from awkward siteations terrsatedly. Tee red of the team worked bad. but of course laboured under a great disadvantage. div.head: HEALTH CHARTER.
div.p: HEALTH CHARTER.
BENEFITS OF THE INSURANCE ACT NOW IN OPERATION.
The benefits of t'.:.e Insurance Act have commenced to flow.

Sickness and maternity benefit came into operation on Monday, medical and unemployment (in specified trades), benefits commenced on Wednesday, "while sanatorium benefit has been working lor long, with the result that much good hus been accomplished already. • Disablement benefit, the last, but very far from the least, does not begin to operate until a person has been insured for 104 weeks, and paid 101 contribu- tions.

Spec;al interest was shown on Monday in births in all psris of the country owing to the fact that babies born after midnight ou Sm,day entitled their parents, if insured persons, to maternity benefit under the Act. •

In an interview with a representative of "The Daily Chronicle" Mr Lloyd George spoke in warm terms of the welcome which had been extended to the Act, as shown by the "shoals of telegrams" he had receiqtd. In 13ptte of the abuse that has been levelled at him by some over-zealous doctors who hate the Act, Mr Lloyd George spoke with warm appreciation of the mea i cal profession. honestly believe," lie said, "that its effect on the profession wll be entirely beneficent. In regard to remuneration alone, the aggres2ate earnings of the profession will be enormously increased. Estimates that have been made for um show that under our capitation fee medical men practising in industrial areas wiil have their incomes increased from 75 to 100 per cent. "At the same time the evils of the old contract medical serviee will disappear. and insured persons will be guaranteed efficient and sympathetic attention during illness. "To the working 01as5e3 the Insurance Act will, I am persuaded, come as an inestimable Noon. Men who tarn small wages have a horror of ill-health because it impairs their earning power, and they dare not call in a doctor for fear of running up a bill. "The relief brought by the Act to a man in this condition of life cannot be easily measured. If he is ill now he can count confidently upon lOs a week from the State Insurance Fund, and he can call in any doctor on the panel without misgiving, and with the full assurance that he has at his disposal the sell ices of a man skilled in the art of healing. No longer will be be under the necessity when ill of crawling to his work in tho morning, and creeping back home, weary and exhausted at night." Mr. Lloyd George spoke enthusiastically of the cordial reception which the Act had received from the masses of the working people. As to the employers, he said, "I cannot speak too highly of the way in which employers throughout the kingdom have behaved. Compulsory contribution was not liked at the outset, but the employers have rapidly adapted themselves to it." "They now realise that the Act will improve the health of working men and that a healthy worker is a more efficient unit of production. Many British employers have always shown great regard for the moral and physical welfare of those in their employ. I am bound to say in connection with this Act that employers in all trades throughout the country have given us their wholehearted support. In SQ doing I think they have acted upon the best traditions of British industry." MEDICAL BENEFIT FOR ALL.

The Insurance Commissioners have received a number of enquiries as to the conditions under which insured persons who are members of approved sccieties become entitled to medical benefit under the /s.ational Insurance Act. They accordingly desire to make it known that all insured persons who are naembers of approved societies (with the exception of certain special classes such as soldiers and sailor snow serving) are now entitled to medical benefit under the Act, no matter when they entered insurance or whether they have since been out of employment. The provision of medical attendanee and treatment for those members who were over 65 veers of age on 15th July, 1912, and who are not entitled to medical benefit at the expense of the State Insurance funds can be arranged privately, as before, by the:r Societies.

div.head: FIRST DAY OF PANELS.
div.p: FIRST DAY OF PANELS.
Smooth Working Assured.

Wednesday was the first day of the medical benefit under the National Insurance Act, and the dsy'a happenings completely disproved the assertion—often repeated by the opponents of the Act that the medical service must break down.

Panel doctors throughout the country were busy signing the red medical tickets by which they under- take to give the necessary medical relief to the insured persohs applying to them. Many insured persons, however, do not understand that they should not wait until they are ill to take the medical ticket to the ioctor, but should select a doctor without delay and take their ticket to him at once for him to endorse.

Already many approved societies have received applications for sickness and maternity benefit, but in many instances the contributor has himself caused delay through not sending with his application the necessary documents for the claim to be admitted. Where there is no local agent to act as an inter- mediary between the insured person and his society the latter should send the following documents direct to the secretary of his society at the registered office: 1. Medical certificate of the doctor on the panel chosen by the member. 2. Claim form correctly filled in for the particular benefit desired. 3. Insurance book and current stamped card. It should also be observed that these should not be sent until the fourth day of illness.

Even if only one contribution has been paid the insured person in an approved society is entitled to medical benefit as from Wednesday, with the excep- tion of persons over 65 years of age on July 15 last, soldiers, sailors, marines of the Royal Navy and married women not being voluntary contributors, who are suspended from benefit.

div.head: MR. P. M. OLIVER'S APPEAL TO DOCTORS,
div.p: MR. P. M. OLIVER'S APPEAL TO DOCTORS,

Speaking at Woodford on Wednesday night, Mr P M Oliver, the prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, said that there was a special appeal he would like to /mike to the doctors of Lancashire and Cheshire. They were giving the Act a trial for• three months, and those three months, January, February, and March, were months when sickness was rife. The calls on the doctor would be many, and the profits small. But the three following months showed on an average much less sickness, when calls on doctors would be few and the profits large. • He appealed to the doctors to give the Act a trial for six months instead of three, to take the good with the bad. If they would give the Act a trial he felt convinced that they would give it a trial for ever:

div.head: THANKS.
div.p: THANKS.

The hearty thanks of the Board was accorded to Mr W C Brooks for his kindness in arranging an entertain- ment for the inmates on the Bth inst. "INDUSTRIAL UNREST AND ABNORMAL SICKNESS." The Finance Committee considered a written state- ment from the Newton Relief Committee, as an explanation of the substantial increase in the out-relief granted in that district, and Mr Billinge, chairman of the Relief Committee, gave a verbal statement as to the various causes which he considered had materially tended to the increase, the chief of which he ascribed to industrial unrest and abnormal sickness. It was recommended that consideration of the matter stand adjourned until the nod of the current quarter and that at that period the situation be again reviewed.

div.head: NEW BEATING SYSTEM.
div.p: NEW BEATING SYSTEM.

The seal of the Board was affixed to a mortgage in favour of the trustees of the Rational Association Friendly Society for the sum of £2,902, being the amount of the loan advanced by that association to defray the expenses of the installation of a decen- tralized system of heating and a new hot water service at the Workhouse.

div.head: CONFERENCE DELEGATES,
div.p: CONFERENCE DELEGATES,

The CHAIRMAN (Jr E L Bent), vice-chairman (Mr A J Jolley), and the Clerk, were appointed to represent the Board at the meeting of the Central Poor Law Conference to be held in London. Miss BROADBENT advanced the suggestion that Mrs Simpson should be one of the delegates but the Board decided to adhere to the usual procedure—to send the chairman and vice-chairman to the conference. APPOINTMENT OF LABOUR MASTER AND MATRON'S ASSISTANT.

In response to advertisements of these positions, 8 applications had been received for the post of labour master and 21 for that of seamstress and matron's assistant. In addition there were 32 applications for the joint appointment of labour master and seamstress and matron's assistant. Candidates applied from all parts of the country. The Board interviewed three selected candidates for tbe position of labour master and five for that of seam- stress and matron's assistant. The respective appoint- roepts were conferred noon Mr 11 Ridgway, labour master of the Clitheroe Union Worknouse, and Mrs A Williams, matron's assistant at the Bridlington Union Workhouse.

div.head: COUNTY EX PMSES.
div.p: COUNTY EX PMSES.

The CLERK reported that he had received the County cleim. It amount( dto £10;,73 7s 7d, as compared with 11.,52.0 is 10d for the corresponding period last year. The CHAIRMAN : I don't know what it will be directly. Mr MATHER : It is scarcely re :tug., as I expected, after reading the reports of the oiscussion at the Pieston meeting.

PAUPERS OVER SEVENTY YEARS OF AGE. The CLERK submitted a return (prepared at the request of the Local Government Board of paupers over seventy years of age (including casual paupers but excluding lunatics in county end borough asylums, registered hospitals and licensed houses), in receipt of relief on January 4th, 1913. The particulars were In the Workhouse or other establishments provided by the Poor Law authorities; 51 men and 18 women, of *hom 10 were old age pensioners in receipt of non- disqualifying relief ; in receipt of outdoor relief,s men and 4 women, of whom 5 were old age pensioners in receipt of non-disqualifying relief. The total number included in the return was, therefore 78, of whom 15 were pensioners in receipt of non-disqualifying relief.

In Mr Bonar Law's THE SURRENDER. reply to the Memorial that was presented to him the other day there is absolutely nothing that was unanticipated. The reply is a surrender, and a surrender without grace. The Conservative leader in the House of Corn mons says that he has discussed the Memorial with Lord Lansdowne, and discloses no more of its character than was already public property. It asks, he says, , that they shall retain the leadership of the party whilst altering in one important particular the method by which Imperial Preference is to be carried out. "It would have been more agreeable to our- selves," he adds, "and in our view more for the interest of\ the party that the change of method should be accompanied by a change of leaders." This seems to.us to be unnecessarily caustic. But it may be Mr Bonar Law's way of ex- pressing modest depreciation of himself. The conclusion is just what it was certain to be. The Memorial is , "such an expression of opinion from such a quarter that it is our duty to comply with the request which has been addressed to us, and this we are prepared to do." In other words, here we are, and here we
remain."

In what position does a reply like this leave the country which has to judge between one party and another? It leaves it in a position almost absolute uncertainty as to the Tory position. Food taxes are not to be pressed at the next General Election. They are to be left over as a remainder. But the Unionist party is still to be Protectionist. If it wins an election by temporarily dropping the Food Tax proposals it will feel at liberty to bring for ward the other features of the policy which it absurdly describes as Tariff "Reform." Without going into the exposure of such a position as this—and, really, further exposure seems unnecessary—may we ask what is the guarantee that, if the Tory party is victorious at a General Election, it will not include Food Taxes in any attempt that it may make to change the fiscal policy of the nation? The pledge now given, it may be replied. But in the light of experience such a pledge, even if it were definite and wholly incapable of being explained away (as it is not), would not be worth the paper that it is written on. The elector who makes notes on political events will say, "Once bit, twice shy." Nothing whatever was to be settled by the " Ending-of-the-War " election except the actual wiping up of the South African mess. It gave us, nevertheless several years rpnetionary Iprriclafinn Tf. Balfour's Education Act. It. gave us an Act which made the liquor trade one of the en- dowed and entrenched interests. Surely that experience must have driven deeply into the public mind the sound idea that the Tory party cannot safely be entrusted with a blank cheque.

It is interesting, in connection with this subject, to find Mr Maurice Hewlett com- plaining that Liberal newspapers devote so much of their space to the struggles of the Opposition to find a policy with which to meet the country. It is interesting, because Mr Maurice Hewlett is an interesting man. His views, however, seem to us, to use his own words, to be jejune. Concerning what he has been told is the indifference of the country to current questions, he says: "It would be truer to say that the country has found out that in themselves they have no interest for politicians who obedient to their caucauses, use them as sticks to Lest each other withal. The country knows quite well that they have been put forward, one and All of them, in the interests of party, and having no obvious remedy it leaves party and them alone."

This, if Mr Maurice Hewlett will permit us to say so, is not merely jejune, it is absolutely raw. The country is not indifferent to current questions. It has made up its mind about them, and for Liberal newspapers to refrain from pointing ont the confusions in -which the Conservative party has involved itself, in an attempt to regain possession of power by smashing up that system of free exchange which has given us our com- mercial and industrial supremacy, would b e to turn away from a great duty and to betray a great trust.

There has never been a HOME RULE Parliament like the THROUGH. present one for legis- -1 a tive achievement. Simultaneously with the National Insurance benefits coming into force, the third Home Rule Bill passed through the House of Commons. The majority for the third read- ing was the magnificent one of 110. No wonder Mr. Bonar Law said You have twice tried to pass the .Bill. You now try a third time—and it will be the last ! Mr. Law told the truth—and got a bigger .cheer from the Government than from his friends. The Commons has finished with that great struggle for the freedom of the Irish people which began in 1874. and has been continued through three bitterly-fought Bills to its present triumph. Barring acci- dents, the Bill will become law in May,1914, when even the veto of the Lords will be inoperative. Four generations of Mr. Redmond's family have been engaged con- secutively and continuously in the Party struggle for Ireland's freedom, and in a message to a London paper yesterday the veteran Irish leader said: The passage of the Bill into law is assured; and the effect of its operation in Ireland will be, not only to inaugurate a new era of peace and prosperity, but to weld together Irishmen of every class and of every creed in an indissoluble bond of brotherhood and of affection for the promotion of the welfare and the happiness of their Motherland.

Lord Haldane's - fore- EDUCATION AND shadowing of a great NATIONAL scheme of Educational WELL-BEING. Reform has been wel- comed by all who recognise that the schoolmaster, to use a generic term which covers everything from the most distinguished University Professor to the humblest teacher in an elementary school or a kindergarten, is one of the most efficacious instruments for turning out a nation well-equipped for the attainment alike of material and moral excellence. Money spent on education, if it is the right kind of education, will be bread cast upon the waters, to return with tenfold increase after not so many days. The Government plan is not confined to the now old-fashioned, though once so novel, ideal of an educational ladder. It aims at making the best of those who will not be able to do more than put foot on the lowest rung.

One of the most striking THE CHANCELLOR'S tributes to the courage COURAGE. and tenacity of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in carrying through the great health charter, comes from a Conservative quarter. In an article which administers a crushing rebuke to those who sought to make party capital by misrepresentation of the measure, the "Pall Mall Gazette," one of the leading London Cons ervative organs says :--- The history of the Insurance Act is full Of political lessons. Nothing is shown more clearly than the value of a pertinacious and determined pressure in the face of prejudice and wanton agitation. When the "Daily Mail" and the " Times " were making their strident appeal to the ignorance and susceptibility of the servants' ball, a weaker man than Mr Lloyd George might have been shaken by the commotion. But the Chancellor of the Exchequer stuck to his plan, undeterred by intelligent and artificial clamour ; the fire of straw quickly burnt itself out, and to-day the very catch-words of the Albert Hall crowd are forgotten. It is scarcely necessary to point in what directions the moral applies. But it is plain enough that the troubles which courage has to face are nothing to those that encumber the retreating footsteps of timidity,

Sir Joseph Lawrence, "RIDICULOUSLY one of the most versa- Low." tile of our Tariff Reformers, has already shown how impossible it will be to remain content with any kind of tariff. Whatever may be the outcome of the present confusion, Whether food-taxes be dropped or not, the Tariff Reform party will continue to agitate for duties on manufactured imports. It was about such imports that Sir Joseph Lawrence sPoke at Mitcham on Dec. 4th. "Mr Chamberlain's idea," he said, "was an average du,y of 10 per cent. ad valorem on manufactures. But 10 per cent. was ridiculously low as compared with the duties charged by some of the biggest foreign countries to which we traded, and we should be justified in dividing our all-round 10 per cent. scale into three categories, as in most of the latest tariffs in other countries, including some of our Dominions, viz: (1) Maximum tariff, 15 per cent. ad valorem duty; (2) intermediate tariff, 10 per cent. ad valorem duty; (3) minimum tariff, 5 per cent, ad valorem duty. He would assign to these three separate scales of duties, commencing with the minimum tariff of 5 per cent., to be charged only to our Colonies who granted us reduced duties; the intermediate tariff to those countries with moderate tariffs not exceeding 50 per cent. average duties, and the maximum tariff to those charglng us duties above 50 per cent. average. such proposals need not be considered seriously. What they are useful for is to ' show that in the opinion of such Protection- ists as Sir Joseph Lawrence ten per cent. is ridiculously low." Already he asks for 15 on goods from certain countries. Not many bioQerlii „ tit-10110 Fttuum utes were previously aiwobb uusuowu I lay, I le. I SUB,

weeks ago the leader of the South African Protectionists spoke of 25 per cent. duties as "moderate." There never was a tariff that was not "ridiculously low " to somebody or other. That is because Protection never does really protect. It sends up prices ; and the man who has to pay increased prices for what he buys naturally finds the profits on what he sells lower than before. Thereupon he clamours for more Protection. Presently, others do the same, and so the game goes on. A tariff is never satisfactory all round.

It is a great thing to A NEW ERA FOR give the worker access THE SMALLHOLDER. to the land, which an unfortunate twist in our economic development had denied him altogether until the Liberal regime, which started in 1906, began, step by step, to retrace a fatal mistake. But something more than mere access to the land only is required. He must be enabled to make the best of the land when he has got there. For this, co-operation and credit are imperative. Mr. Runciman's arrangement with the joint- stock banks to give credit to co-operative societies on the best possible terms is a reform, though quietly carried out by administrative process, which may be looked back upon in the future as the opening of a brighter era for the rural districts of this country.

The Insurance Act must mean immortality for the Liberal Party. It is the Epiphany star of social reform.—Sir George Scott Robertson, K.C.5.1., the distinguished soldier.

* - Mr Lloyd George has consented to receive a deputation of working women on the ques- tion of suffrage. rhe deputation will include women from all parts of the country, and the meeting is fixed for Monday next at noon.

* - A London correspondent says that so superstitious are they in London that one half the streets have no number 13. On the other hand this superstition has so little influence upon Lloyd George that he commences his Insurance scheme on the 13th day of the 13th year of the 20th century.

"His Majesty's Government have no intention whatever of adopting the system of compulsory service for fighting units. Far from abandoning the voluntary pripciple, they intend to foster, encourage, and extend it by every means in their power. This, then, is final so far as we are concerned, and I go further and say that no alternative Govern- ment that could be formed would come to a different conclusion at the present time."— Colonel Seely.

A correspondent sends a timely suggestion re Victoria Park on behalf of the numerous devotees of model-yachting in Warrington The park is sadly in need of development,and it is to be hoped that the Council will see their way to provide an artificial lake, with accommodation for boating, bathing, and model yachting. Now that additional access to the park has been provided, the demand for further outdoor attractions cannot fairly be ignored. *

The Chairman at the annual dinner of the Norwich Licensed Victuallers recently declared that "Tariff Reform was as dead as Balaam's ass." There was "always enough money to make it stand.on its wooden legs "; but" such an everyday thing as the food he eats and the clothes he wears" was too near the elector's daily experience to hoodwink him upon. There is something almost prophetic about this speech, for it was made before Mr. Bonar Law went down to Ashton- under-Lyne. •* * _ _ _ _

"There is no country in the world which has made such rapid strides as Great Britain in the reduction of its pauper and death rates in the prevention of disease, and in the care of the poor. . . . We are determined that in the next quarter of a century, consumption shall be as little known as are now smallpox and typhus. We want to do away with workhouses and infirmaries, and hospitals, and when, at the next election, Tariff Reform becomes the first plank in the Tory platform, let us see that the food-taxers walk it."— John Burns. *

It may not be generally known that Ruskin's father and mother rest in the Surrey churchyard close to Croydon where as a boy 'much of John Ruskin's holiday time was spent. A contributor to this month's Young Woman" supplies the wording on the memorial: Here rests, from day's well-sustained burden, John James Ruskin. Born in Edinburgh, May 10, 1785, he died in his home in London, March 8, 1864. He was an entirely honest merchant, and his memory is, to all who keep it,. dear and helpful. His son, whom he bved to the utter- most,'land taught to speak truth, says this of him. Upon the east side, on the marble, are the words : " Here, beside my father's body, I have laid my mother's : nor was dearer earth returned to earth nor purer life recorded in heaven. She died December 5, 1871, aged 90 years." * o

By the death of Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith, the well-known Liverpool barrister, who passed away at Colwyn Bay on Wednesday, the Northern Circuit loss one of its most promi- nent members. The deceased gentleman was a sound lawyer, and his special knowledge of commercial law caused his services to be in great request in this class of case. He had much county court practice, and figured frequently in the Court of Passage as well as in Crown and civil cases at the Assizes. His knowledge of the law affecting workmen's compensation cases was very complete, and on points arising in actions of this kind he was a formidable opponent. The late Judge Bowen Rowlands, during his last illness, deputed Mr. Cuthbert Smith to qdjudicate in his stead at the Warrington County Court, and in this capacity Mr. Cuthbert Smith, dealing with the numerous compensation cases which come before that court,evidenced his grasp of the law affecting employers' , liability, * * *

Nothing comes amiss to the wide-awake antiquarian. Our contributor A.M. begins in this issue to show us the historical interest of our children's games and nursery rhymes. It is one of the last quarters to which we should have looked to find history and the news about Sally Waters will come as a pleasant shock to most people. Two other articles are promised ; one on "The House that Jack built " and another on the sad fate of" Cock Robin." But we hope our contributor may be induced to .carry us still further into their delightful realm. After what we have read we shall want to know the identity of Jack and Jill, of Little Jack Horner, and the Man in the Moon, to say nothing of Mother Hubbard and the Old Woman .who lived in a Shoe. We have already began to suspect that they came over with the Danes or were among the Knights of the Round Table.
