Every insured person should at once take his or her medical benefit card to a doctor on the panel, for endorsement. Should they delay this step until they are actually doctors may justifiably decline to accept them as patients under the Act. *

It appears that the type-written epistles, to which reference was made in our last issue, were not the full extent of the anony- mous correspondence which caused so much feeling at the last meeting of the Town Council. Several letters of a more personal tone and in ordinary handwriting, were also received by several members of the Council. A letter was also sent to the wife of a prominent Alderman, warning her not to allow her husband to attend the Council meeting in view of the exciting scenes which were anticipated. * . *

Where are the enemies of the Insurance Act? A few months ago their name was legion and their tongues were busy with "half-truths " and full-blown terminological inexactitudes about the Act. To-day it is being hailed on almost every hand as the greatest social welfare legislative enactment of the British Parliament. There are still grumblers to be found who talk of" a tax on industry," but they have been silenced to all intents and purposes by the very real and substantial benefits which have come into force this week. There are thirteen million people who have cause to bless National Insurance. Their's is the voite to listen to ! * •

The greatest furore has I?een caused by the maternity benefits, largely, of course, because they appeal to the sentimental side of man and womankind. All over the country prospective fathers had excellent reasons for studying the clock on Sunday and speculating on the nature of the " blessings " expected on Monday. After Sunday midnight the poll, was open and bounty babies rolled in bountifully. In Warrington the new corners for the first twenty four hours arrived liter- ally with silver spoons in their mouths., thanks to the generosity of Mr. A. H. Cros- field. The normal daily birth-rate in War- rington is six, but thanks to the healthy competition induced by Mr Crosfield, on Monday there were no less than nine who arrived with a valid claim to the silver spoon. Their mothers of course, come in also for the thrice-wel come State benefit of 305., as will the wife of every insured person at future maternity. Add to this the sickness and unemployment benefits both for male and female workers, and one gets some idea of the amount of sunshine that Mr. Lloyd George and the ,Liberal Government have introduced in the homes of working people. * *

Unemployment was low in December, as might have been guessed, but the figures for the whole of 1912 are affected by the abnormal conditions brought about by the coal strike in March. In that month the percentage of unemployed rose at a bound from less than 3to more than 11. Thus we have an average figure for the year of 3.2, as compared with 3.0 in 1911, although the only months in which the figure was actually more than 3 were March and April. We may confidently say that, had it not been for the disturbance in the coal trade, 1912 would not only have seen the smallest margin of unemployed we have known, but would have brought us to the point where there was an actual dearth of labour in several of the principal industries. It may be reserved for 1913 to show us those con- ditions prevailing. As satisfactory as the low amount of unemployment recorded is the fact that wages at last showed a steady upward inclination, an increase of £131,611 a week being distributed between 1,712,000 workers.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
Annual Congregational Gathering.

Opinions differ as to the advisability of holding socials and tea meetings in connection with places of worship, but if all such functions took the same delightful form as the annual parochial gathering of the Warrington Parish Church there would be few to condemn the practice. This year's tea was held at the Fairfield Schools on Thursday evening. The rooms presented a gay appearance, haviaig been tastefully decorated by willing hands. At the tea 157 persons sat down and many more attended at the later proceedings. Mr Frederick Harding carried out the catering, and among those who assisted at the table were Mesdames Willie, Hopkins, Walton Harding, S Taylor, and the Misses White. The clergy present were The Rector (Rev Canon Willis), the Revs A J Bratt, T Vickers and J M Buckrnaster. After tea whist drives were held in the upper schoolroom,and dancing was the attraction in the lower room. A concert was also held in another room. Mr R W Autwiss acted as M.C. for dancing and.the music was provided by Mr N Brandreth (piano), and Mr A Shaw (violin.) There were two whist drives, lasting two hours, each of 24 tables. Mr G W A Brown was the M.C. and the general assistants were Councillor J G Craik and Mr Edward Isherwood I(church wardens), Councillor Locker and Messrs J Hill, T Harding and others. The prize winners in the First whist drive were:— 1, Miss A Brimelow and Mrs Stansfield ; 2, Miss A Hope and Mr F Dale. Second drive : 1, Miss A Hope and Miss Mitchell; 2, Mrs Farrell and Miss Frangleton. The concert included the following items:—Pianoforte duet" Barber of Seville," the Misses White ; songs, Master H Sankey; violin solos, Miss Reynolds; songs, Mr .1 H Draper and Mr William Dennett; pianoforte solo, Mr F M Darby. At the conclusion a play entitled" Granny" was given in a very pleasing manner. The part of Maud was to have been taken by Miss M Broadbent but a slight accident prevented her attendance. Her place was taken by Miss D Brown. The other characters were :—Oscar Morris, a young artist, Mr Brian Dickson; Colonel Hammersley, Mr Marston ; Mrs Rattenshaw, a country woman, Miss Sylvia Broadbent. The proceedings which terminated ut midnight were of a most enjoyable character. THE RECTOR'S ADDh ESS.

At the tea the RECTOR gave an interesting address, remarking at the ontset that they all knew he was just 70 years of age, and oa Good Friday he wouYd have been Rector of Warrington for a quarter of a century. (Applause.) They were making an addition to the church by building a new vestry, and he was very grat,4ul for the help they had received. They had about £575 in hand and on promise, and the estimated expenditure was £620. In all probability the amount they would want would be £7OO altogether. With regard to the Easter vestry, the Reetor thanked the officers for their kindness, and remarked that they had decided this year to have the meeting in the evening instead of mid-day, to enable all, and especially workingmen interested in the church, to attend. The church cifertory gave satisfaction, being about £570, the same as the previous year. Continuing, the Rector spoke of tbe missions of the church, and said they had reasons to be thankful that their congregations were crowded, and that they had a large number of communicants. They must be prepared for building another mission upon a site which had been given them near the barracks by Colonel Robert Ireland Blackburne, but it would be on a larger scale. In all probability it, would be for a church and vicarage for a new parish in time. Referring to the Church Institute, be said they had the beginning of a Church Institute on the Manchester road. There was at present e room for billiards and games but that was only an instalment of what they hoped would be a library, gymnasium and parochial hall. They had decided at the Parish Church Council to fence the whole of the property round, so as to be able to use the land for the benefit of parishioners. The last point referred to by the Rector had reference to a new finance scheme, He bad brought before the Council a new scheme called The Archbishop's Finance Scheme the main point of which was to make the diocese the unit, instead of the parish. All the rural deaneries would be assessed to see what portion they would pay to the diocesan fund and all the parishes would be assessed in accordance with the population and endowments. The object was that there should not be rich and poor parishee, but that all should be provided for according to what seemed right. That scheme would in all probability come into operation in all the diocese of England during the course of this year. He would, however, keep the Council well informed on the matter. (Applause.)

The Union of Liberal Clubs. Mr. A. C. Doran of Rochdale presided • at the fifth annual meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Union of Liberal Clubs, which was held at the Audenshaw Liberal Club, Guide Bridge. The Warrington District Federation ef Liberal Clubs con- sisting of five of those institutions in the Warrington, Widnes, and St Helens districts was admitted to membership on formal application. Various subjects respecting the affiliated clubs were discussed, but the chief business of the meeting was that of making arrangements for the annual meeting of delegates to the National Union. This is to be held on March Ist and is to be attended by representatives of clubs in all the federated districts. It was agreed to recommend the Cheshire and Derbyshire Federation's executive to arrange for the meeting to take place at Stockport. Officers for the ensuing year were elected as follow: President, the Right Hon. W. L. S. Churchill, M,P.; chairman of committee. Mr. C. A. Doran; bon. secee- tary and treasurer, Mr Councillor J. Cook; hon. auditor, Mr. G. B. Hellas; hon. solicitor, Mr. H. T Pullen (Bradford). Warrington Photographic Society. Anyone who has seen Mr G E Thompson's coloured lantern slides at the exhibitions will not be surprised at the great reception he received at the Academy on Tuesday. About 50 members and friends were regaled with his lecture "Round a French Lake." It is the Lake of Annecy in ilea° Saveie, nestling in the old world country at the foce of the Savoy Alps, nine miles from Gineva. The pictures took us from Grenoble through Chambery to the Lake and its charming neighbourhood. The present colour prccesses in photography will have to travel, far before they reach the level of these beautiful hand coloured works of art shown on the sheet as they were by the Society's new electtic projector. Besides the delightful lake scenes are chateaux, convents, monasteries, old markets, and the rarest of old houses and villages with their quaint customs and fairs, all of which were portrayed with excellent photographic effect. The matter and manner of the lecture were equally attrac- tive and nothing could exceed in quiet humour his dream of how be, as a subject of His Majesty Henry VIII., would have been received at the chateau where he was now allowed with such courtesy to practice his art on the most sacred subjects and bring away pictures from the cestle that must be unique. Mr Th ompson was heartily thanked at the close. FOR MODERN FIREPLACES and Cooking Ranges corn bining economy with simplicity try J. S. GARLAND Ironmonger, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Sons of Temperance. This enterprising Friendly Society, despite the inclemency of the weather, held a moat successful Temperance meeting on Saturday in the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Lecture Hall. The chairman was a local veteran in the person of Bro. Judson, of Earlestown. --In the course of his remarks he advocated the claims of the Order, testifying to its usefulness and healthy condition from personal experience—The speaker of the evening was Bro. Mclntyre, of Manchester, who in a very spirited and vivid manner shorted that the Sons of Temperance were first and foremost a Temperance organisation, and that many people had been induced to sign the pledge as a result of its propaganda. The low sick rate of the society of nine days per member for the past 50 years, was alluded to in order to show the' healthy position and the good financial state of its funds ; alsoahrough the State Insurance Act it had considerably more than doubled its membership. He also emphasised the interest he had taken in the I children's section, pointing out that there was a cadet membership of a early 100,000 children who met every other week arid conducted the whole of the business themselves. They read sound Temperance teaching coupled with the fact that they were insured for the fullest amount possible which the law of the land allowed for qd. per week. At the age of 16 they we:e transferred to the adult section. Out of every 100 so transferred 95 per cent. were in the Order and were total abstainers at the age of 30 - truly a wonderful record. On the adult side he showed that tor the lowest contribution the highest benefits could be secured to suit all purses because of the Order's low sick and death rates. The meeting closed with votes of thanks, and it was announced that further informa- tion could be obtained from the local secretary, Mr. A. Wardrean. of 49, Amelia-street, or every other I Saturday at Bewsey road. would instil in him a further desire to promote the I great cause of Forestry.

div.head: Golden Wedding.
div.p: Golden Wedding.

Mr and Mrs Joseph Madeley, of 4, Forest-street, Latchford, celebrated their golden wedding on Sunday. They were married at St Michael's Church, Rushall, near Walsall, on January 12th, 1863. Mr and Mrs Madeley, who have been living for some years in Latchford, spent the major portion of their married life in Walsall. Mr Madeley has been in the iron trade all his life, beginning to work at the very early age of eight, and was in the employment of one firm over 40 years previous to his coming to Latchford. He is still working at his trade. Mr and Mrs Madeley, who have been the recipients of many good wishes and presents, are in excellent health and look forward to the celebrating of many more anniversaries of their wedding. The fortnightly meeting of the above s,ciety was held in the Old Academy, Bridge Foot, on Wednesday evening last, when, to a good attendance of members and friends, Mr B S Townroe, 8.A., read a paper on "The ethics of Imperialism." The lecturer, in the course of a most interesting and provocative address, endeavoured to point out the meaning and justification of the policy which goes by the name of Imperialism, and claimed that no question more vitally affects the future welfare of this country. Leaving antouched the narrower issues of tariff, political federation, and militarism, he dealt ably with the broader aspect— the moral or ethical side of the question, and emphasized the desirability of closer unity between the Colonies and the Mother Country, strengthened as it was by the thousand interests and community of thought in almost every relation of life. Mr Townroe pointed out the responsibilities which devolve upon the citizen in bearing the burden of Empire, and said that legislators, statesmen, and permanent officials could not alone perform this task but that there must be behind them a trained political opinion, realising our national responsibility for one- fifth of the population of the world. At the conclusion of the address a keen discussion ensued, in which Messrs A H Rathbmste, E G Burgess, Dr S A Mellor, N Nield and Dalby took part, and the policy of Imperialism came in for much criticism, both adverse and favonrable. A hearty vote of thanks to Mr Townroe terminated tlte meeting.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. SAM HASSALL.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. SAM HASSALL.

The news came as a painful shock to many Warring- tonians of the death of Mr Samuel Thomas Hassan, who passed away at his residence Elmhurst, Latchford Without, at I 30 on Wednesday afternoon, after a very short illness. Mr Hassan, who was chief salesman at the Hightield Tannery, Runcorn, was attending to his duties as usual last week--in fact he made a journey to London. On Monday last he complained of an influenza cold and decided to stay at home for a few days. The next morning his wife found him lying unconscious in bed. Dr ttohinson, who was consulted, called in a specialist but all efforts were unavailing and Mr Hassan died at the time stated, without having regained conscious- ness. The cause of death was an abscess on the ',rain. Mr Hassell will be greatly missed, particularly in local circles, for music was his great hobby, arid he had taken a special interest in the Warrington Male Choral Union, of which he was the conductor. The circum- stances are made the more distressing by the fact that it was only three months on Thursday since Mr Hassalt was married at St Helen's Church, Hollinfare, to Miss Lucy Davies, a well-known vocalist, to whom the deepest sympathy of all will go forth in her terribly sudden beredvement. Mr Hassan was thirty-eight years of age. He was a native of Kidsgrove, in Staffordshire, but came to Warrington in boyhood. He at once joined the cboir of the Workingman's Mission and became the leader at the age of seventeen. For the greater part of his life he remained closely associated with the mission and its work. About fourteen Tears ago Mr Hassan was instrumental in forming the Warrington Male Voice Choir and became its first conductor. He held the position up to the time of his dk ath, although latterly he had shared the duties with Nir W S Nesbitt, of Manchester. Mr Hassall bad frequently led the choir to victory at
LliE LAI:r.; MR. HASSALL.

competitive festivals and nobody was more delighted than he with the creditable position which it attained in the northern musical world. He took a prominent part in bringing about the amalgamation with the old Apollo Male Voice Chior, under the title of the Warrington Male Choral Union. Mr. Hassell was an acceptable tenor singer, and had long been a member of the Warrington Musical Society. He had taken part in several of the productions of the operatic section. During the interval at the society's concert on Wednesday evening the conductor (Mr F H Crossley) informed the members of ,the death of one who had been esteemed by them all, and many and sincere were the expressions of regret and sympathy. For the past twelve years Mr. Hassell had been associated with the Highfield Tannery, Runcorn, and had gained the confidence and goodwill of the firm and work. people alike. He acted as conductor of the male voice choir formed in cooue3tion with the works. Before taking up his position at Runcorn. Mr Hassell was a member of the staff at Messrs Fleming's tannery, Fennel-street, Warrington. He led a remarkably active life but, notwithstanding his many interests, he found time to indulge in outdoor recreation and was a member of the Warrington Cycling Club and the Frodsham Golf Club. Of a frank and genial disposi- tion, he was a favourite with all who knew him, and his death at such an early age will he felt by many as a , heavy personal less. The funeral will take plane at Grappenhall Church this (Saturday) afternoon. The cortege will leave the house at 2 o'clock.

div.head: CHESHIRE EDUCATION.
div.p: CHESHIRE EDUCATION.
Sidelight on Village Housing:

The Cheshire— Education Committee, at Crewe, on Monday, received a letter from the head teachers of the Cheshire secondary schools drawing attention to the fact that the wilaries at present paid to assistant teachers in several Cheshire secondary schools were not sufficient to attract or retain the services of able and qualified teachers, and that in the interests of higher education in the county some reform seamed urgently needed. The secretary for higher education was directed to prepare a return showing the salaries of assistant masters and mistresses] in secondary schools in the county. The Elementary Schools Sub-committee reported that they had considered a resolution passed by the managers of one of the schools in the Chester area to the effect that "the headmaster is desired to punish children for misbehaviour during the dinner interval and on the way to and from school." The committee decided "that no action be taker, as it is considered that the powers of teachers in this ou,Lior are already sufficiently defined." Attention was called to the appointment of a head teacher in the Congleton area conditional on his resid- ing at Buglawton. Ms. J M Yates, K.C., who resides in the district, declared amid laughter that there was no place in Buglavvton where a teacher could reside. There were cottages with either two rooms up and one down or two rooms down and one up. At the present time they had not a single vacant house in the place, and on account of the prosperity of the fustian-cutting industry at Congleton there wse no likelihood of there being cottages vacant so long as that lasted. The committee decided not to approve the condition /squiring the teacher to live at Buglawton.

div.head: QUERIES OF ANSWERS.
div.p: QUERIES OF ANSWERS.

OUR READERS are invited to send legal queries to be answered week by week. Inquiries must be short. concise, and plainly written, and the name and address of the writer given to show that the inquiry is genuine. The replies are by a member of the profession, and every effort is made to secure accuracy, but we cannot assume any responsibility for the opinion or advice given. Mark all envelopes containing queries " Legal," and address them to the EDITOR," EXAMINER," WARRINGTON. If you do not wish initials to be used in the reply please suggest a nom-de-plume.

STAMPS.—You certainly can claim under the Act. You did not claim exemption and you have had your card stamped. The fact that your husband is now on full time makes no difference. SLAVERY.—You had better see the Officials of the Approved Society; they will give you everymassistanee. The doctor must be one of those on the panel. If you have any difficulty write us again. V f CTI n.—lf you cannot defend the action you will have to pay the costs of the County Court summons. Certairly your creditor did not show you much consideration. P.J.—The full is. 61 and free medicine. W.B.—lt is difficult to advise you in the absence of the documents. You appear to have contracted for months' supply and you are bound to accept delivery. It is no excuse that prices have gone against you. Why not try to compromise? DIVORCE,—At present you can only proceed in the Superior Courts. If you wait you are in danger of kming your Suit on that account, MORTGAGE.—The Mortgagee can sue you personally as well as realize his security. He can also foreclose. Can you not secure another lender? You should act quickly.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
Concert in Parr Hall.

The Musical Society's concert in Parr Hall on Wednesday evening, though it drew only a meagre attendance,is noteworthy in that it made us acquainted with the most recent important work from the pen of the late Mr. S. Coleridge-Taylor—a cantata, for soli, chorus and orchestra, entitled "A Tale of old Japan." Wedded to a narrative poem by Mr Alfred Noyes, quaint and pathetic in character yet redolent of the cherry-blossom fragrance of the land forming its locale, the music must be regarded as a further and startling revelation of that rich vein of melodic and harmonic beauty which Coleridge-Taylor has already so pleasantly made us familiar with in his "Hiawatha." " A Tale of old Japan " is, indeed, a most charming work of its kind, and its relationship with the work just mentioned merits enquiry in its promise of proving both interesting and remarkable. Conceived on the free and quite distinctive lines characteristic of its composer, it will be gathered that nothing in the nature of contrapuntal formality is to be found in it, place being given, on the other hand, to a wealth of engaging structural themes and a kaleidoscopic range of brilliant orchestral effects which prove at once a source of unalloyed delight to the listener. The telling of the sad story of the ill-starred love of 0 Kirni San is cleverly divided in a continuous way between tho solo voices singly and together and simul- taneously with the chorus, the character of the unhappy girl-heroine being, of course, taken by the principal soprano, while to the tenor and bass fall naturally the parts of Sawara the pupil, and his tutor Tenko the painter-artist. As a test of choral singing the cantata taxed the capabilities of the musical society's vocal members on just their strong side—their power to deal with difficult detail—and from the intricacies of choral parts often deeply involved in the complexities of the music for the solo vocalists, they emerged in a most creditable way, the numerous crucial points calling often for both great restraint and great intensity of expression, being made with iutel:igent emphasis and discrimination. Mr. Crossley, to whom acknowledgments of these points of excellence are due, is to be further congratulated on obtaining from his chorus some delightful contrasts of tone, as may be instanced in the picturesque "Peonies, Peonies, crowned the May," "Lying on the gold sand," and the poignant recital of passages like that commencing "Small and terribly drifting." The orchestra had a most onerous task in playing, with neatness and due expression, Mr. Colerridge-Taylor's dainty yet, at times, dangerously overloaded orchestral parts. Yet, except occasionally when the band was simply and frankly too loud, the society's instrumental members, led and assisted professionally as usual, came through the ordeal most satisfactorily, incidentally earning for themselves a full moiety of the laurels of a highly creditable and entirely adequate presentation of the work. It is due to say that Miss Leah Felissa, Miss Nellie Anderton, Mr. John Booth and Mr. Hamilton Harris proved themselves, jointly and severally, fully competent in interpreting the somewhat exacting music for the principal voices. Of the two part-songs in the second half of Wednesday's programme the most interesting was unquestionably the unaccompanied one entitled " Sleeping " (German.), and this calls for special men- tion in that it was sung with marked taste and expression and the attainment of a well-nigh perfect balance of the various parts. The orchestra further distinguished itself in Mozart's " Zauberflote " over- ture, albeit the tempo adopted was much slower than is usual in present-day performances. Miss Felissa sang with dashing brilliance the Faust Jewel Song,and Miss Anderton shelved marked ability in investing with a certain amount of interest the rather dreary song "Sabbath morning at sea" by Elgar. The tenor and bass vocalists gave some excellent songs in quite an excellent way, the former, " Maire, my girl" (Aitken), and the latter, "Had a horse &c." (Korbay) and "How deep the slumber of the floods" (Loewe), encore numbers being demanded, during the evening from each end all the four principal singers in turn.

div.head: TO A DEAD MUSICIAN.
div.p: TO A DEAD MUSICIAN.

By the courtesy of to distinguished poet Mr Alfred Noyes we are able to publish the harmonious and touching verses which will be engraved on the tomb of the late .Samuel Coleridge-Taylor (1875-1912), the Anglo-African composer, one of the most genuinely spontaneous musicians Of his day and a gentle and lovable nature, whose sudden death was a shock to the English musical world last September.
tribute was paid to his meMory by a festival concert held in November at the Albert Hall, London, at which

the profits (over £l,OOO net) are said' to hive exceeded those of any concert held there. One of the dead musician's latest and best works was a setting brimming with melody,picturesqueness,ind the tender, affectionate feeling of Mr NO3 03'S charming poem "A Tale of Old Japan."

(FOR THE MEMORIAL-STONE TO COLERIDGE-TAYLOR. Sleep, crowned with fame, faarless of change or time. Sleep, like remembered music in the soul, Silent, immortal; while our discords climb, To that great chord which shall resolve the whole.

Silent, with Mozart on that solemn shore; Secure where neither waves nor hearts can break; Sleep, till the Master of the World once more Touch the remembered strings and bid thee wake . . . Touch the remembered strings and bid thee wake.
ALFRED NOYES.

Some extremely interesting statistics are given in the " Neue Deutsche Theateradressbuch " which serve to show the relative popularity of various composers and dramatists in Germany. We are not surprised to find that Richard Wagner is the most popular of composers, with no less than 1,815 separate representations of various of his works. A very bad second comes Puccini, with 850 nights, which is, nevertheless, a considerable record for a living master. Germany, how- ever, ,suffers no less than England from the übiquitous musical comedy, and the author of" Parsifal " even is overwhelmed by the 3,100 representations of Franz Lehar and Leo Fall, and almost equalled by the 1,379 of the "Waltz King." Johann Strauss. But it is no small tribute to Germany as a musical nation that Wagner can claim nearly 2,000 performances.

A woman factory band, named Phcebe Clarke (32), pleaded guilty at Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tues- day, to stealing 193 Id and a purse at Widnes. The child of respectable Warrington parents, prisoner, at the age of tlnelve, commenced robbing little children of' money. After a few years she disappeared fur a and then returned to her old practices, and now had no fewer than GO convictions against her. Prisoner was now sent to prison for nine months.
lhe prosecution was conducted by Mr Lcanb.
SHOWMAN'S CRUELTY. A DISAPPOINTMENT IN MARRIAGE. THE SEQUEL.

A curious defence was made by a loquacious middle-aged amusement caterer, whose wife summoned him for persistent cruelty at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair) and other magistrates. The defendant, Henry Bodycot, was described as a travelling amusement caterer, of The Siding, Bank Quay, and bad a stand with bagettelle and billiards on the Fair Ground near the Fire Station, The wife, Mary Ann Bodycot, alleged that owing to his cruelty she had been compeiled to leave him on the Bth January. Mr tv R Roberts, who appeared for the applicant, said that the parties were married in November, 1910. lie believed she was the:defendant's third wile,and that there were no children by the marriage. The defendant had a van and went from fair to fair with bagettelle and billiards and did very well. They both lived in a travelling van and the wife had not been married to defendant very long before she found out that he was an habitual drunkard. He soon began to StIOW signs of a vicious disposition when in drink. There was not much room in the van and the defendant had turned his wife out at night, no matter what the weather was. On occasions she had had to go out to escape his brutalit3. She, along with a daughter of defendant, had bad to spring out of the waggon to escape the threatened violence of the man. Indeed, the nights of those two women seemed to have been spent in spring- ing out of the van and crawling in again. On tht, 7th inst. the defendant brought his waggon to Warrington and it was situated on the railway embankment, along Parker-street. He announced his intention of going to have a look round the town, but his wife had been in the habit of going to public houses several times to ask the attendants not to serve her husband, because when he was in drink he was a raving maniac. She was successtul in debarring him from drinking in some puhlic-'nouses, but unfortunately, he escaped his wife ultimately, and when she got home she knew what was going to happen. He made use of the most abominable language atm he was not fit to he at large. The wife asked for a separation order. Mary ADD Bodycot, the wife, who is residing at 1, Flag-lane, corroborated the statement made -ioy Mr Roberts.

The defendant, who Lai been making voluminous notes all througb,objected to Mr Roberts " kading "the complainant through her evidence. He did not think the solicitor was entitled to "tutor" her. The Chief Constable: She would wander all over the place..

COmplainant stated that her husband treated her very badly when in drink. He had struck her in the mouth with his fist and had chased her with an iron bar. If he was steady for one week she had a month of misery. The defendant said that the breakfast things were left unwashed and alleged that his wife had run away with money and left him practically destitute. The breakfast things were not washed up from a week ago. Here the defendant produced documents stating "This is her character and these are mine before I married her." (Laughter). After other corroborative evidecce as to the defendant's cruelty had been given and the defendant had subjected each witness to a long cross- examination, he stated his case to the Bench. tie met his wife two years ago and took an instant liking to her. Being well possessed, he proposed marriage to her and was accepted, expecting that everything would go on straightforwardly. Instead of that, he found out that be had married into a " hot- bed of pollution " right through. Every day the moment the daughter got up she sat scratching herself and biting her nails for three hours and the hreak fast things were left. His wife had worn a pair of stocaiegs for three weeks, being too lazy to change them,and the daughter was equally lazy. IteAing novels, going to theatres end music-halls was all they required. He was very sorry he had got into such pollution. He did not deny that he had used bad language, but his wife had been equ illy had. Complainant was granted a separation order with an allowance of les per week, and defendant was also ordered to pay the court costs and the advocate's fee.

SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN. At the Liverpool County Sessions on Tuesday, Lucy Hickman (38), a fustian cutter, of 10, Portland-street, Warrington, was charged with n.3glecting her children in a shocking manner. Tile children were James (14), Thomas (12), Eva (10), end Gladys (G. Medical evidence was to the effect that the children were badly clad, the clothing being quite insufficient fer the weather. The two girls were verminous, and till sleeping rooms were in a filthy condition, whilst the bedding consisted solely of a dirty old quilt. In the doctor's opinion, the condi- tions must cause injury to health and unnecessary briefly suffering. Defendant, he said, had the appearance of a habitual drunkard, and at the time of his visit, on the sth of December, she was suffering from the effects of drink. John Hickman, a son, aged eighteen, who gave his evidence somewhat reluctantly, said that his mother had even sold food to obtain beer, as also she had pawned clothes. An Inspector of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children who had visited the house said that the bedclothes were black and stiff with dirt. Defendant, he said, had told him that her husband would not give her money. the terms of the preceding statement constituted the defendant's defence, adding that her husnand had beaten her. The Inspector said that to his own knowledge the woman bad been given money by her husband, but she only spent it in drink. The woman was found guilty of neglect. She was then charged with being a habitual drunkard, and, this being proved, she was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for neglect and three years in the Inebriates' Reformatory Home at Langho for being a hatitual drunkard.
SATURDAY.—Before Mr J W Hayward (in the chair) Messrs R 'l' Fairclough, A J Jolley, NV Furness auJ T Pemberton.

GIRLS IN TnotrinE.—Mary Muller (13), 97, Fair- dough's Avenue and Annie Green (12), 5, Gilbert- street, appeared in answer to a charge of stealing during the previous week, a quantity of ribbon of the value of TOs. from 74, Church-street, the property of Annie Clinton.—The Chief Constable stated that the girls were seen the previous day to be acting in a suspicious Opftlatler.outside a show case at the above address. The police were informed and subsequently the girls were brought to the police ststion. They had apparently been stealing in a wholesale manner from ail kinds of shops abut the town, and it wits essential that the case should be adjourned ;a order to make inquiries. They had taken things from practically half the stalls in the market.—The case was adjourned. SEittous ASSALTLT CASE.—A sordid story of brutal assaults was related when Frank Tansey, 58, Tanner's. lane, was charged with assaulting Charles Fletcher, 37, Gladstone-street, on Christmas Day. He was further charged with having committed an aggravated assault on Mary Ann Gannon, 23, Portland-street, on Boxing Day, end with assaulting Julia Ann Gannon on the sae day.—Mr Stec!, who appeared for the defendant, M pleaded guilty.—The story as related by the Chief Constable, was that about one o'clock on Christmas morning Charles Fletcher was proceeding home from a party and saw a crowd of people in the street. He went to see what was the matter, and found a young girl (who it transpired was the prisoner's sister) leaning against a wall crying. lie asked her what was the matter, and immediately after the prisoner struck him a violent blow in the mouth, cutting his lip and loesens lug two teeth, with the result that he had to go to the Infirmary for treatment. The other cases of assault took place about 2.30 on the morning of Boxing Day. The prisoner went to the house of Mrs Gennon and her daughter, and asked for his sister. He was told that she was not there and that he could search the house. He was allowed to go upstairs. Mrs Gannon was coming dowe, and the prisoner struck her a violent blow in the face. Afterwards he came down and struck the daughter a heavy blow in the mouth. They put him outside, but in the struggle the prisoner was injured. Mrs Gannon and her daughter were Po much upset that they got themselves ready to go to the Police Station to report the matter: They left the house, and when going clown Dallarn-lane the prisoner struck Mrs Gannon a severe blow across the head with a poker, felling her to the ground. The daughter stooped down and the prisoner deliberately struck her a heavy blow across the hack with the same instrument. The mother and daughter returned to the home and a doctor was called in. Mrs Gannon had been under his care over since. Mr Steel said it was a very so h did story. The prisoner had had some drink, and his sister had been out all the evening and there had been a quarrel between them. He was trying to get her to go home when Mr Fleteher ' came up. Tausey was under the impression that in the struggle in the hcuso he was struck on the head with a jug, but Miss Cannon said the injury was caused by him coming into contact with the wringing machine. Prisoner was extremely sorry for what he had done. He had not been in trouble :iefore, and haei been in custody since hristruas.—Tansey vas fined £6, includ- ing costs, and the magistrates said they were much praiseworthy conduct. impressed with Fletcher's

div.p: CLARION ET A;

At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, John %A ebb (33), shoemaker, pleaded not guilty to stealing a gentleman's silver lever watch, a clarionet, an overcoat, &c., the property of Allan Royle, of Warring- ton. Mr 3 Openshaw (instructed by the Town Clerk of Warrington) prosecuted. Evidence was to the effect that at the end of April, 1912, prisoner came to the shop of Royle and asked for work, which was given him. His bedroom was the back one, and Royle occupied the front one. On May 11th, Royle stated he got out of bed at 6 a.m, because he was suspicious, having heard Webb get up, go downstairs and move (thou'. Finding the drawer in the kitchen open, as also the yard door, he roused his nephew, and a search was instituted, with the result that they found the articles, together with a revolver, missing. Prisoner's explanation was to the effect that on the night in question he went downstairs to let in a man whum he had met on the tramp, and whom he put in a chair to sleep. Later, thinking he heard the man moving about, Webb alleged he went downstairs, saw what had happened, and, picking up the revolver, gave chase after the man. Thinking that he might himself be accused of the theft, he was afraid to return. Prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair) Mesrs C Jackson Holmes and T Locker.

"NOT FIT TO BE Loo-s-E."2-13atTrick Farrell, 11, Paradise Place, was charged with breaking seven paces of glass at the dwelling house of Sarah Ann Unsworth, 41, Golborne-street and doing damage t 9 the extent ot :is. on the 13th Jaunary.—He pleaded guilty. He was further charged with assaulting P.C. Thomas Barr whilst in the execution of his duty.—This charge Farrell denied.—The officer stated that at 7.10 the previous day the woman, Unsworth, asked him to go to her house as the prisoner was causing a disturbance there. He (the ofFcer) ejected the prisoner and cal ed again at 8.15 when the woman told him that she had had to get another officer from Sankey :street to put the prisonEr out,as he had returned. The prisoner had smashed the v,iodows and on the way to the police station he tried to trip him. (the officer), several times and struck him on the side of the head.—Sarah Ann Unsworth stated that the prisoner had come to her house for his wife who was her daughter. His wife had come to her for protection,—Prisoner alleged that his wife had said she would " knife" him.—The Chairman said : In the interests of yourself, in the interests of your wife tind in the interests of everyone else you will go to prison tor one month. You are not fit to be loose.

TIIIIRqDAY,—Before Mr W Roberts (in the chair), Councillor Locker, Messrs W Richardson, J Upson, and J Jolley. THEFT or METAL.—James Brailey,carter, 10, Pinner's Brow and James Fielding, lodging-house Stanley. street, were charged with stealing on the 14th January seven wire,drawers steel plates, value 155., the property of Messrs Rylands Bros. Fielding was also charged ith receiving the goods knowing them to have been stolen. Chief Inspector Williamson said that in conse- quence of information received Detective Sergeant, Holland went to see Fielding who, when questioned denied having got the plates and sold them again. He said he had got two little bits. However, four plates were found in the backyard of the house 29, Howley. lane and when this fact was made known to Fielding he admitted he had put them there the previous day and also that he had sold the other three to Toole's for Is. 7d. He admitted that be got them from Brailey who was employed to cart rubbish from R,ylands works to a refuse tip at Howley. Fielding had asked the other prisoner how much he wanted for the plates saying that he had only two pence,ba Brailey said that would do for a drink.Ho did not know Brailey had stolen them. When charged, Brailey said " I did take them but be never gave me twopence for them but said that he would give me the price of a drink.l am innocent. —Brailey ',vas find 203. and costs 10s. in all and Fielding was ordered to pay ICs. and costs a total sum of .Cl. . _

A YouNG OFFENDER.—Amy Barnett (IC), 47, Dudley- street was sumrnonen for stealing on the 4th January the sum of 3s. the monies of Gladys B Wilkinson, from a stall in the Market Place.—Chief Inspector Williamson stated that the proprietors of the stall, Messrs the Penny Bazaar Co., Ltd., had employed the girl for three years. For a considerable time past they bad been missing money from the stall where the girl was the assistant. Inquiries were made and it was found that the girl had been spending money more freely than one could reasonably expect her to do. The manageress of the stall, Blanche Wilkinson, saw the defendant serve a customer and get a two shilling piece and give Is lid change. The girl put the two shi tinge underneath her apron. Later on, the same night, she disposed of a Is in a similar way. Miss Wilkinson took the girl iute the lavatory and asked her bow much money she had. The girl pro- duced a purse contaiuing small silver, but after Miss Wilkinson had still further pressed her she pioduced the 3s and was allowed to go. The company had found that they had lost and were losing money, and the summons had only been taken out in the hope that it would act as a deterrent to other Orls.—The girl admitted that she had been taking money from the stall during the past four months. The largest amount she had taken was the 3s. mentioned in the charge. She had had about .£1 altogether, and out of that she bad bought a scent bottle end gone to places of amusement often.—The case was dismissed on payment of costs, and on the girl promising not to repeat the offence. 'YOUNG GIRLS' THEFTs.—May Mullee (13), 97, Fairclough Avenue, Annie Green (11) 5, Gilbert-street and Martha Daly (13), 7, Robson-street, appeared in answer to several charges of stealing small articles from shops to the value of about 3s. during the last three months.—Chief Inspector Williamson stated that the police had first got to know of the offences on Friday afternoon last when a Nliss Clinton of Church- street reported to Detective Clough that two girls had stolen ribbon from her shop. laquiries were made and as a result the girls were seen and subsequently Green admitted the offence. Mullee was brought before Miss Clinton, who identified her along with Green as the girls she bad seen running away from the shop and one of the girls had some of the ribbon in her hair. Whilst pawning a pair of boots which they had stolen they took a shirt, blouse and petticoat. The thefts covered some dozens of shops and stalls but only one or two articles were found in the house of Daley. The girl Daley stayed outside to keep watch most of the time. The three articles stolen from Mr Houghton's shop were found displa .rd for sale in the shop window of Mrs Mullee. Mrs Nlullee,said she did not know anything about goods The defendams hadtnade an admission to the police that they went to the market every Saturday and took what they wanted. They must have been carrying on for :eyeral months, on tbe same business.—The Chairman, in fining each defendant 203, raid it was a terrible thing for young girls like them to be brought there on such horrible charges, and they thought the parents had not exercised that control which they ought to have done.

FEUD AV.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst, and Pierpoint, Messrs. S Wright, and A J Jolley, G Pilling and T Locker. SERIOUS THREATS. —John Wm Canney, Forster- street. was summoned for using threats to his wife on New Years Eve.—Mr W B Forshaw, prosecuted and slid the case had been before the court previously wh-n the defendant had been committed on a 11 days order to the workhouse in order that his state of mind might be inquired into. The doctors had been unable to certify that he was insane. Mr Forshaw then went on to relate that the defendant returned home on New Years eve and after he had bcen in the house a short time he made use of the remark "It is no u:e, you and the children will have to die to-night." He brought a knife out of his pocket and opened it but the wife struggled with him and held his wrist for ten minutes. She became faint and rushed into a neighbour's house. If the defendant was not insane he was very dangerous and the wife was afraid he would carry out his threats. After hearing witnesses the magistrates bound the defendant over in two sureties of Lb U or one month's imprisonment. NEGLF.CT.—James Noonan, of no fixed address, was summoned for running away from the County Borough of Wa:rington and leaving his child chargeable to the Union on November 21st.—He pleaded guilty and was sent to gaol for one month.

div.head: SOLDIER'S CIGARETTE.
div.p: THE SOLDIER'S CIGARETTE.

GENERAL OFFICERS DISCOURAGE SMOKING. Jn all the eight commands of the British army the general officers are imposing more or less stringent regulations by means of beat orders to check the habit of cigarette smoking among the troops. Surgeon General Sir ST L Gubhins, Director General of the Army MedicarService, and Surgeon General Sir Alfred Keogh before him, in their annual reports on the health of the home army have emphasised the importance of taking steps to reduce cigarette smoking by soldiers. The men, as a rule, it is said, buy the cheapest kind of cigarettes, and smoke them constantly when not actually exercising in the field or on duty in barracks or in camp. The Surgeon Generals state that the use of the cigarette, among young soldiers especially, gradually but quite perceptibly develops heart trouble, and that in the interest of the army as well as the individual soldier the habit should be greatly checked.

div.head: VICTORIA PARK.-A SUGGESTION
div.p: VICTORIA PARK.-A SUGGESTION
Sir,—l wish to draw your attention to the following extract from the" Clyde Notes "in the " Yatchsman " for the 9th instant :

The New Year regatta on the Municipal Model Yacht, Pond at Largs was a complete success. Fifty models were brought forward. The weather was very suitable in every way, and a crowd,that would have done credit to a July day, turned out to witness (and to enjoy) the sport. The sailing was exceedingly keen, as all the crack Lugs makers and sailers of boats were present, while there was a strong contingent present from Fairlie with a few of the best boats belonslne to the world-famous village. Nobody had any chance, however, against the boats made by the various members of the blever Ninian family, of Largs, as they had won four of the first prizes, three of the seconds, end one of the thirds. The Fairlie boats on te other hand failed to secure a first among them. This pond cost the town of Large over £5OO to make, but it is safe to say, few, v.,ry few £soo's were ever spent to more advantage in it. Why not one in Victoria Park? - -
There are many good model yachts (not toys) in this town, l) ing idle for want of a suitable sheet of water.
I think it would stimulate the youths' ingenuity, be a delight to the elders, and help a mite to keep alive that splendid old spirit " Britannia rules the waves." I',.IODEL-YACHTER.

div.head: LYMM BILL.
div.p: THE LYMM BILL.

Sir,—As one who was unable to be present at the ratepayers' meeting held in the Lymna Council Chamber on the Bth inst, owing to an important engagement, I read with interest your report of the meeting. At the conclusion of its perusal I was sur- prised to find that several matters had been passed by those present at the meeting; for example, Mr G L Welford quoted £BOO as the annual profit (Water- works). What about the boating rights that were to be charged? and the open-air baths that were once mooted ought also to add to the annual revenue? Again there is the question of electricity. Would it not be within the rights of the owners of the lake to undertake a supply of electrical power for the district? Another point that caught my attention was Mr Molesworth's statement " What on earth did they want with parks at Lymna ? It was a piece of folly." Is that so? I think not! It has been my belief for some years that one of the most Important things the Lrlllll Urbtn District Council can do is to procure one or more playing folds for the children of Lytnm. As it is they have to play on the streets where they run grave risks of being killed, I, myself having seen some marvellous escapes of children from being run over. I cannot remember any road fatality but I believe that several of the children who have been drowned whilst playing on the canal side would have been living to day had tlrere been a proper ployground provided for them. We are often asked to support funds for giving town children a day in the country and yet these very children have got what the country children have not—a "park." It is rather strange that only this week Miss Molesworth has been out collecting for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. I am reminded that "Charity hegins at home!" Whilst giving the L.U.D.C. my hearty support with the present Bill I should like to see them move in the matter of providing recreation grounds for the children of the Lymm District.--Yours
A CHILDREN'S WELL-WISHER. Lymm, Jdnuary 16th, 1913.

div.head: PROHIBiTION AND DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: PROHIBiTION AND DRUNKENNESS.

Sir,----The address delivered at the British Women's Temperance Association meeting at Lynam reported in your issue of the 11th inst., favourably reviewing the results of New Zealand "Local Veto " is so contra- dictory to a report which appeared in the "Manchester Guardian " of the 28th December, 1910, that I think your readers would be interested if I quoted from it, written as it was, on the spot, by an individual who had apparently taken considerable trouble to make himself acquainted with the facts : "What has been the effect of no-licence, and does the extraordinary success of that movement lead 1.13 to anticipate the carrying of Dominion prohibi- tion within a paetically measurable distance of time ? To give a hurried answer in the affirma- tive, as the onwatd march of the no-licence voting might suggest at first glance would involve shutting one's eyes to facts. The chief of these is, that notwithstanding the advance of no-liconce voting drinking has substantially ii,creased. When only 37.82 per cent of the voters favoured abolition of licences the annual expenditure per bead on liquor for the whole population was £2 19s 8d ; when the aggregate vote against licences had grown to 42.23 per cent the Drink Bill had gone up to .0 4s 9d per head. In the next three years no-licence voting jumped up 665 per cent, but the increased appetite for liquor was then represented by an average expenditure of £3 lOs 3d. In 1905 and again in 1908, the growth of the no-licence vote was still accom- panied by greater indulgence in alcohol." "Thus ' no-licence ' has not reduced drinking in the aggregate. If liquor consumption has diminished in 'dry ' districts, it has gone up in even greater ratio elsewhere than the official figures indicate. The removal of drink from the public house bar where it is subject to official oversight, to the private cupboard and club locker where it is not, may or may not be desirable. It is maintained that there is a greater degree of law and order in no-licence than

div.head: ROMANISM v. PROTESTANTISM.
div.p: ROMANISM v. PROTESTANTISM.

Sir,—Phil Squod is disgusted. Well I am sorry, and more so, if he thinks I imputec dishonourable motives to himself, as I consider true charity requires that we accept that those who differ from us in religion do so in good faith. He certainly attacks the Catholic Church very strongly, and to little purpose I think, as pulling down is not building, for if he considers that Church is constantly changing and therefore wrong,he might say which he does consider to be the true Church, what should be its constitution, and where it is to be found.

He expounded the idea in his last letter but one that because some Catholic countries are not materially prosperous, therefore the Catholic Church is wrong, conveniently ignoring that one of the most prosperous countries of the present day, Belgium, is Catholic. Now he changes his ground and takes up a far weaker position, viz., that because abuses exist.d or are alleged to have existed in monasteries at the time of the Reformation,therefore—the abuses were stopped. Of course if abuses did exist they should have been stopped, and by the authority to whom the monas- teries owned allegiance; but to coelly assert that they were sacked by Rome and its servants, thoit Henry VIII. and Thomas Cromwell were the servants of Rome, well, Mr. Editor, I think you and I know differently, and so do most of your readers. Now if a few policemen went wrong and became thieves, we would not say that the constitutional laws of the country were wrong ; and if so SOLD,' Catholics or a great many either have been bad, it has proved nothing to the detriment of the integrity of the Church. In both cases it is the fault of the individuals. But to hark back to the real question at issue : Conduct of individuals does not matter nor is the teaching of any particular 'Church the point at isaue. What matters is the nature or signs of the true religion established by Christ. I think we all agree that it is only possible for Him to have founded one, and the vital question for all of us is the consequence of having the true faith, serving God as He desires, and thus being on the certain pith to eternal bliss. The religion established by Christ, must have been established to last until the end of time, and coining from Him who is truth itself, must necessarily have been a perfect code of definite, explicit, and compre- hensive tiuths.

He must also have delivered this charge to an authority which He established for delivering His message to mankind, to be preserved intact by that authority and handed on to their successors in that perfection and completeness in which they received it. And so, being Christ's Church, that perfect system of truths has been handed along the centuries and must exist somewhere, and I beg to venture that the Church which preaches these truths should be charac- terised by the following marks : (1). Unity• The Apostles having received their charge firma Christ Himself, knew exactly what they were to deliver and consequently there was perfect, harmony and unity, and so that which is the true Church must know its own mind and teach with a complete unanimity. " (2.) Universality or Catholicity: That alone which has perfect unity can spread and become. universal while retaining its original nature. God would have all men to be Paved and so Ile commanded His servants to "Go and teach all nations." Therefore that Church must be found in all countries.

(3.) Infallibility or certainty of Feing right : The Apostles leceived the charge with certainty and explicitness, and handed it on to their successors as they received It has been likewise passed along, and the Church now delivering the message must be doing so with the same confidence and emphasis as did the Apostles, nay as even Christ did. Now, Mr Editor, tngether with Phil Squod I submit the matter to the judgment of your readers and would ask : are not the marks suggested above what must reasonably be expected to denote that Church which Chi ist instituted, and which is that Church? And in conclusion may I observe that if any Church does not claim those 'narks, it is only a sign that it is without them.— Yours &c., JOHN RICHARDSON. SG, Buttermarket-street, Warrington.

Sir,—Were Phil Squod's desire for truthfulness without supression of fact or misleading statement wholehearted, be would avoid such sinister ambiguity regarding Dr Newman's lecture on Popular Pro- testanism, given previous to his conversion to Catholicism. His isolated quotations from Macaulay are boar misleading and misrepresentative, for although a historian of a purely: Protestant epoch, Macaulay was forced out of justice to give due credit to the Roman Church. Hence he says, "To this day in some countries where negro slavery exists, Popery appears in advantageous contrast to other forms of

div.head: From Reynolds' Newspaper.
div.p: From Reynolds' Newspaper.

Christianity." " How great a part the Roman Catholic ecclesiastics subsequently had in the abolition of villenage we learn from the unexceptional testimony of Sir Thomas Smith, one of the ablest Protestant Counsellors of Elizabeth." "So successfully had the (Roman) Church used her formidable machinery that, before the Reformation came, she had enfranchised almost all the bondsmen in the kingdom except her own; who, to do her justiee, seem to have been very tenderly treated." "There can be no doubt that our forefathers were by far the best governed people in Europe." Statements like these, Mr Editor, are very comprehensive, especially when one reflects on them as being the production of a Protestant age. Further- more the Roman Church continued her utmost to better the condition of the masses by encouraging the oppressed to hand themselves tog,-ther, and showing them how to form guilds and societies, the objects of which were social improvement and protection from oppressors and misfortune, and even to-day the Roman Church continues her good work at which she has never ceased to labour from the earliest days of Christianity. How, then, can the statement that learning was stunted by the Roman Church have any truth in it at all? Surely no learning could he widespread unless opportunities in life were opened to all classes; and the Catholic Church paved the way for the progress of learning by her successful efforts in placing all classes, even to the lowest, in a position to take advantage of the chances offered them. More evidence still that the Roman Church has not been inimical to the popularisation of art or science is manifested by her zeal in encouraging art, by expending vast sums for the prccurement of all that is best iii sculpture, art, Sc. All the best works of the great masters are in her possession,incleed many of the finest productions in the world would never have been accomplished had not the Roman Catholic Church stimulated the love of art by her lavish expenditure. Proofs of what she has done are evident in every European country, and no less in ours wh se smiling valleys are greatly enhanced by adornments placed there by Catholic hands. Still more numerous and more stately would the grandeur be to-day had not Cromwell's vandalism (a period, by the way, of Phil Squod's glorious epoch of Protestantism) effaced so much fine art, and caused so much destruction that necessitates, even in our generation, great expenditure of public money for restoration.—Yours
EUREKA.

div.head: CLASSES AND THE MASSES.
div.p: THE CLASSES AND THE MASSES.

Sir,—ln your last issue you gave a report of a sermon, preached by the Bev B Percival, vicar of St. Peter's Church, and headed as above. Text taken " Let us consider one another." Good! Let us! The spirit of coheiliation, seemingly, is forcing its way to the front, even in our churches. Contrary to two ther local ministers—Dr Mellor and Rev H Ogden— reported in y,.ur columns, the Rev B Percival, after his summing up is left with the dumps. Bad! Let as consider. Great ideals are decaying ; proof— decline in public worship, family prayer, and Bible reading. Are there no great ideals apart from these expressions of Christianity ? The Church has no place to r ffer to-day for an earnest practical individual. I myself was fed on .hristianity up to the age of 25 years then gradually received light not from heaven, hut from the earth. To-day, lam a Social Democrat ie. a proletarian held in servitude because of my economic position, knowing that my emancipation is dependent on that of my class also. What has the Church to offer rue ? "From praying and fasting' we have turned to thinking arid working." The salvation of the workers does not rest on any belief in the saving power of a Son of God, or of God. The material on which we base our hope of salvation is here on earth. It rests in the amazing powers that, we see to-day of producing, the wonderful power of man when applied scientifically to Nature ; this, our inheritance, has grown out of the accumulated labour of past ages, and is the Redeemer of Mankind. The Socialist cognizant of this, urges the masses to grasp the power, already by them, and thereby carry out their emancipation. A privileged class—a minority— stand in the way, hut only so long as the majority remarn ignorant of their power. The Rev. B. Percival; and all his kind, simply apply the aruesthetic, the chloroform, " the opium of the people" religion— and so perpetuate this ignorance. Keeping the masses subdued by fixing their attention on matters transcendental, supernatural, etc.

The decline ie church attendance, Sze., is due to the simple fact that humanity is advancing. "The height of man's superstition is at the same time the depth of his ignorance" "Decay in ideals"— where in heaven or earth or anywhere else is there an ideal as moral, AS reasonable, and as sublime as international social demociacy ? Only from the abolition of class-rule, frirn the transformation of the selfish capitalistic organizations into co-operative instruments of produc- tion will issue the true brotherhood of man, the true morality and justice. In the place of religion we put humanity. Civilized human society is the supreme being in which we believe. In place of a Heavenly Father, Who protects and defends His children, we are striving for a society which shall assist the help- less individual in all his needs.—Faithfully yours. ISAAC SHAW.

div.head: OLD ENGLISH TRADE UNIONS.
div.p: OLD ENGLISH TRADE UNIONS.
LECTURE BY MR. J. DALBY.

Mr Joseph Dalby, M.A.,delivered the first of a course of four fortnightly lectures on " 0:d English Trade Unions" at the Socialist RO3MS, Wilderspool Cause- way, on Monday evening. Mr G Chamberlain presided over a good attendance. The subject of the lecture was the trade guilds of the Middle Ages and Mr Dalby presented a most interest- ing picture of the life of the time. He pointed out that to-day we saw a great clash between the ideals of the people and the economic system in which they lived, but in the best period of the \fiddle Ages the IDEALS AND TILE FACTS OF EVERYDAY LIFE WENT

HAND IN HAND. The one was the expresssion of the other. No historical student could help feeling, toe, how closely bound up with labour religion vies then. We must get out of the way of thinking of the Middle Ages as a dark, gloomy period, a kind of prison house out of which we were delivered by the glorious Reformation. It wits nothing of the sort. How did he know? Partly from reading history but partly too from using his own eyes. He refused to believe that a great Ctthedral like Lincoln Cathedral or the many others scattered over England and the Continent were built by people who were herded to their work es our factory workers were to-day. The very idea was atsurd. Ho wished he could show by the lantern how beautiful and lavish was the work put into a Cathedral then. Parts that did not show were about as c irefully and beautifully done as parts that did The marks in the stonework showed clearly that whole p irtions of the Cathedral were rebuilt 100 or even 50 years after t'aeir list construction. Because they were rotten? By no means. Merely because the architect and the body of his workmen took an absolute delight in working and making a beautiful object. It must be remembered that the masons were organized co-opera- tively as a guild—just those who were working at that particular job. They were set on by the architect and paid by him in wages, but the fact that they were banded together in that way made a difference and he believed they were allowed considerable freedom. Besides the architect was an artist and not a speculative builder. El they wanted a contr ,st, take the Pyramids of Egypt. Servile labour was written on the face of them. Mr. Dalby next touched upon the religion of the time, which he said was not at all Roman in the sense of na, darn Romanism. There was no organised Protest-int Church then. It was better to call it simply Catholic. That religion was definite, and on the whole consistent. What little science they knew they had no difficulty in squaring with their religion. The Church was not a petty religious society such as it is now. It . spread its influence through the whole of life ; educa- tion and poor relief were just functions of the Church. The Chu-ch taught that all men were brothers, ail being equally servants of Clyist. The Guilds supplied that need for brotherhood by little soc'eties of men who could make their brotherhood mean more to them by realising it on a small scale. The guilds, at first entirely religious, came afterwards to have a trade basis. Men found that they could best REALIZE THESIS HUMAN boLIDARITY THROUGH CRAFT

SOLIDARITY Not that they ceased to be religious when they became craft cons3ions. When a guild brother died, a fixed levy was laid on all brethren to pay for Masses to be said for his sc,ul. Each brother had to give alms to th 3 Poor too, on that occasion, that the poor who received Money or bread should in return pray for the departed. Many of the guilds which appeared were simply religious and charitable societies and nothing more. AB of the trade guilds had a religious basis, an! those who had Studied the subject were not agreed as to the extent to which pure craft consciousness and craft interests entered into the mediasval guilds. We should have to be on our guard constantly against imagining the medi:eval guild to be anything like cur modern trade unions. The tires were different. England was hardly the England ot to-dsy. Industry was only just beginning and it wes not true, as it was now, that the great bulk of men were manual to sn workers. Mr Dalby then briefly traced the ri,e of the walk's and pointed out that Speaking generally, the mediwval guild system had three stages—the Merchant Guild, the Craft Guild and the Journeyman Guild. Of these the second—the Craft Guild—was far away the most important. The great London companies—the Fish- mongers, the Goldsmiths and all the other institutions for the fattening of the capitalist, that he might make a tasty dish for the militant workman, were degener- ate survivals of the ancient craft-guide, The earliest of the three —the merchant guild—arose out of the desire of those in any town who possessed land—they Were the majority—to band themselves into a society for the purpose of mutual aid in trading and in order' to protect themselves against the " foreigner.' By the 'foreigner" they meant not only a Frenchman or a Fleming, but anyone from another city. As crafts developed an artisin chase arose, ashi,h procured the goods whose sale ewes arranged by the old privileged citizens of the alerchant Guild now become a little aristocracy. Those artisans were,a3 often as not,free reen,and they determined to strengthen their position in the only way known to Lute men of the benighted Middle Ages—by co-operation forming a Craft Guild. The weavers led the way and all over Western Europe weave's' guilds fought against the old governing bodies. The London weavers and the Oxford weavers were both given their charter )I)3Y King llenry I. Later these valiant craft guilds ecame in their turn tyrannous, but as yet we °lll3l saw th,--m fighting against the monopoly of the Merchant Guildsmen. As late as 126-5 an order of the Merchant Guild of Leicester Prohibited the craftsmen of that town from weaving for the men of other places so long as they had suffi- cient work to do for the burgesses of Leicester. As the craft guildsmen grew stronger, they gained power in government of themselves, borne of them—most-- forbids their members to go to the town court before bringing their case to the brethren. Sometimes there Was a fully constituted guild court. But what were Most interesting was the regulations laid down by the guild as a whole for their work. No work was to be done except by daylight. Woile Candlelight was strictly forbidden. No doubt the primary object of these regulations was the e„nsuring of tne good quality of the wares turned out. r rnat was necessary, if custom was not to be lost, but s„aother element and a very important one entered here. "-tie Guildsmen had a very high sense of the honour of their trade. They were banded together, as their statutes said, for a religious object—the honouring of the Holy Trinity or the Saints—and their religion did Beeill to have affected their trade in a way which most. Seem very strange to the MoDERN COMMERCIAL MAN ,Who did not at all worship Go! or the honour of his 'rade and substituted fa: -the floe old mottoes 9f the guilds the stirring banner " Business IS business.' When we came came to the number of Working days of medise val workmen, we be gan to realise What all our talk of progress amounted to. I he number 0f working days of a workman in Florence Italy) was I:f_as 275 out of the 365. That, of course, was due to kne observance of Holy Days which we now called rlidays. and though some of those present wsuld Vubtless prefer the modern name many would swallow ue old name if they could have the thing With it-90 holy days in the year. Sundays were included, of course. Work always ceased at noon ?i,ll Saturday, and also before special holy days. Ahe London weavers 'might not work betwecn hristrnas and Candlemas (February 2nd) nor the uutters of Hallamshire during the 28 days fol'oesing August Bth of each year and from Christmas to January ""cd- What was exact'y the position of those mediwval Workmen as regarded capital? Tney did not work entirely co-operatively, of course, and yet we c mid 11°t. say they were wage-earners. As a matter of fact, 111?‘0,130 of our modern terms applied to them at all. hen the Guilds were at their best the great majority tf the members were independent master craftsmen, anded together under certain common rules. They !ere paid independently for the work they did, but the :.erY fact of their Guild organization prevented—for a !'lme at least—any eection of them from becoming 7ealthy capitalists. The Guilds degenerated very much tater—end necessarily so—as industry and wealth increased and as there was a greater demand from all Tasses for =lam:Allred goods. The Guilds themselves weecante close corporations. Sons of the Guildsmen admitted without any test or apprenticeship, tb. some trades apprenticeship itself became a log only open to the rich or the well- !_onnected just as in our modern system the manager's l'iuen was rushed through all the various shops, so that ap, might know as much as possible about the 11;;sti'l trade processes before he went on to his _ ster position. All this time, from many causer, the Wicultural workers were pressing into the towns. the:Cgs we gut a class of msn who knew their craft erf,"4°uslily, were good workm, n but outside the Pro euorn of the Guild, servants or journeymen with no sos Pref, of ever becoming independent workmen, free aer_v:gork for whom they pleased. In short, we got a Nev,tie class, as hopelestly cut off from freedom as the si'nern wage slave Having di alt with the rise and Nvetliine of the Journeymen's Guilds, Mr Dalby said we told that competition was a law of life, that srr.an nature was essentially competitive, and we were sus;en to the conclusion either that those who said ithiegs were saying what they knew ayes not true, se that they had read no history. Co-operation I pa.? just as much a law of life as competition— an!, More. Men could he got to substitute the honour thu_ dignity of their calling for a base desire to enrich in elves in a senseless, mad way, and when we read diteval ordinance "that everyone Inuit be pleased ttn'euoalß• work and uo one shall, whale doing nothing, ,;:ds.pritate for himself what others have produced by !lation and work, because laws must be a shield for et'Ae Cation and work," we began to feel what a thing our civilization was and what walithe h°Pei thtal must inspire us in our tremendous task.
