div.head: WOODEN WEDDING,
div.p: A WOODEN WEDDING,
THE GENESIS AND LIFE HISTORY OF TARIFF REFORM.

Mr. Ernest Williams author of "Trade in Germany " relates that: "In the closing days of March (1903) I.was directed by the Editor of the "Financial News " to undertake a vigorous propaganda in that journal on behalf Protection,and I was requested to supplement that journalistic work by getting together an organization formed for the same end. . . A meeting was called. The -meeting did more than discuss; it formed itself straight- way into the Protection League. Not a soul present had aninkling that the very next day Mr Chamberlain was going to light his torch at Birmingham We rose to it by altering the title of our league. Prejudice had gathered round the word Protection, and under the new develop- ment it was no longer well to use a word, however reasonable, which created prejudice We realised that under Mr Chamberlain's leadership a great national movement had begun, and that we had to go out and capture the masses forthwith, and not be content with the suffrages of the chosen few who were already emancipated from prejudice. So our Association became The Tariff League. ,At the next meeting of our committee we changed our title once again, and hence the Imperial Tariff Reform. A Committee of Members of Parliament resolved itself into an organisation which came to the Imperial Tariff League and offered amalgamation. The Imperial Tariff League accepted, and handed over its membership, its effects, and its goodwill to the new men, and so gave birth to the Tariff Reform League."

div.head: WOODEN WEDDING OF
div.p: THE WOODEN WEDDING OF
PROTECTION AND TARIFF REFORM.

Ten years ago there lived an old maiden lady called Protection. She sprang from a family of that name who long years ago were held in honour, but who for their mis- deeds were exiled by statesman who occupied high place in our land, by name Nei, Cobden, Bright, and Gladstone. But as with the Bourbons in France, and the Stuarts in England, there was always a remnant who adhered to this family and its fortunes, and made efforts to restore it to influence and povier. Their efforts were unavailing until ten years ago an inspired statesman back from the veldt and the wars became foster- parent to a youth called Colonial Preference, now generally known as Tariff Reform. This youth was ambitious and strove to attain power. Realizing he could not gain his ends unaided, he devisec: the plan of forming an alliance with some old family,so he wedded the lady mentioned. Miss Protection was nothing loth, and by no means coy; she was getting somewhat the worse for wear, and had made at least two serious attempts to change her name! Moreover Tariff Reform hoped by a union of forces to beit able to secure the support of the populace'. Now while their united forces were naturally greater, some of the youth's adherents objected to the habits, principles, and especially to the name of the lady. It was explained that Miss Protection had surrendered her name, bought a new bonnet with ribbons of blue and merged her identity in that of Fiscal Reform. Nevertheless many of the youth's followers, objected, and when the banns were cried, cursed the proposed union, by bell, book, and candle, and deserted the united standards. They asked" Can a leopard change his spots and be other than aleopard,and can Protection be other than Protection though called Fair Trade, Reciprocity, or Tariff Reform ? " But the worst misfortune to the happiness and ambitions of the allied pair was when those who remained loyal began scrapping among themselves. The adherents of the lady con- tended that while they were willing to change their name even seventy times seven if desired, they were not going to change their principles or their methods. Among these were "Make the foreigner Pay," "Find two jobs for every man," "Make everything dearer for him who sells, and everything cheaper for him who buys "and the like. Now since the followers of the lady' were much more numerous, self-interested, and self-assertive, than those of the young man they soon gained ascendancy, and have now made it clear that while they are quite willing to secure all the credit they could get from the name and character of the youth, it was Protection they were out for and Pro- tection they will have or have nothing. They are not therefore a very happy family, as you can imagine. Unfortunately at the time of writing there are great differences in the rival sections, and even• among the sections themselves there is heard the clash of spears. Part of the Protection section is made up of those who till the earth that it may produce bread for all, but the larger part is composed of. those engaged in making by machings, raiment and other necessary things for the comfort of life, but who are consumers of the equally necessary food products of the soil. Now while such are quite ready to believe the foreigner can be made to pay in the matter of manufactured articles,they have doubts about their ability to make him pay the taxes on the foodstuffs they buy. Hence a lively quarrel has arisen and whether peace will be restored time only will reveal. Still the union has lasted ten years and Fiscal Reform and Protection are about to celebrate their Wooden Wedding. We consider the pair ill-matched, but we are against divorce unless there is grave cause, and we trust these twain will be able to patch their differences, enjoy their celebra- lon, and live happily ever after. .
C.E.P.

div.head: 'ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
div.p: 'ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
THE CURIOUS CASE OF "SALLY WATERS."

We made the acquaintance of Sally Waters very early in life. She was the kind lady who gave us our first good excuse for kissing desirable members of the other sex, and we worried not the least about her identity. Nor did we,when the giddy days of kissing- rings were over, suspect,that interest would ever awaken or that Sally would ever give us a moment's anxiety. But the unexpected has happened. Sally turns out to be an interesting and most elusive individual, and years of desultory thinking have only revealed enough to make her more and more attractive. Let the reader scan the following disjointed hints and see whether he too does not feel the haunting power of Sally Waters. First let us take a look at Sally as we made her acquaintance in Warrington in the Long ago Come Sally Sally Waters Come springing in a pan, Now do you like water Just for a young man, Come pick one, come choose one, Come pick the very best Now those two's got married I hope they will enjoy A son and a daughter A kiss and a smile. If this were the only version of the Sally Waters song we might give it up at once as meaningless, but happily there at least fifty others, all different in their details, yet all, in their chief features, the same. One that probably preserves best the original features is sung by the children in Dorset. Sally, Sally Waters, sprinkle in a pan, Rise, Saily ; rise Sally and choose a ycung man; Choose for the best, choose for the worst, Choose the pretty girl (or boy) that you love best. And now you're married we wish you j ty, First a girl and then a boy ; Seven years after son and daughter, And now young people, jump over the water. All the country over children play the marriage game of Sally Waters. The boy or girl in the centre of the ring choosing a partner from the rest (we mention the procedure for the benefit of uninitiated if such there can possibly be) the choice being sealed by joining hands or kneeling on a handker- chief or with a kiss. Older people will hardly be prepared for the suggestion that children's games make material for serious study.' But it _must be remembered that usages which now belong only to the playground were once sober occupations. Dances for instance were at one time very serious proceedings.Ogr forefathers undertook them as a means of warding off evil spirits, of securing the growth of their crops, and the banishment of disease. At fixed seasons, such as the spring time, they danced to an accompaniment of suitable rhymes andiactions, calling upon the sun and rain to do their work. At weddings they danced to the happiness and fertility of the marriage,and gave copious loses of sprinkling and incantations to the bride and bridegroom. Scores of old rhymes for the use of farmer, doctor, wife, and indeed for everybody, crop up among the clay books of Babylon and Assyria dating centuries before the Christian era, some of which in their substance and almost in their very form are in use among the children of to-day. The first Christian missionaries to our shores had to condemn and forbid the "carols",a word that then stood for the dances of our rough ancestors. This much being demonstrated it is very interesting to raise the enquiry whether we have not in the " sprinkling " of the Sally Waters rhyme, and in the pious wishes for a son and a daughter a relic of a marriage "carol "and whether this scrap of verse may not belong to a very remote past. Certainly its allusions could not have been invented by children. None save the antiquarian can guess at the meaning of "sprinkling a pan," and references to a seven year marriage and coming out of water if they mean what they seem to mean carry us far before the dawn of Christian teaching. Let us analyse the expressions used in 'Sally Waters." In forty-four out of fifty versions that hav e been collected there is a mention of Sally. She is Sally Walker in _

Shropshire, Yorkshire and SCotland, Sally Salter in Lincoln, elsewhere she is Sally Sanders and in Liverpool Polly Sanders. Obviously Sally Waters is the original name. Examining the versions with a view to obtaining a clue to the meaning we are struck with the fact that the best versions of the song—indeed the only ones that suggest any meaning—belong to Somerset, Devonshire and Dorsetshire. Here in all probability we shall find the original home of the song. Let us put alongside of this the fact that the famous waters of Bath were the "Aquae Solis" of the Romans, or the Solis Waters of the Britons. The word solis stood,not for the sun,a male deity, but for Sul, the presiding female deity of the bath. The Roman temple built there was dedicated to the goddess Sulis-Minerva and the name Sul can be still seen among the inscriptions as well as on an altar in the form Sulevw. Possibly the Sulevw were the attendant sylphs of Sul, who in Roman lore were the tulelary divinities of rivers, fountains or roads. It is well known that the Romans gave the name Sulis to a similar spring in Brittany, famous for its healing qualities and to this day can be seen the enormous stone basin in which the pilgrims dipped. Both in France and in Britain in Roman times there were " Sulis waters," and the fact that our song appears to come from the neighbourhood of Bath is very sugges- tive as a clue to "Sally Waters," but beyond this we cannot go. And now let us examine the wording. The song is obviously a marriage song and we shall derive our best help in a study of ancient marriage usages. Sally is first urged to sprinkle the pan. This comes before the invitation to choose a young man, and as it occurs in thirty -three out of fifty versions it may be regarded as part of the original. Let us see it as it stands in the version used in Buckinghamshire. Chorus : Sally, Sally Waters sprinkled in the pan What did she sprinkle for ? For a young man. Girl's Mother: 6priukle, Sprinkle daughter and you shall have a cow. Girl: I cannot sprinkle mother, because I don't know how. Mother: Sprinkle, daughter, sprinkle, and you shall have a man. Girl : I cannot sprinkle mother, but I'll do the best I can. Chorus : Pick one, choose one, but don't pick me. Pick the fairest you can see. Girl : Ihe fairest I can see is . . . . Come to- me. Chorus: Now these two are married, etc. In this form of the game some one impersonates the girl's mother and urges her to sprinkle, promising that she shall have a

div.head: e cow and a-husband runs as follows :
div.p: e cow and a-husband runs as follows :

Whittle daughter, whistle, whistle for a cradle, I cannot whistle, mammy, 'dt ed I am not able. Whistle daughter, whistle, whistle for a cow I cannot whistle, mamtny 'deed I know not how. Whistle daughter, whistle, whistlelQk a man, I cannot whistle, mammy ; whew! Yes, I believe I can.
The old meaning of" whistle " is to utter magical or imprecatorary words in a low voice, a practice associated with witchcraft and regarded as uncanny in a woman. This is the meaning of,

A whi•tling woman and a crowing hen Are neither fit for God or man. Sprinkling the pan therefore was something that showed a woman to be fit for marriage. What the sprinkling was we have not yet guessed. Sally Waters rs next advised to make her choice of a young man, to "choose east and choose west" as some versions have it, or as in most of them to "choose for the best and choose for the worst," a phrase curiously like the " for better or worse" of the marriage service. ' _

_ . Next comes the wish for " first a girl and then a boy "with the curious addition "seven years after son and daughter." Here we touch something of decided interest. In sixteen of the versions it is definitely given that the marriage is for seven years. In another marriage game popularly known as" Pretty little girl of mine," this is also stated, and it occurs in "The Lady of the Mountain" also. We are far back indeed when touching a period in which marriage ties were but of seven years duration. It is a period indeed upon which there is but little light to be obtained, but we shall perhaps be safe if we assume the meaning to be that unless a son and daughter had been born within the term the marriage would be broken off.
--- Those who kn ow the remote country dis- - -

tricts will know that the seven years limit still lingers in tradition. A woman whose husband has left her assumes him to be dead after a period of seven years and asks that the bell be tolled for him. And we shall hardly need to tell our readers that among country folks marriage is popularly regarded as incomplete until there is the "son and the daughter." The last line whilst the most puzzling has perhaps the greatest interest of all. - In the Dorsetsh ire version quoted it reads. And now young people, jump over the water. Somerset has it Kif a each other and come out of the water. Shropshire says, Kiss, shake hands and come out of the water. And London children sing, Kiss bef,re you go out of the water.

The last versions appear to be the true ones. Dipping was a common ceremonial in heathen times and was used for various objects. It was a test, for instance, of witch- craft. May not the dipping have been an accompaniment of the heathen marriage ceremonial? _
Kiss and come out of the water" is very suggestive of a dipping process. And is there not a hint of the same thing

in the Cornish saying "The first of May is dipping day," a phrase which has survived in spite of fact that it has been meaningless for centuries. The first of May was the great season for making marriages in the far-off past and would be the "dipping day " for new married couples._ Curiously enough a cere- mony of dipping—merely a piece of horse- play in modern times—has been practised in many places as a May-day usage. In North- ampton, for instance, it was a piece of May- day gaiety until very recent years. The only clue to the meaning of "dipping" is in the Sally Waters verse. And we think we have suggested the correct one. Did they dip the bride and bridegroom in the Salis Waters at Bath? And was the original version of the song" Come to Salis Waters ? " This is an interesting question, but we do not suppose it will ever be answered. The kneeling down upon a handkerchief opens up another long train for inquiry, for it connects " Sally Waters" with the old Cushion Dance. Let those who are interested glean particulars of the old game. They will come to the conclusion that it is first cousin to the marriage game of Sally Waters. Perhaps we have written enough to prove our point that Sally Waters is a bewitching lady. Her reference to seven-year marriages and wedding-day dipping proclaim her a heathen,but she is none theless attractive for that. She is a little pagan waif from a dim, and uncanny misty past. Do some of our great families boast that they were here before the Conqueror? That is nothing to Sally. She was here before the Missionaries. A. M.

Report of the 201 th quarterly district meeting was held on Saturday at the Blue Lion Hotel, Market Place. Bro T Roden, D.C.R., was in the chair and Bro R B Healey, occupied the vice-chair. The various courts were represented by the following brethren : Court 138, Bros W Hipkiss and W Roylitrice •, eourt 240, Bros J Davies and G W R Baines; Court 43/0, Bros Councillor J Chrimes, W James and F. Clayton; Court 431, Bros H Perdue and W Lightfoot; Court 491, Bro J Gatley ; Court 475, Bros T Hollins and E Hollins ; Court 9335, Bros A Tilling and GI Maybury. The District Secretary read a lett.er of apology from the District Treasurer (Councillor Bro Peter Peacock), who , regretted it was impossible for him to attend. Bro J ' Walsh (senior district trustee), was thereupon asked to kindly officiate in his stead for the day. The cash account was then tal,en which showed a further considerable inc:ease in the cistria funds and was finally approved. The return of new members was submitted and as was the case last quarter, the number was too large to deal with at that meeting and it was decided to accept the return as written by the district secretory. Various matters of importance to the district were then dis- cussed, and all points which could not be settled that day, were relegated to the Advisory Committeo to arrange before the next district meeting. A very pleasing ceremony then took place in the form of a presentation to P.D.J.R. Bro. G. W. R. Baines, of a handsome framed emblem. Councillor Bro. J. Chrirnes in making the presentation spoke in high terms of the splendid work which Bro. div.head: IS FEMINISM GAINING GROUND?
div.p: IS FEMINISM GAINING GROUND?

For the last quarter of a century there has been a majority in the House of Commons in favour of Women's Suffrage, but women have never had the leverage necessary to turn academic sympathy into anything more practical. They have not been able to get the vote for the simple reason that they have not got the vote to get it with. Nevertheless, though the vote is a necessary link in the chain of the feminiitic movement, its absence has not prevented the forging of other links. The general move- ment is gaining ground; barriers are falling fast. Women have the municipal franchise; they can be guardians. councillors, mayors; they can have a good education and take degrees. They can be doctors. The age of protection for girls, though still culpably low, has been raised. A recent Divorce Commission declared in favour of equality of treatment between men and women. There are signs, above all, that the double moral standard may go by the board. All these changes have come about well within the memory of man. The difference between the pogition of women to-day and those of 100 or even 50 years ago, is stupendous. In 1813 Mrs Elizabeth Fry catne out into the world to champion the cause of waifs and strays in prison, and was considered an unwomanly woman for not finding all the interest she needed in the four walls of her own home. To-day she is one of the most honoured of her sex. A howl of derision met Miss Florence Nightingale, when it was announced that she was going to the Crimea to nurse her fellow men, without a chaperon. It was improper. She was a husband-hunter, and that was all about it. To-day her name is treated with peculiar reverence. The whirlgig of time brings in its revenges, though sometimes too late to be useful. An elderly lady once told me that she remembered the time when Josephine Butler was considered a woman not fit to be spoken of. She was ostracised by a certain section of society. She went about the country in danger of her life. Her husband brought up the question to which she devoted the best years of her life at a meeting of Church of England clergy. He was howled down. The public opinion of that day considered it a more grievous wrong to speak of existing evils with a view to removing them than to acquiesce in them by silence. What was not too bad for a young child to be allowed to suffer, it was considered too bad for a grown woman to know, or for a serious man to speak of. The feminist movement has done one thing: it has dealt a crushing blow to prudery and hypocrisy. To-day in the Lady Chapel of the Liverpool Cathedral there is a window in which appears the likeness of Josephine Butler, with the legend : "To Josephine Butler and all brave champions of purity." Lately the assembled clergy of the Church of England passed a resolution in favour of the White Slave Traffic Bill. Upon these questions public opinion is expressing itself unequivocally. Why? Because women throughout the country have preached from street corners the doctrine of moral equality, and the right of women and chilO.ren to the protection of our laws. This is not the vain dream of one steeped in the Suffrage movement. It is a dream of Mr. Alexander Coote, who has devoted his life to combating the social evil. He was asked to what he attributed the wave of popular feeling which moved the House of Commons to pass the White Slave Traffic Bill, and answered that he considered it due to the agitation of women, especially of the Suffrage women. He also declared publicly that he considered that Women's Suffrage would mean the solution of the moral question. The importance of Women's Suffrage becomes apparent in view of such considera- tions. We are on the eve of another great trial of strength. The Reform Bill goes into Committee next week. It is to give every man of 21 a vote. Not a single woman is included as it stands. A clause in favour of granting some women the vote may be embodied in it through the amendments. Surely our fellow countrymen can never again talk of a British sense of justice unless some such amendment succeeds. The three

SOME USEFUL TREES. I know that boys and girls like to read about wonderful things, and I thought they might like to know a little about some remarkable trees. Of course we have fine trees in England,trees that are big strong and beautiful. And we have very useful trees also, but not trees which are wonderful in the way that some tropical trees are. Take first the case of the bread-fruit of Ceylon, a remarkable tree. The fruit is baked and eaten by the natives as we eat bread, and is equally good and nutritious. In Barbatu, , South America, is a tree which by piercing the trunk produces milk, with which the inhabitants feed their children. In the interior of Africa is a tree which produces excellent butter. It is said to resemble the American oak, and its fruit, from which the butter is prepared, is not unlike the olive. Mungo Park, the great traveller, declared that the butter surpassed any made in England from cow's milk. Sierra Leone has a tree which produces cream fruit, which is agreeable to the taste. At Table Bay, near the Cape of Good Hope, is a small tree, the berries of which make useful candles. It is also found in the Azores. The vegetable tallow tree also grows in Sumatra. In the island of Chusan large quantities of oil and tallow are extracted from its fruit, which is gathered in November or December,when the tree has lost its leaves. The weeping tree of the Canary Islands is a kind of arboreal freak. This tree in the driest weather will rain down showers from its leaves and the natives gather up the water from the pool formed at the foot of the trunk and find it pure and fresh. The tree exudes water from innumerable pores situated at the base of the leaves. There is another very wonderful tree about which I will write a few lines next week. It is perhaps the most useful tree of all. Now I wonder who can guess before- hand which tree I am about to describe.

WHEN SHE WENT OUT TO TEA. My little girl, I hope you tried Your very best to be; Quite ladylike and well behaved, When you were out to tea; "And that you said, Yes, if you please,' When things were offered you; Or, No, I thank you,' quietly, Just as I told you to.' "Well, mamma dear, I smiled and said Yes, thank you,' so polite, And, 'if you please,' and sat up straight, And always acted right. "I didn't say. 'No, thank you,' though Because, mamma, you see, I wanted all they helped me to, When I went out to tea." THIS WEEK'S STORY,

Sir Ernest Shackleton at the luncheon in his honour given by the Pilgrims in New York was talking about a piece of geographi- cal ignorance: "It was incredible. It reminded me of a little waiting- maid. "As she brought me my tea and toast and bloater one morning I said to her: "'What a rainy morning, Mary! It's almost like the Flood.' . "'The Flood, sir? said the little maid. She looked at me with a puzzled smile. "'Yes,' said I. The Flood —Noah, you know—the Ark—Mount Ararat.' "She shook her head, and murmured apologetically. "'I ain't had no time to read the paper lately, sir.'"

Opal aid Dark Sindes.—Paacock colon:legs and embroideries Lave slowly made a place fc,r thmmelves in fabrics to be used for evening dresses in the early spring. Many of the newest shoes are of these shades. to match dresses. Dark shades, especially in combina- ti )ns of moire and velvet, are quite a feature of this year's evening dresses,possibly the prevalence of black, accounts for this tendency. Opal tints, which are mc at delicate and pale, an.' quite a contrast to the dark tons are in high favour also. The New Stumped Nets.—A new material, intended to replace beaded end sequined nets, has a pattern stamped on it to simulate beads and sequins. This it does so well that is close examination is necessary to distinguish between the real and the imitation. One great drawkack to the heads, in this connection, is -their weight, which renders a somewhat heavy net a necessity and another is their tendency to tear on the slightest provocation. These drawbacks are obviated in the new nets, which are very line, and as they are with- out beads, very light in weight. Scarves for summer wear are being extensively manufactured of this charm- ing fabric, and as it bids fair to have a vogue, it will doubtless t e put to other uses as Spring ndvatc?.s. A New Jabot.—A quite novel jabot is really a small laced-edged fichu, worn close to the throat where it is crossed under the chin tind 'tied with a ribbon bow. Made with good old lace, it is particularly effective, for it is a copy of that worn by a noble lord who flourished in later Tudor times, before machine made lace had come into use. Although the weather, so far has been unusually mild, fun have been worn quite so much as in the coldest easons, and many pretty and new models for neckwear, have been introduced. Among others is a deep collar that falls in long points on the shoulders. This also is a copy of a 15t'4 century fashion. A collarette of fur, shaped like an Eton collar, and tied with cords and tassels is another novelty.

Fashionable Coiffures.--The hair is still worn flat and !close to tho head, which makes it eezessary to study the hair and hat together, for much care is required in this connection. Coiffei,rs made every effort to start the New Year with Pompadour modes but So far with- out succes9, and 83 all the now straw hats are close fitting there will he no change in present styles. Hair- dressers introduce new styles to suit mature faces, and girls adopt these to suit themselves. Ornaments are worn on evening coiffures low down on the forehead. Sometimes these take the form of a pear-shaped pearl, which falls from the centre of an ornament of the Regency period. A soft Curl under the pearl has a becoming and s dtening effect. The 'ram-o'-Shanter flat.—Any doubts that may have been entertained as to the popularity of the small hat when it was first introduced must have long since been laid to rest. Its ro3ition in the world of millinery. is assured. It is worn by everybody and adapts itself especially to fur which this season is most artistically manipulated in combination with tinsel brocade, or woollen embroidery in Indian patterns. The Tams have large soft crowns which can be altered to suit any ,type of face, and have been so improved since these 'were first introduced that they n:ay be described as universally becoming, and this fact must be generally recognised since they are ES popular for morning wear as well as later in the day.

forms of town vegetation. Ash trees in the purer parts of Leeds often retain their leaves six weel s longer than those in the more contaminated di-Aticts. Thus, on September 18th of last year, in IluLslet, with suspended matter 1,5651b5., and acidity 901bs. per acre, all the ash trees which were alive, were found to have shed their leaves, while at Roundhay, with suspended matter 901bs. per acre, and acidity cii, practically all the ash trees were in full leaf at the beginning of November. This year, in the more polluted parts of Leeds, many of the leaves of ash, sycamore, birch, beech, ribies, oaks and plane trees were showing signs of smoke damage before the end of May. If, therefore, we look upon the leaf as the fact-ry of the plant, we find that, owing to smoke pollution, the factory is ac.ually closed for six weeks out of the four or five months of its working year, while during the remainder of the time, as our assimilition experiments show, it will be working at less than half its normal pressure. The tree automatically keeps a record of its yearly growth, and the presence of any inhibiting factor will make it-elf known hy the narrowing of the annual rings. This is well shown in the case of the sectim of the Sco eh fir. The tree in question was grown at Broxburn, where shale retorts were opened in 1893. Coineiden- with this, as can be seen by counting back the number of rings, is a sharply defined check in the yearly growth.

The presence of smoke contamination is wanly made manifest by an increase lisulphur content in the leaves of trees. In the case of leaves or the same ago and frcm the slime plant, collected from localities where he ainoutt of smoke pollut:on has been previously determined, a striking correlation is cbserved l'etween the percentage of sulphur present in the dry matter of the leaves, and the annual deposit of oxides cf sulphur as previously determined. Oct. 14 Sept 18 Oct. 11. 215 ... 6.61 ... 181 ... 322 will not grow Woodhouse Moor 131 ... 288 ... 149 ... 199 ... 324 Weetwood Lane Ribstone Park It would appear, therefore, that in the more smoke infested areas, rot only is there an increased deposit of sulphur compounds with the spot upon the sui face of the leaves, but that there is also an increa-ed intake of sulphur dioxide, probably through the stomata' openings. Now sulphur di aide is a powerful germicide ; it will kill (if bactelia good and bad ; it is absolutely anathema to the enzymes which play so important a part in the growth of both animal and vegetable matter ; and so will tend very con- siderably to lower, the stamina and vitality of both plants and animals. It is this sulphur dioxide which gives to town fog is acrid and irritating effects, and in contact w ith air and moisture it passes rapidly into sulphuric acid. This acid is a strongly corrosive substance. It attecks mortar fabrics and metal work, and is highly injur'ous to vegetation. With the object of ascertaining the effect of free acid on plants, Tiniothy grass was sewn on May 12th, 1908, in a series of boxes 1 foot equate, filled in each case with 861 from the same field. These were watered at rates correspcnding to the average rainfall of 25 inches with Garforth rain water neutralised, Leeds rain water (the acidity of which varied from part to occasionally during fog as much as 10 par's per :00,000), and also with waters containing 1,2, 4, p, 16 ar d 32 parts per 100 000. In the case of Leeds rain water, and of those waters containing the higher degrees of acidity, germination was distinctly checked, aid the delica'e green of the young grasses quickly changed to a yalow or brown. The grasses watered with water whose acidity was 32 parts per 100,000 were killed cff in little more than three months ; and not a trace of vegetation of any kind was visible in the following spring; while the water whose acidity was 16 parts per 100,000 proved fatal in less than a year. It was also shown that while the final ffect of acidity was to destroy vegetation altogether, smaller amounts had the Effect of reducing both the quantity and tho quality of the herbage. Thus in every case a larger amcunt of acidity meant a decreased yield, an increased fibre content, indicating that the grasses were indigestible ; and a decreased protein content, indicating a low feeding value. The effect of the acidity in the soil itself was shown roost markedly in the reduction in the number and activity of the soil bacteria, of which the most valuable and at the sauce time the reo-t sensitive ale the nutrifjing rganisms. The following table, giving aftr three years, the yield on dry matter of grass and the number of bacteria per gram ef the soil, shows what powerful factors bacteria are in infleencing the fertility of the soil, and also suggests still another way in which smoke pollution may damage vegetation. The results, so far as they are to hand, prove conclusively that smoke pollution does actually and definitely exert a very prejudicial influence upon garden crops. Health-Week Campaign.—A national health wee 77 programme is to be organised on a more extensive scale than last year. The experiment will be repeated In April, and it is hoped to enlist the co-operation of all the municipalities and social welfare organisations In England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales. The campaign so far as Trelaud i 3 concerned, is to be undertaken by the Womens'Nat ional Health Association; of which Lady Aberdeen is the head. The main object of the campaign is to raise the social well-being of the people, and to interest the poorer classes in improved methods of living. To lectures)sermons, and leaflets will be added cinematograph displays dealing with two aspects of the movement,—public health and personel health gees- tions. There will also be a series of Mothereraft Competitions, on a large scale and instruction to parents in the upbringing of children, so that a healthy race may be fostered. The Agenda Club is rendering a distinct national service by the organisation of this campaign, in which it is hoped that medical officers of health, sanitary inspectors, doctors, nurses, the- clergy, and representative bodies, will all help. The sinews of war are being largely provided by the Life Insur- ance Companies who have a ssecial interest in improv- ing the health of the community at large. The Wife's Allowance.—The economists have laid down certain rules respecting the relation of rent to income, and a learned judge, the other day, carried this principle farther, and said that a mite's alloeance for dress should not exceed the rent of her home. Most women wculd be plessee if the annual budgeting allowed half as much. House rent should not be more than one-sixth, to one-tenth, of the family income, according to the number of people who have to be fed, clothed and educated, but in the average middle class home, the wife has to do with considersbly less than this proportion for her own attire. If the family grows, and expenses increase, it is she who has to "do without." The husband must keep up appearances, for the sake of his husineret, er position, end most women have to manage on a smalltr float cial margin, than the husband, father, or brother. That is why they tumble, over one another to secure a bargain at the sales, pro- ceedings which the lordly man, with his better-lined pocket, is apt to regard as evidence of feminine small- mindedness. Poyal Playwrights.—Many years ago, King Nicholas of Montenegro wrote a flay entitled the "Empress of the Balkans" which was produzed with some success in Germany. He is not the only monarch of to day to figure as a playwright. The Emperor of Austria and the Emperor of Germany are both Royal dramati as, as is also "'Carmen Sylva," the Queen of Roumania, who is eminent as an author, poet, painter, musician and writer of popular plays. There is some talk of producing King Nicholas's play in London, and its title recalls the fact that there is living in the Metropolis a lady who claims to be "Empress of the .E.sean Isles." he is the widow of a Colonel in the British Army, end declares that she is the direct and only surviving descendant of the former rulers of the iEgean Islands, before they passed into pessession of the Turks. She submitted her view of the matter to the Peace Confer- enee, at St. James's Palace, and claims that the release of the Islands from the Turkish Empire will revive her sovereign rights. Sale Hints.—At this time of year the woman with a frugal mind makes a point of going thraugh her ward- robe, and deciding what she requires, before she begins her campaign on tbe shops. At sale time it is often wise to avoid big things, nicre especially if made in a fashion that has been prevalent for some time, as they may be hopelessly out of date when required to be worn some months hence. Little things generally pay to buy in advance, and it is surprising how a sash, a belt, a flower, some good lace, or even contrasting hose and shoes, will transform au evening dress that, may seem incapable of alteration. A fresh set of buttons, or a new jabot work Wonders, when put on; or worn with a suit or coat that have seen their best days, Some good fur, when deftly arranged, will lengthen the life of a 4sif-worn theatre or evening gown, and all these things

Evergreens sufftr most in this respect, because thy have also the winter smoke to contend with ; of the evergreens the most susceptible owing to thdr characteristic sunk stomata are the conifeis. Conifers • planted in Bunslet, with a total deposit of suspended matter equal to 1,565 pounds per acre per annum, I have seen completely kill, d off by smoke pollution in less than three months. Some time° years ago more than twenty conifers were p'anted in the grounds of the Leeds University, where the annual deposit of suspended matter amounts to roughly 400 pounds pr acre. At the present time not one of them is alive. The enly two localities in Leeds in which conifers attain even moderlte growth are th 09.3 a-ound the two stations, liounchay and Weetweod-lace, which stand out clearly as possessing the least smoke- polluted atmospheres. If the plant obtains the greater part of the material of which it is composed from the air, through the assimilation of .carbon dioxide, the measurement of that asAmilation, by a unit area of leaf in unit time, should give its measurement of effective growth. It was interesting, therefure, to compare this assimila- tion in the case of laurel leaves of the current year's growth, grown in different parts of Leeds. Taking those grown in Westwood-lane as the standard, it was found that on the same day, with the same temperu- ture, and the same intensity of light, the assimilation of different leaves from the same locality will vary day by day, depending upon the temperature and intensity of light • in other words, the cloud of soot and smoke continually hanging over an industrial area will have, in this respect, a very marked influence in limit- ing the growth of pl u ts. If, again, the as-imila- tion of leaves grown in the Westwood-lane is compared on the same day with that in some more impure district, it is always found that the, leaves from the purer district possess the greater power of assimilating early n dioxide. The points, therefore that I wish especially to emphasize are : _

I. That it is possible to get a measure not only of the amount of smoke pollution, but also a measure of its effective damage to vegetation. 11. That the factors in smoke pollution which prejudicially affect vegetation are : (a) The smoke cloud limiting the available sunlight. (b) The tarry matter coating over the leaves and choking the stomata. (c) The presence of free acids in the pair,

principally the sulphur acids, tending generally to lower the vitality of the plant. (d) The effect of the free acids, falling upon the soil, and limiting the activity of the soil organisms, prircipally the nitrifyikg organisms, The last factor can very effectively be dealt with by a simple application of lime, whilst the first two can only be met by checking the output of smoke, and using every effort to lessen the air pollution which is the ruin of many of our crops. A. G. RUSTON, 8.A... B.Sc.,

I did not bear Mr Champion in the Patten hail on Monday, and I do not know what line he took. I cannot, however, imagine an illustrated lecture on this subject without abundant reference to the work of the Keartcris, and I suppose Mr Champion would have not a little to say about the amazing success of those most ingenious and successful photographers. No doubt he would at the same time be able to tell of amateurs who have done wonders in the same line. I have the pleasure of knowing two or three such. Foremost among these I put Mr Bradley, who has for many yea's had charge of the school at Stanbury, a little village in the Bronte country, situate, in fact, on the very outskirts of Haworth itself. A great authority on the Brontes, Mr Bradley is more widely known as :a keen nature student who has somehow managed to make most of his scholars almost as enthusiastic nature lovers as himself. When not actually engaged at the school, or acting as guide, philosopher, and friend to visitors to the Bronte shrine, Mr Bradley generally rambles over the moors in the company of kindred spirits from regions beyond, or ensconses himself in some wood with his camera and patiently awaits opportunities for ran) snapshots illustrative of wild bird life. The last time I had a chat with him I found he had accomplished some really extraordinary feats of this character, and some of the lantern slides he has secured in this way would favourably compare with any of the Keartons in the fume line—and higher praise it were surely impossible to bestow. The reproducticn of the local younWsters Christmas essays a we,k ago reminded me of another set that lately came under my notice. In this instance the children were required to describe an outbreak of fire, and many of them did their best to be graphic. Here are two or three samples :—" The firemen rushed upstairs with great angelity and velocity." " The policeman telephor;ed as hard as ever he could." "The fire engine was seen dashing along full of pride and proudnes3." "The i uffing of the engiLes and the shouting of the people fair thffenctl. you." CONCERNING SPELLING.

" Deffened" is good, but " angenility " is better. Tho other week I herrd a University don declare that it did not matter twopence how a writer spelled a word so long as every no knew what the word was. I recollict Sir James Donaldson insisting that all should be allowed to spell as they like, "ju t as Shakspere did, and just as our ancestors did." Of a number of intelligent boys tested as ready for situa- tions with commercial firms only one could spell " prejudicial" and only one could spell" responsi- bility." No doubt these would be ready to vote Sir James Donaldson a brick or a trump. There is a way out of the difficulty which may serve the ordinary correspondent wh3 is uncettain in this regard. I may illustrate it by reference to a very ancient story. An old lady, as she sat writing letters, drew a line under a word and said : "You know, my dear, when I don't know how to spell a word I underline it like this. Then, if it is spelled wrong it passes for a good joke, and if it is spelltd right it doesn't matter." I am acquakted with at least cne lady who wtites le ttets accorCing to that plan.

THE SANATORIUM QUESTION. On a previous occasion I have urged that the responsible authorities ought to move cautiously in view of the vast expenditure which the provision of sanatoria for the treatment of consumption will certainly involve. There i 3 somewhat widespread misapprehension respecting this undoubtedly great scourge whicii one wontl fain do something to dispel. It is true that so lately as 1907 vital statistics showed that the land was Lterally decimated by consumption. Pulmonary disease of the lungs alone.claimed upwards of 50,000 victims per annum ; and, as the dread malady attacks various parts of the body, there is no reason to suppose that the estimate that half a million people in the kingdom are at present suffering :from some form of tuberculosis is exaggerated. An eminent doctor has des- cribed it as a vicious by-product of an incomplete and ill-informed civilisatioe. It is well then that we should have one National Association for the Pre- vention of Consumption to compare notes year by year and pub'ish the results broadcast ; also one Departmental Committee and other organizations for the acquisition of facts and figures, the conpilation of reliable data, and the spreading of information as to the precautions to be taken against so formidable an enemy of the race. Let it be cheerfully granted that all this is to the good, and deserving of the utmost encouragement and support. Assuredly most of us would go further and heartily commend the experi- ments which are bring made in the way of open-air treatment of consump'ion. At the same time those who have had ample opportunity of observing the methods followed at the sanatoria, nnd are as yet far from satisfied with the results, may at least be excused if they decline personally to favour the multiplication of these costly institutions forthwith. My own opinion based on info:mation derived from sources that, are beyond question, is that the powers that be ought to confine their operations to existing establishments until this important branch of medical science has advanced far beyond attainments to date. When there is no longer any doubt as to the efficacy of sanatorium treatment along the lines indicated, none would be likely to hesitate about oenerou.s expenditure of public money thereupon : but nothing like that standard has yet been reached, and in this matter our representatives should be content to " hasten slowly." The foregoing was suggested by what appeared in the minutes of the Ileal,ll Committee published in the last issue of the " Examiner," and there was one other item of the report of that same meeting of the Town Council respecting which, being myself a regular and persistent and unrep3ntant anonymous writer, I must le allowed a few words. I refer to the tremendous fuss made Ly some members because a typewritt.-n circu'ar, signed "A Ratepaper " had bee n addressed to them. Were the contents of this formidable document rea'ly " scurrilous " and " dis- graceful," and was the act of the sender" dastardly'? Was the writer justified in preserving anonymity ? The answer to this final question depends, of course, upon the true answer ti the otl:er. Let us consider the subject as a whole—generally on its merit, that is, apait from this rather pitiful local instance. THE COWARD'S REFUGE.

The pulpit has bcat cynically &Eel ibcd as "Cowards Castle," but I think the term might be more appropriately applled to the position taken by a malicious writer who is "willing to wound " and not "afraid to strike "so long as be can bide his identity behind a noun de perm. This will illustrate what I mean:

" An act most despicable," said The little lady, and Before I'd do a deed like that I'd cut off my right hand." "11l write and tell her what I think," She said in tearful voice ; And in her pluck her faithful friends Most loudly Wd iejoice. "j will, I will," she then declared; " You'll see that I am game" She stra;ghtway wrote the letter—but She did not sign tar name

As a Wesleyen minister of my acquaintance observed only the other day, anonymous letters, unfortunately, usually have a bad odour about them. They often leave a bad taste in the multi], and that is because they are used for attacks or insinuation which is meant to wound or distress. Such let!ers are a coward's refuge and have well-deserved scorn. A candid criticism, where a man signs his name, no one needs to fear, but a stab in the dark is the weapon of a low-born sneak, xs ho has no claim to the title of a man, let alone a Christian. What I deny is that this can be fairly applied to the average anonymous letter appearing in the correspond- ence columns cf this and other respectable newspapers. Suppose two " Examiner " readers engage in controversy through this medium One of them may for perfectly good and sufficient reasons prefer to withhold his name from publication. But if the other, writing over his own name, happens to get the worse of the argument, he is pretty certain

to cover his retreat under the pretence that he cannot continue the discussion svi; h one who has not th, "manliness "to append his proper signature. This may have nothing whatever to do with the matter in, dispute, and there may be no earthly reason why higi opponent should disclose his identity ; still it serves: its purpose. But who, in such a ease, is the real' coward? Stippse, again, that " A Ratepayer," instead of multiplying cupies of his precious epistle, address' ing them to various members of the Town Council ,had forwarded it direct to the Press in the form of a letter; to the editor. Would our scandalised public repre-i ' sentatives (who should not he thin skinned but shoulcC rather cultivate the hide of the pachyderm)have for one; moment thought of denouncing such an act as " das-! tardly," "scurrilous," " disgraceful " ? I trow not. JUSIIFIABLE ANONYMITY. There is such a thing —altogether apart froc3l. journalism. I was chatting with a police?' superintendent the other day, and he confessed to we! that some of the most valuable bits of informatial he ever read came in the form of anonymous letters' He never neglected such communications because the, were unsigned ; he could quite understand that there might be an excellent rea,on for the omission, and be invariably caused investigation to be made into hiute and messages thus conveyed. Mc reover, as one whore I have previously cited put it, there are other and very different cases where au snonymous letter can be of service, as when a n.inister receives a note on a Monday morning, whin he is feeliag limp and washed-out after Lis Sabbath dull informing him by a " Well-wisher," that his message has done good and that someone has beelll st.engthened by his words. To a brief message of tbie' kind a man need not sign his name, Lr there is eel sinister motive in such a missive. A minister once' received a commentary on a certain part of the Scriptures, anonymously, with the words : " Pei haPe, these notes on the Scripture yiai were expoundial may be if service." Turning over the leaf, thel recipient found pinned two bank-notes, and tbe words' "lii gratefui. appreciation " wi it'en on aaslip of paper attached. The acknowledgement which was to he sent to " X.Y Z." at the post office, stated that the, commentary was •invaluable, and that the "notes were the most "pi actical and lie pful " on thell particular passage which he had ever received. expressly except journalism and literature general, as the anonymity so commonly practised WI regular writers for the press and often 14 to a certain point by mahers of books is generally obvioiply justifiable; but if I were at liberty to extend inquiry into these realms it might be interesting. As a fellow scribe observed a while ago, over since printicg was invented there have bees writers who, for one reason or another, have veiled their identity by a pseudonym. 'I here have beet various grounds for anonymity. Modesty, of course. has been, and ever may be, one. Diffidence, whizh it not quite the same thing, is another, and cowardice 6 third. In old days, however, there were wiser reasons Before Milton lashed rut in favour of freedom ef speech and wiining, anonymity was often the onli course of safety, and even that was nit always prudent Ecclesiastical and civil censure often came down upoti a writer with a heavy hand if it caught him daring 0' itieise constituted authority, or to discuss forbidden' questi as. The stake, and liter ill) pillory, was coal sidered fit punish crnt far any such venturesoree! individual. Apparently there are members of our, oiv n Town Council who feel lather like that toware "A Ratepa: er " wliJ ventures to send them anent mous communications. Without pal ticularly defend' ing, and assuredly not c mmencling, that precis, method of attempting to influence our " City Fathers, I suggest to these estimable representatives of a more or less appreciative community that they school there' selves to be not so eas ly ruffled, and to treat such in'erposition as one of the inevitable incidents of n pablic career.

div.head: BOYS AND THE CARTRIDGES. 4100 DAMAGES AGAINST A WARRINGTON
div.p: THE BOYS AND THE CARTRIDGES. 4100 DAMAGES AGAINST A WARRINGTON
AUCTIONEER.

Judgment was given by his Honour Judge Stanger K.C., at the Salford County Court on Monday, in an action brought by Reginald Goulding, aged ten, of Oldham-street, Warrington, claiming £lOO damages for the loss of one of his eyes from J Mainwaring, auctioneer, of Bridge-street, Warrington. The hearing took place in the Warrington County Court, and occupied two days in December, and the giving of the decision at the Salford Court was in accordance with the desire of the parties. Mt Dehn was counsel for the Plaintiff, and Mr M'Cleary for the defendant. The Judge reviewed the evidence and legal arguments in considerable detail. The case(he said) was one of _

exceptional importance, which it %;ould not be unreason- able to take as far as the House of Lerde. The defendant was the owner of certain land in Warring lon, Which had been formerly used as a brickfteld, and on Which there was a concrete bed, which had been neces- sary to carry the engine used in the brick-making. In order to develop the land he employed a man named Rowe to dismantle the bed. Explosives had to be used, and on September 13 last Rowe placed a box of detonators in a sin. metal pipe, which he coveted with his coat while he went to explode a ()barge. In his ' absence the box was discovered by three boys, who carried it away and spilled tbe contents in an adjoining street. On the following day the plaintiff and another hey found some of the detonators, took them into the Yard of the house where plaintiff lived, and began to hammer at one of them, with the remit that it exploded and blew out one of the plaintiff's eyes. There were three questions of liability to be decided, the judge sale. The first was whether Rowe Was a servant of the defendant or an independent contractor and whether he had been negligent; the second was whether his negligence was the cause of the injury, or whether the accident, which was the immediate cause of the injury, was too remote; and the third was, supposing these were answered in the affirmative, whether defendant ought to be held responsible for Rowe's negligence. As to the first of these, he agreed with Mr Dehn, that in a place where highly dangerous articles like these detonators were used consummate care was incumbent on the person who had the custody of them. Rowe used these detonators for blasting purposes on land which was open to the Public, on all sides, and which was, as he and defendant both know, the habitual resort ann playing ground of very young children. There were various means by Which Rowe could have kept the cartridges out of the teach of the children, and he had come to the conclu- sion that Rowe had been negligent. The next point was whether the accident to the Plaintiff could be said to have been caused by Rowe's uegligence. After referring to the various authorities cited _qn both sides, the Judge pointed out that it Mast b within the reasonable anticipation of anyone rho-thought about it that serious mischief might i°lloe, upon such explosives falling into the bands of ctuddren. The argument was raised by Mr M.Cleary :at' the children who took the explosives were • "censees, and that the landowner was therefore not rbesP°fleiblei but the question at issue here was not one etsveen the defendant and his licensees, but as to 'whether the defendant and Rowe owed a duty to the public,. He agreed there was no relationship of master and servant between defendant and Rowe, but he did not agree with Mr M'Cleary that only liability which rested on the defendant concerned the actual blasting itself. He considered that there was a duty owing to the public in connection with the placing of the detonators as well, and that the defendant could not tid himself of hie rasponsiiiity, by delegating to an independent contractor the duty of keeping these ,explosives in a careful manner. The amount claimed 157 the plaintiff was reasonable, and there would con- a,e(l, neatly he judgment for .£lOO end coats on the C ‘uighest) scale. A stay of execution for fourteen days, pending appeal, Wall granted on Mr M'Cleary's application.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"Mid Pleasures and Palaces."

Mr 0 Watson Mill's drama, presented at the Royal Court Theatre on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday !3venings, is not conceived on the orthodox lines which itB title might suggest to the case-hardened playgoer. It deals with the life of an heiress who, ignorant of the fact that she is entitled to untold thousands, is brought 11P by thieves in the under-world of Paris. She, of ccurse, never accommodates herself to the wrong•doing of her associates, but gains au honest livelihood as a flower girl. How- she marries a thief who, on discovering thEit she is the victim of a conspiracy, cleverly out- the Chief of Police, who has planned to get the fortune within his own grasp. The play is full of exciting situations, and the beautiful stage pictures are a striking feature. Mr C Watson Mill played the Part of Raoult,the Thief, with the necessary alternating totes of emotion and sang froid. Miss Joan Ellis laaPersonated Ircma, the heirest, with grace and charm, and Mr Edward E Louis gave a convincing Portrayal of the unscrupulous Chief of Police. All the other parts were in capable hands. The weird APache dance was Cleverly performed by Freda and Frank. _
On Thursday and Friday evenings the Warrington Dra.tnatic Society presented "Sunday," which will again be the attraction this (Saturday) evening,

div.head: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
div.p: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
COMMON SENSE ADVICE BY A DISTING UISHED SPECIA LIST.

. ". Acid " stomachs are dangerous because acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the stomach, thus hindering and preventing the propPr action of the Stomach, Bnd leading to nine-tenths of the cases of stomach trouble from which people suffer. Medicines and medicinal treatments are useless in such cases, for they leave the smiles) of the trouble, the acid in the stomach, as dangerous as ever. The acid must be neutralised, and its formation prevented, and the best thing for this purpose is half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia, a simple antacid, taken in a little warm or cold water after eating, which not only neutralises the acid, but also prevents the fermentation from which acidity is developed. Foods which ordinarily cause greatest distress can he eaten with impunity if the meal is followed with a little bisurated magnesia, Which csn be obtained of any chemist, and should :always be kept handy.
RESIGNATION OF LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS CHAIRMAN.

At the Liverpool County Quarter Sessions on Tuesday Mr C P Scott Barrett, deputy chairman, announced that Sir William Forwood, the chairman of the Court, had resigned his position on account of ill-health. The regret of Bench and Bar at his retirement was expressed. For forty Nears Sir William has been one of the leading figures in the public life of Liverpool. He first held ..he Mayoralty in 1880, and was knighted three years later. In 19.02 he was presented with the freedom of the city.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 18, 1913
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 18, 1913
MOORE.

WESLEY GUILD.—A social evening was held in the school on Wednesday evening, which proved to be highly successful in every respect. The programme was opened by a short musical programme consisting of pianoforte solo, by Miss Edith Done; songs by Miss Alice Lawton, Miss Clare, Miss Ruth Tanner and Mr John Banner, and a duet by Miss Clare and Mr James Antrobus. At this stage refreshments ware served which had been tastefully prepared by the ladies of the committee. The competition proved to be very interesting, well known xidvertisements being repre- sented in character. The winners were :—Mr Horace Wilkinson and Mr Massey Cartwright. The rest of the evening was spent in games, which were much enjoyed by all present. The Rev 11 Middlewood (the guild president) performed the duties of chairman. R,ISLEY•

INDLPENDENT METHODIST CHURCH, FEAR'NHEAD.— The annual prize distribution took place on Saturday evening. Mr Joseph Bate (one of the school superin- tendents) presided, and in the course of a very helpful and suggestive address, mentioned the increase of scholars and the good work, dcne by the teachers in the past year which gave him hope and encouragement to face with fresh zeal the duties of the coming year. He then called upon Mrs Joseph Mason, to present the prizes to the childreu. There were 32 first awards, 3 seconds and 1 third. Mrs Mason in a very pleasing speech commended the great effort that had been made by the scholars and also the mothers. Great credit, she said was due to the mothers for such good attend- ance, ani but for their energy they would not need many Sunday school teaches. Mr Joseph Mason pre- sented three special prizes to members of his class, Ist to ME Monks for best•tiaper given during the year ; 2nd, to Mr F Bate ler most regular attendance; 3rd, for best attention to A Worrall. Recitations, solos and games were enjoyed up to a late hour. • WIN WICK. PANTOMIME AT THE ASYLUM.—On Tuesday and Friday evenings last the patients of thb County As,ylum, Winwiok, and a few friends, were entertained with per- formances of the pantbmime "Cinderella," by members of the staff and outside employees. Miss Kitty McDermott was a distinct suacess in the title role, both in her acting and singing. "Nobody knows when I am lonely," sung with feeling and deservedly encored, was certainly the best song of the nigbt. Miss Amelia Kane made a very charming " Prince " and sustained her part well all through. The role of Baron Balder- dash was entrusted to Mr John Woods, who enacted it in a very capable manner. A word of praise is due to Messrs Bolton and Joe Hopkinson for the very clever way in which they portrayed the twe ugly sisters. A special feature was the song and dance by Mr Hopkinson, a very clever dancer, having we understand, followed that calling as a member of the Theatrical Association. Miss Emily Hobin was very dainty and carried out her duties as Fairy God- mother in a very pleasing manner. The humour was supplied by Messrs B. A Chandler and 3 T Cannell with their thought-reading and quaint songs and patter, and Mr F W Uncles as Police Constable X.Y.Z. of the Winwick Division. The dresses were beautiful and the songs were well chosen and up-to-date. The fact that everything went off without a hitch is, to a largo extent, due to the very capable stage-managership of Dr Hopwood. The orchestra under the control of Mr E Haynes excelled themselY es ; they were always subdued in the accompaniments to a singer. while their overture was received with rounds of applause.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WEStEY GUILD.—The usual weekly meeting of the Guild was held on Monday evening,and,it being the first meetieg of the month, was of a devotional character Mr F Wright presided and a thoughtful and suggestive paper was read in vigorous style by Mr Parkinson of Leigh. The subject was,' The influence of the Psalms on three great Englishmen," Cromwell, Milton and Bunyan. The roll was called by Mr H Tomliu and the thanks of those present to the speaker were voiced in suitable terms by the Chairman. THE LATE MR. PETER HIGHAM.—The remains of the late Mr Peter Eligham were laid to rest on Sunday afternoon. The first part of the ceremony took place in the Wesleyan Church. The ten children of the deceased gentleman and a number of his grandchildren, brothers, and other relatives were present, as well as a considerable number of friends and neighbours. The Rev E Morgan officiated throughout and spoke in a few choice words of the character and worth of the deceased. The interment took place at Christ Church, the body being followed by a large company, including Alderman Bennett . and Messrs Walter and Leonard Bennett. Mr William Bennett, who was indisposed, sent his carriage. A number of beautiful wreaths were sent, includiug one from the employees of deceased, Messrs Bennett Bros. PARISH COGNCIL.—The quarterly meeting was held in the C.E. schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr R ' Denham presided and there were also present, Dr Bennett, Messrs Critchley, Houghton, Howard and Potter.—lt was reported that the C.L.C. had withdrawn their scheme for the formation of a road and bridge over the railway from Padgate-lane to Tidal-lane.--The Clerk was instructed to obtain a list of prices payable by the R.D.C. for the cartage of cinders to different parts of the township.—The following important resolution was carried unanimously on the proposition of the chairman seconded by Mr Houghton— That this Council protests most strongly against the proposed sewage scheme for the township of Poultou-with- Fearnhead for the following amongst other reasons : '(1) The heitlth returns for the township for many years past have been most satisfactory. (2) There have been no diseases of en epidemic nature beyond the usual children's diseases which occur in the most up-to-date sanitary districts. (3) Thatan increase in the rates of anything like the sums mentioned would mean the deitopulation of a very large portion of the township, and thereby a considerable burden upon those left to pay the rates. (4) That any accumulation of sewage matter in the brooks in the township could be easily removed by a systematic cleaning of such brooks at a very small expense to the township.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PARK TENNIS CLUB.—A successful whist drive and dance was held in connection vith the above club in the Penketh Infects School on li'riday, January 10th. Members end friends to the number of between 50 and GO put in an'appearance. The evening's enjoyment com- menced at 7.30 and continued till 1 a.m. The M.C.'s for the evening were Messrs Dwerryhouse and H Molynenx. Th,l music was supplied by Messrs J and F Hall. The following were the prize winners :—Ladies, 1, Miss A Davies ; 2, Miss Elsie Colley ; consolation, Mrs B Ireland. Gentlemen, 1, Mr H Molyneux ; 2 Mr 14' Kimberley ; consolation, Mr W Lightfoot and Mr A Hanstock.

div.head: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.

The ordinary meeting of the alaove Council was held on Monday evening in the Council schools. There villa a good attendance of members which included the foliovsing :—Dr Murray (chairman), Mr J G Withinshaw (vice-chairman), Messrs W Davies, J Ditchfield, R lioutledge, J Woodward and E Foster (clerk). A DANGEROUS CORNER.

The Chairman introduced the subject of the Station- road arising out of the minutes. As reported in the "Examiner," the Council had passed a resolution that it was to the interest of the parishioners generally that the corner in Station-road opposite Mr J Ditchfield's cottage (which is a dangerous one) should be taken off and the Clerk was instructed to write the owners of the land in question re juesting them to see whet could be done in the matter. Dr -MURRAY in his remarks pointed out that the owners of the land referred to had no right of frontage and unless they were prepared to take over the road which was now in the hands of the London and North- Western Railway Company, he did not think they would be successful in their desires to improve the dangerous corner in quostion. Mr J (.3 WurffiNsx,o.v 'proposed that the Rural Dis- trict Council adopt the road. Mr Davies seconded. Mr Ditchfield moved as an amendment that the road be left id the hands of the London and North-Western Rai 1,. ay Co Mr Woodward, in seconding, said it was only a road to the station and if taken over there would be the same difficulty at the Railway Station. The road would have to stop there. The original proposition was carried and the Clerk was instructed to write to the Rural District Council. A DANGER SIGNAL. _ _ _

Mr Davies moved that the danger signal for motor drivers &c. re school) be removed nearer the school. Mr Withinshaw seconded and the motion was carried, the signal to be fixed between Mr Woodward's shop and Mr Jones' shop (butcher.) The Clerk intimated to the Councillors present that they would have to seek re-election next March, the Parish meeting taking place on March 17th.

div.head: WHAT A YOUNG ENGLISHNIAN DID.
div.p: WHAT A YOUNG ENGLISHNIAN DID.

In England it is once a farm labourer always a farm labourer. In Ontario it is far different. That province offers farm workers the opportunity of becoming managers of businesses without it being necessary to make an outlay of capital. The following item gives just one instance of what a young Englishman has done during the last season. He worked for a farmer for a short time and proved his ability. Then his employer made him an offer to enter into a proposition on equa' shares, and the result is given below :

dols. Cost of building greenhouse 339 Fertilizer Baskets for market produce The early plants were raised in the greenhouse, then set out on 21 acres of land. The produce sold for I,loBdols, and half the profit, viz., 319.90d015, or £l4, was the amount earned by the young Englishman in five months, leaving him still seven months to carry on other work. Although this was a case of intensive agriculture involving tbe building of a greenhouse, there are many similar opportunities in all branches of farming, general dairying, mixed and fruit. It should be noted that the entire cost of the greenhouse was deducted from the,first year's income.
