imposed. LIBERAL TEA PARTY AND DANCE. CELEBRATING "INSURANCE DAY." The great social event of the Lymm Liberal calendar for the winter session of 1912-1913 is now a thing of the past, but the memories of it will live for many years to come, not only because of the happiness it gave but on account of it being held on that memor- able 'date, "insurance Day," Wednesday. January 15th, 1013. The venue was again the Drill Hall, which had been gaily decorated with flags and bunting, the plat- form having a choice array of plants on each side, whilst the tables looked resplendent with red centres, flowers evergreens, etc. (the handiwork of Mrs Champ, and the Misses M Champ, Moston, M Priestner and Welford.) At these tables over four hundred persons sat down to do justice to the ample and choice supply of edibles that had been provided, and judging from the quickly emptying plates, smiling faces, and commendatory remarks the catering committees had-every cause to feel pleased with their efforts. As soon as V- a was over the room was prepared for a little speech-making and entertainment. The chair was taken by the President of the Lymm Liberal Association, Mr G L Welford, who was supported by Mr J D B Smith (chairman), and Mr R Barker (hon. secretary). Mr Smith informed the audience that the following ladies and gentlemen had sent letters of regret at being unable to he present :—Mrs Dedds (Penketh), Mrs Jones (Stretford), Mrs Miller (Oughtrington), Mr W Long (Thelwall), and Mr W E Thompson (Altrincham). Mr Welford commenced his address by congratulating the committees on the Access that had attained their eflorts and said that the Liberal Party had no need to be down-cast, as was shown by the good attendance. He expressed his pleasure at seeing so many young people present because it was to them that he looked for recruits. He was glad to see the ladies there for it would pay to look after them in the future as they would soon be having their vote and he wished them to imbibe Liberal principles. (Armistice.) He then pro- ceeded to talk about the National Insurance Act the benefits of which came into operation that day, and its utility and beneficence only the future would show. He thoought it was the best Act that had ever been placed on the Statute Baok its provi ions, which were on a most liberal scale, would do an incalculable amount of good and many people would thank his I lajesty's Government, and Mr Lloyd George in particular. (Prolonged anplause.) He said that he always regretted that the Conservative party had not joined hands with the Liberals in passing the measure as he would have liked it to have assured a non-party aspect. However, certain members of the , Conservative party had thought to make election capital out of it and whilst they achieved a certais measure of success now that the Act is assuming more popularity they have discovered the error of their ways and wish to back out. He said that it would be an easy task to dwell on the awkward position teat the Conservatives were now in, and thought they were reaping the " fruits "of Protection. The Con- servatives had put their party before their State,whilst the Liberals put their State before party. He spoke of the progress that had been made with the Home Rule and Welsh Church Bills, and said that though the Lords might send them back to the Commons, yet ke expected they would be placed on the Statute Book within two years He expressed his hopes for the speedy passing of the Franchise Bill and said that then there would be more equality and that Division would once more be Liberal. (Hearty applause.) He hoped they would maintain their interest. " Keep your powder dry ! " He announced the big Liberal meeting to be held in the Drill Hall on February 20th, when Mr George Nicholls' ex-M.P. for Northampton is to be the speaker. After expressing the hope that they would all enjoy themselves he said that it was his desire that Liberalism should be as popular as ever and that they would repeat their great victories. (Applause.) The eniertainment was opened with a recital by Mr Norman Blackett whose elocu- tionary efforts, together with the songs of Mr Arthur Leyland, at the last Liberal party warranted their being r e-engsgad for the present occasion. Mr Norman Blackett's first items. were two cleverly given character studies, "'Little 'orphant Annie," and "'is pipe." Later on he gave the humorous recital "Babies," which earned the well deserved encore that took the form of a musical monologue, "Coming home." This too, evoked such hearty applause that Mr Norman Blackett had to make another appearance when be gave a characteristic encore piece The fearful night." Miss Minnie Barlow of Altrincham was the lady singer for the evening, when her cultivated soprano voice and pleasing manner charmed everyone. Her items were (including encores) "I must die," " To Sylvia," "Songs my Mothar taught me," and "Autumn." Mr Arthur Leyland, a bass of much promise, was very acceptable with the songs" Go to Sea," "A Soldier's Song," and" My Old Shake' Mr T M Eastham played the pianoforte accompaniments with his usual taste and judgment. Mr JD B Smith whilst proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, artistes, and workers, endorsed Mr Welford's invitation to the February demonstration, and said that the Secretary would be pleased to have more members in the Lymm Liberal Association., Mr R Barker seconded the proposition, buebefore putting it to the meeting Mr Smith added Mr Barker's name, remarking upon the excellent service he had performed in connection with the present gather- ing. Mr Welford briefly replied, after wbich the room was cleared for dancing and in a short time many couples were gyrating to the sound of the music pro. vided by Mr George Underwood's band. The bright red ties, bows, flowers, etc. that were worn all added to the beauty of the gay scene over which Mr George Holt jun.. was an efficient M.C. Mrs T Wyatt and Mrs J Radcliffe were in charge of the refreshment room The following ladies took prominent part in preparing. the tea :—Mesdames C J Barnes, J Brearley,L Broadey, F Brown, H Champ, J Clare W Cross, D Daniels, Guest, G Holt, jun., T Knowles Leigh, W Mclntyre, Jun., W Mort, F. 0 Moston, W Moston, W Seymour, It tV B Whiteway, and the Misses E Barker, D Barker, A Brazendale, M Brazendale, Egerton. Glaze, Mclntyre, Moston, M Moston, Smith, Stott, Welford and Wright. The Gentlemen's Social Committee consisted of Messrs R Barker (hon. secretary), C J Barnes, J Brearley, D Daniels, F A Merris and W Seymour, who were assisted by Mesers F Chain, Joe Clare, P Clare, 03 W Cross, A B Edwards, F Guest, J H Mather, C Moss, W Moston and S Moston.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

TOBOGGANING.-It is not often that Lymm can rival the Swiss winter resorts and yet anyone passing down the "Private Road " on Monday or Tuesday would have been shrpassed to see bow popular tobogganing was, for in the fields on both sides .of the road were a large number of young people enjoying the sport on a large variety of sleighs. The " chute " in the field nearest to Dane Bank was the cause of much fun and
excitement.

INSURANCE.— THE MEDICAL BENEFIT.—Tn connection with the National Health Insurance, Cheshire Insurance Committee, Lymm and district, the followidg arrange- ments have been made for the administration of Medical Benefit. The panel of doctors that has been formed for the above disrrict consists of:—Dr Burrows, Whitbarrow ; Dr E M. De Jong, Portland House, Lymm; Dr L Thorp and Dr H Thorp, Foot's Gray, Lymm, also at Mill-lane, Heatley, and at Broomedge. Medicine ittc., when ordered by a doctor on the panel, can be obtained from either of the following chemists :—Mr F E Evans, The Cross, Lymm ; or Mr E N Owen, Old Post Office Place, Lymm. WESLEYAN MOTHERS' MEETING.—On the 9th inst the members of the Wesleyan Mothers' Meeting and Sewing Class were once more kindly entertained in the schoolroom by Mrs J H Pawlyn. The gathering was mot quite so large as in previeus year., but those present had a most enjoyable time a splendid knife and fork tea followed by a good entertainment being provided In the unavoidable absence of the Rev J H Pawlyn, owing to indisposition, the proceedings were I presided over by Mr Finch. The concert consisted of songs by Mrs Lewis, Miss Liles Finch. and Mr T Newton ; recitations by Miss Moston and Mr Finch ; and children's dances by the Misses Gladys and. Lilian Naggear. THE WELSH CHURCH BILL.—On Friday evening of last week a protest meeting against the Welsh Church Bill was held in the Parochial Schools under the presidency of the Rev G B Thurston, M.A., rural dean of Bowdon. Either owing to the belief that the Bill is too far advanced for the protest meeting to affect it, or owing to lack of local interest in the measure, or other reason, there was only a small attendance. The chairman after a few remarks as to the purpose of the meeting introduced the speaker of the evening, Miss Pryce, of Bangor. Miss pryae dealt largely in generalities and though her remarks were favourably received by the sympathetic audience they would probably have had little weight with the supporters of the Bill. No resolution was formally submitted to the meeting. Mr Broadbent also spoke briefly on the subject. A vote of thanks to the speaker was proposed by Dr Burrows and seconded by Mr Hirtley. _

CONGREGATIONAL CHRISTMAS PARTY.— We are told that "everything comes to him who waits," and so it was with the scholars of the Congregational Sunday school last week when on Thursday and Friday evenings their eagerly anticipated Christmas party attained a visible form. On the Thursday evening the elder members of the school had their tea after which came the annual concert and distribution of prizes. Mr J H Holt presided over the gathering which was of a miscellaneous character, songs, recitations, etc. being given. The prizes were banded to the fortunate winners by Mr It H Gotobed. On Friday the younget.scholars had their turn at the festivities, when they too had an enjoyable time at the tea tables. A visit to the school- room after tea made one feel quite envious of the happy little ones as they marched round the room with their teachers singing "For I'm the bead of the army, etc," and participated in the various surprises that had been prepared for them. The school has many kind friends amongst whom are Mr J E Bedell of Bowdon, who for many years has generously given a supply of toys at each annual party, and Mr R Gotobed who kindly sent a stock of sweets by his little bon Erie, ho was dressed up as Father Christmas Besides receiving a toy, each child was presented with a parcel containing some article of apparel. An impromptu concert consisting of gramaphone selec- tions, recitations &o. was given by the children.

"SHALL LYMM HAVE A POLL ?"—lt comes RS ratber,a surprise to many local residents to learn that despite the clear case for the purchase of the water- works, etc , that was made at the ratepapers' meetirg last week, and that a majority voted in favour of the resolution, c irtain local persons have been at work and secured a requisite number of signatures to 'cause a poll to be made. These signatures having been presented to the Clerk of the Council within the seven days a poll will now take place, and incidentally, more public money will be wasted. It will be a great pity if the Bill is rejected for in addition to the loss of money that has so far been expended on the promotion of the measure it will mean in all probability that Lymm will never have such a favourable opportunity of possessing its own waterworks. Should the Bill not be accepted then what is to prevent the whole scheme from being sold to a public company who will turn the Dingle and lake into a pleasure retort; a Beni° railway in the Dingle would be quite popular with a certain class of visitors. The question of supplying Warburton ahpuld not cause any fear of shortage for Lymm as the present out-put easily meets the demand and can be increased if necessarl We also understand that by securing the water supply and lake the Connci) will be able to make a consider- able saving to the rhtes on such items as taxes, ground rents, and fees for water power. It seems a pity that the amount of £BOO per year should go out of Lymm into private pockets, when in forty six years time it could be placed towards reducing the rates. If the persons who are opposing the Bill would only realise what the present increase of rates to the tune of three pence in the £ will mean in reducing the rates of the suture surely they would be a little self-sacrificing. FREE CHURCH COUNCIL SERVICES.—The annual week's united services held in connection with the Lymm Free Church Council have taken place in the Primitive Methodist Church this week, when, with perhaps the exception of Wednesday night, they have been.well attended. The meetings have been of a most helpful character, the spiritual tone being of the highest order. • The whole of the arrangements have been carried out in a most satisfactory manner and reflect credit upon the hon. secretary. Mr J D B Smith. The first service was held on Sunday night when the Holy Communion was adminis- tered by the Rev R W B Whiteway. A powerful address was given by the Rev H Ogden on the valae of the ordinance of the Lord's Supper.--On Monday night the chair was taken by the Rev it W B White- way and the .Rev George Curtiss was the preacher. He chose as his text 2nd Timothy i. 12, pg win power of Jesus.—The as Mr H Holt, and the the Rev E Morgan, who after giving several cd wh aeil rl mi nu% cohni e flTyu eosnd atyh en gkhe et preacher, illustrations he had come across in reading the life of Gipsy Smith spoke on the subject of "the presence of Christ," and showed bow that this was the highest form of Divine presence."—On Wednesday evening Mr R Hewitt presided whilst the preacher was the Rev W Reid, who based his remarks on the story of the boy Jesus' first visit to Jerusalem. (Luke ii., particularly verse 40.)—Thursday night found Mr J D B Smith in the chair, with the Rev J Hamilton, of Cheadle, as the preacher. The text on this occasion was 2 Cor. v. 17, "If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature." The preacher said that these words defined the term "Christian," which was his topic for the night. He said that all men sought happiness though their methods differed. After giving the stories of Faust and Sir Gallahad and their search for the ideal be said that the ideal was only to be found in Christ. He further defined a Christian as one :—(1) believes in certain fundamental things. e.g., Christ ; (2) is the spirit of Christ; (3) loves and serves his fellows. Let us be and do like Him. On Friday night a meetiug to further the interest in the work of the Free Church Council was held, a report of which will be given next week.

div.head: PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY —Before Mr A Watkins (in the chair), Messrs T J Ridgway, A W Callender, W G Groves

and H Holden. - - No RED LIGHT.--John Rowlands,Clay-lane,Timperley, was fined 2s 6d for allowing a light other than a red one to be seen from the rear of his vehicle. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—Harry Johnson, Agden Bridge. Lymm, was summoned fer using obsence language and carrying a gun without a licence.—A fine of 5s includ- ing costs was imposed. A MOTORIST'S OFFENCE.—Richard George Hinchcliffe, Bedford-street, Liverpool. was summoned for driving a motor car without a rear light and also for failing to produce his licence when requeated to do so on the night of December 28th. Mr Harding, Liverpool, appeared for the defendant and pleaded guilty. lt was stated that the motor car was seen without a rear light. lOn an officer whistling, the defendant stopped the car and when asked for his licence he said be had left it at borne. He had, however, sent it on by post since. Mr Harding pointed out that the defepdam had pulled up straight away wben the officer whistled. It was not his own car and he had left the licence in the pocket of his overcoat. The lamp had gone out owing to the rough state of the road. Defendant was ordered to pay 5s and costs in the first case and the costs in the second case. ALLEGED WIFE DF.SERTION.—Janot Prosser, The, Rookery, Booth's Hill, Lymm, summoned her husband- Thomas, 19, Park Plage, Cross-lane, Salford, for des tion. Mr Kay appeared for the comnlainant and stated that the parties were married in 1901 and seven months later the wife loft her husband. They came together in June 1911 and in April 1912 defendant left her and did not return. Complainant admitted that her husband had written asking her to go to Salford but she refused•—Defehiant denied desertion and said be had asked his wife to make a home in Salford but she refused.-1 le magistrates dismissed the case. 7HEFT 001 TIMBER.—Thomas Tighe, Cadishead, wos summoned for stealing four pieces of timber from the Partington Steel Works, the property of Simon Cawers, of Manchester.—lt was stated that the defendant, who was employed by the firm, was seen to take the timber away without having obtained permission to do So.

div.head: HATTON.
div.p: HATTON.

DRATH OP MRS. PARIL—It is with deep regret that we announce the death of Mrs Parr, wife of Mr James Parr of Hatton Hall, who passed away on Sunday morning after an illness of three weeks, caused by an attack of paralysis. The decased lady would have been 80 years of age in February. The interment took place on Thursday at Daresbury Parish Church. The tenantry and workpeople sent a handsome wreath as a token of their affection. Mrs Parr was a lady of quiet habits and by her kindly disposition made many friends.

div.head: WIDNES OFFICIAL'S SUDDEN DEATH.
div.p: WIDNES OFFICIAL'S SUDDEN DEATH.

Mr John Flo!book (54), of 4, Elliott-street, Widnes, left business shortly after four o'clock on Monday afternoon, and on reaching home shortly before five died suddenly. He was an ex-police constable of the Lancashire Constabulary, and held the office of County Court bailiff for Widnes. WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. MOTOR-BUS QUESTION.

The Mayor (Alderman F eil) presided over the monthly meeting of the Council held in the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon. Mr Lewis moved an amendment asking the committee to take back a resolution to increase the fere& The stages had been augmented considerably, and in some cases the increase had gone up 20 to 40 per cent. He contended that this would not solve the question or wipe out the serious deficit. The maintenance charges failed to maintain, and they hunk heavily around the motor-bus business. Upon the chairman of the Bus Committee agreeing to take the minute back for further consideration the amendment was withdrawn.

div.head: CONSUMPTION OF WATER.
div.p: CONSUMPTION OF WATER.

During the hearing of the Gas and Water Committee minutes, Alderman II S Timmis drew the Council's attention to the amazing consumption of water. During the four weeks ending December 25, 108,102,000 gallons were consumed, or 8,250,000 in excess of the previous month.

div.head: BOUNDARY EXTENSIO'S,
div.p: BOUNDARY EXTENSIO'S,

The General Purpoves Committee offered an extension scheme, and Alderman 0 Neil said the time had arrived for the Council to take immediate steps to effect an extension of the present boundaries. , The names of the districts to be absorbed were yet under consideration, but many of the townships adjacent, enjoyed the many improvements recently carried out in the borough. They were about te spend £56,000 upon works extension, and there was a strong and grow- ing feeling among toe inhabitants of the borough to extend the boundaries where the field of usefulness might be increased. ° The matter dealing with the above was referred to the next meeting.' RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday Mr C E Linaker presiding.
MOTOR CAUTION POSTS.

At a meeting of the Weston Parochial Committee a letter was read from the County Surveyor stating that the Couyty Council would comply with the Committees request that motor caution posts be erected near Weston House, and school signs be erected near the Council schools.jr.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL SEWERAGE.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL SEWERAGE.

The Clerk read a letter from the Gro.ppenhall Parish Council in which they drew attention to the Open sewer running-from the end of houses in Mayfield-road. As the sewage scheme would take some time to com- plete, they were of the opinion that the sewer mentioned ought to be dealt with at once. Mr Farringdon (inspector), had visited the place the previous day but owing to the snow, he could not make proper investigations. He suggested that he should report at the next meeting. His report was adopted and his recommendations acted upon.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr Adams, medical officer, stated that the Grappenhall schools were closed for a fortnight on account of mumps. At Westol7 Point there was an epidemic of measles developing and it might be-necessary to close the schools before the next meeting. The report was adopted. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr J Spruce presiding.

THE LATE MR. THOMAS DEAN. Before commencing the ordinary business the chair- man moved that a vote of sympathy be passed with the widow and daughters of the late Mr Thomas Dean, of Runcorn. Although Mr Dean had not been long with them they were all unanimous that he wss a most desirable Poor Law Guardian and was thoroughly adapted to the work. Mr Wood seconded, and siid be had known the decsased gentleman for 30 rears and had always found him to be a straightforward genial man. It had always been a pleasure to he associated with him in any kind of work The work he most delighted in was such that he found to do amongst the poor. In the welfare of the poor he always took a keen interest, and they all deplored his death. The resolution was passed, all members rising. A NEEDFUL RESOLUTION. The Easingwolf Union passed the following resolu- tion and asked thle Guardians to give it their support : —" That proceedings may be taken by the mother or the Guardians, to obtain an order against the putative father of any bastard child born in a workhouse, to pay the costs of Confinement, and to contribute towards the mother's support during the whole period of her residence in the Workhouse both before and after the birth of the child. That in the event of the death of the mother or in cases where the evidence cannot be obtained, the Justices shall have power on the applica- tion of the Guardians and on proof, to make an order on the putative father to contribute towards the child's maintenance When chargeable to the Union. That the Guardians shall have power to detain for a period of six months any woman who shall give birth to more than two illegitimate children in a Workhouse." Mr Hallows moved that they support the resolution. He had bean through the Workhouse that morning and bad been surprised at the number of illegitimate children they bad in their institution. Some had been brought in that morning. Something ought to ho done for the unfortunate women. _ _
09 Mr Antwis seconding, the resolution was sup- ported.
FORTRESS RESIGNS.

Miss E Wormold, portress at the Workhouse, wrote resigning her position. On the motion of Mr Linaker (junr.) seconded by Mr Mclntyre the reEignation was accepted and it was decided that the usual steps be taken to obtain a suco:.ssor.

div.head: BOARDS' CONTRIBUTION.
div.p: THE BOARDS' CONTRIBUTION.

The Secretary of the National Children's Home and Orphanage wrote stating that the certificate for the reception of Poor Law Children at the various branches of the institution bad been raisgd by the Local Government B ard from ss. to a maximum of 7s. per bead. This advance was readily approved on their submitting to the Lt,cal Government Board a reasoned statement as to the considerably increased costs of maintenance since the sum of ss. was approved by them nearly 30 years ago. The Clerk pointed out that they had one child in the homes at Luton in respect of whom they were con- tributing ss. per week. Mr Linaker (inn): Did'nt we grant another Is, to the Pant asaph Orphanage? The Clerk : Yes you increased it from 4s. to ss. Mr Hallows said that the sum mentioned for the Nationel Children's Home was excessive.

The Clerk : The maximum is 78. per head. The Clerk suggested that they should write and ask the Orphanage what they were asking for the mainten- ance of the child they had there. Mr Antwiss . What age is the boy? A Relieving Officer : Nearly 14. It was decided to act according to the Clerk's suggestion.

div.head: COUNTY PRECEPT.
div.p: THE COUNTY PRECEPT.

The Clerk reported that the county precept amounted to £72,437 lis 6d. All the items were the same with the exception of that for general elementary educational purposes; that amount was id in the £ down. (Applause). Mr Antwis : What a surprise ! Mr Pilling : What will it be next year. (" Hush !" and laughter). The Clerk: It is something new. FEEBLE-MINDED. The Master reported that there were five boys and two girls, feeble-minded, in the Workhouse. They
were suitable cases for removal to the Farndon Institution. It was agreed that they be removed at the expense of the Board.

div.head: HALTON PUBLIC VACCINATOR.
div.p: HALTON PUBLIC VACCINATOR.
It was decided that Dr Maxwell be appointed as publics vaccinator for the Halton _district.
DELEGATES.

On the motion of Mr'Wright in the absence of Mr Woodward, seconded by Mr Antwis, it was decided that the following gentlemen be appointed as delegates to the Central Poor Law Conference: Messrs 'l' Baxter, C B Linaker and the clerk. The Conference takes place on the 11th and 12th of February.
_ SUPPLIES FOR CHILDREN'S HOME.

A sub-committee consisting of Mem% Wood, Booth, Hayes, and the master was appointed to discuss the tenders for the supplies to the Children's Home.. Thee recommended that the tenders of Mr Alfred Dodd, Runcorn, of £96 12s led, for blankets, drapery, Stc., by accepted and also that the bedsteads (50) be obtained from Messrs Leslie and Son, Warrington' for the sum of £27 lOs and also that 20 forms and five tables be obtained from Mr John A Wood, Manchester, for the sum of £27. The re commendations f the sub-oommitee were acted upon.

div.head: ST. HF LENS. PRIEST'S SUDDEN DEATH.
div.p: ST. HF LENS. PRIEST'S SUDDEN DEATH.

The Rev Father William Splaine, S.J., r priest at Lowe 'House Catholic Church, St Helens, aged 66 years, was found dead in bed on Monday morning. The deceased came to St Helens on the 2nd inst. from East Shilton,wbere he had been stationed for twelve months aP missioner. He appeared to be in good health when he retired to rest on Sunday night, and should have said Maas at seven o'clock in the morning, but as he did nct appear Father Riley, the rector, went to his room and found him dead in bed. FUNERAL OF MR. T. GLOVER.

The funeral at St Helens on Monday, of Mr Thomas Glover, es-M.P. for the borough, was the occasion of a remarkable demonstration of regard. Notwithstand- ing the inclement weather there was a large attendance. Mr It &Atlie, president of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain, was present, with Mr S Walsh, M.P. and Mr T Greensll, president, and Mr T Ashton, secretary of the Lancashire sod Cheshire Federation. Miners' lodges all over the district were represented. Mr Robertson attended on behalf of the Scottish Miners' Federation, and Mr J A Seddon on that of the Parlia- mentary Committee of the Trade Unions Congress. The Mayor (Mr Crooks) and tbe borough and county magis- tbates and representatives of local Labour clubs were also present. BRISK INSURANCE BUSINESS.

ST. HELENS WOMAN'S FAMILY POLICIES. • At St Helena Police Court on Monday, a widow. named Ellen Atherton, of 167, Rivington-street, St Helens, sued the National Standard Life Assurance Corporation, Limited, 38, Church-street, Liverpool, for the recovery of two sums of £lO 16s and £1.4 18s in respect of policies granted to claimant on the life of her mother, a Mrs Margaret Wilson, aged eighty years. The case fur the claimant was that for twenty years or so she had had her mother insured in the Prudential and the Victoria Legal Friendly Societies for similar amounts, and last Match three of the defendants' agents of whom her own son was one induced her to transfer her mother's policies to the company for the sums claimed. At the same time she banded over ten other nolicits which she held in other societies on the lives of her sous and members of the 'family, and insured them with the Corporation, on the understanding that she would only have the same premiums to pay, would: get full benefits, and that in the event of death there would be prompt settlement. Afterwards, however, the claimant continued to pay and kept alive the policies. with the Prudential and, Victoria Legal societies, and when the old woman died the liabilities were met by the two societies named. On the other hand the, defendants took no notice of letters sent to them or of the claims male.

For the defence, it was contended that the claimant was not entitled to succeed, inasmuch as she had. already drawn £25 for her mother's funeral expenses, who was in the workhouse at the time she was insured with the defendant corporation. She was not seen by the agents, but the proposal cards were filled up, the requisite answers being given by the claimant who knew they were lies, and Wl3O also made a mark, repre- senting it as made by the old woman. The Claimant said an agent, , named Pitman, who knew the old woman was in the workhouse, filled up. portions of the proposals.- The Chairman (Mr J B Leach) said the bench had unanimously decided to make orders for the company to psy the amounts claimed, with costs.
CANADA'S IRON AND STEEL INDUSTRY AND THE UNITED STATES STEEL TRUST.

The growing consumption of iron and steel products in Canada during the last few years is reflected in the development and prosperit, of the local iron and steel industry, which has become one 0f the first importance. The production of pig iron for 1911 has risen to just on a million tons, and that of steel ingots and castings to 682,000 tons. This output, however, does not supply more than 30 per cent of the tonnage of the iron and steel consumed in Canada. Im orts into the country of this class are valued at one hundred million dollars., The Lulk—two thirds—of these imports comes from the United States and the share of the United States cor— poration alone of recent years has ranged from 31;0,000. to 400,000 tons a year, representing a value of twelve to fifteen dollars, the average duty on which has been between six and seven dollars a ton. It is now announced (cables the "Daily Telegraph "financial correspondent) that the Steel Trust 'sill shortly invade Canada by establishing a plant to cost twenty million dollars at Sandwich, Ontario, on land of about 1,500 acres which was purchased by the corporation five years ago. By taking this step, the company will save several millions of dollars annually in import duties..

THE DEBACLE OF THE FOOD TAXERS.

By Mr. A. H. Grosfield. Turning to the Westminster Gazette the other 'day for news of the progress of the fiscal contro- versy, my eye caught the following headline LATEST COVENANT.' I had been looking forward to reading the docu- ment that has been presented to Mr. Bonar Law, and I therefore immediately looked. to see what this latest covenant contained. It runs as fol- lows: At enormous expense and telepathic trouble we have obtained a copy of the document now being signed by Unionist M.P.'s. Its form comes as no surprise seeing that an Ulsterman (Mr. Ronald McNeill, M.P.) is in charge of it. N.B.—This cancels all previous covenants, pledges, undertakings, referendums, "dodges," and statements of any kind or sort whatever made at any time, date, or place. Being convinced in our consciences that Free TrAde is disastrous to the material well-being of Great Britain, as well as of Ireland, des- tructive of our prosperity, and perilous to the unity cf the Empire, we, whose names are underwritten, men of Union, loyal followers of our dearly beloved leaders, hereby pledge our- selves in Solemn Covenant in this our time of threatened calamity to stand by one another in defending, for ourselves and our children, our cherished hopes of winning the next General Election, and in using all means which may be found necessary to defeat the present treacher- ous and peace-loving Coalition; and, in the event of victory being then at last achieved, we further solemnly and mutually pledge our- selves to impose no food taxes until at any rate victory has crowned our banners a second time. In prayerful confidence that Bonar Law will not make such a mess of it at Edinburgh as he did at Ashton,' we hereto subscribe our names, and further, we individually declare that we are not members of the Opposition Front Bench." Now whether that is the authentic document itself of which Mr. Boner Law is the recipient, or whether the Westminster Gazette has been wickedly poking fun at a leader and his party, who are in a sad, not to say ridiculous plight, I must leave your readers to judge. Perhaps before this reaches the Examiner they will already know from the answer which Mr. Bonar La it is to give to the memorial of his party; or will the secret be kept a little longer, say until the eagerly- anticipated speech—eagerly anticipated, I may add, in every quarter—which Mr. Bonar Law is to deliver ten days hence in Edinburgh. Referring to that event, I see one Unionist paper, after the nowadays stereotyped a,nd regula- tion reference to the commanding position which Mr. Bonar Law occupies, adds that "all eyes are turned on him," and that he "will not fail to give his followers and his cause a strong lead." Is the wish father to the thought? Taking all the circumstances into consideration, what an ex- quisite note of irony there is in this expressed wish or thought. Becanse hitherto Mr. Bonar Law's lead has included such extraordinary con- tradictions. He has said that he believes in food taxes, ' and will not abandon them; and then at Ashton-under-Lyne he announced that he would leave them to be decided by the Colonies; while now he is being invited to recant and renounce them. With regard to the Referendum, he has on one occasion or another said that he did not want it; that he accepted it; that he rejected it; and that, as he proceeded to expain another time, it was wholly impracticable. Now, how on earth is the poor man under these distressing and dis- tracting conditions to give his party a strong, clear and definite lead? It would be difficult to conceive a picture at the same time more ludicrous, pathetic and even tragic than that of Mr. Bonar Law sitting down to compile his Edinburgh ora- tion. He would be a bold man who ventured to predict what that speech at Edinburgh is likely to contain after the experience we have had recently of Unionist evolutions and gyrations. The Union- ist and Tariff Reform Party's record in that res- pect for the last ten years is admirably summed up by Sir John Simon's speech at Rochdale. I quote the following verbatim from the Manchester Guardian: "In ten years," says Sir John' Simon, "they have invented twelve excuses for imposing these food taxes, and it is useful to call to mind and set in order what those excuses are. First, that the consolidation of the Empire requires it. Second, that it is the foreigner who will pay the tax. (Laughter.) Third, that maize and bacon will not be taxed so that the food of the very poorest may not be made more expensive. Fourth, that taxing food makes it cheater. (Laughter.) Fifth, that the taxes are to be very small ones—l suppose to prevent the food being too cheap. (Laughter.) Sixth, agriculture will be stimulated by the farmer getting better prices. Seventh, that the price of the untaxed supply always remains the same. Eighth, that the increased price of food will be compensated for by the remission of other duties. Ninth, that no food duties will be imposed until there has been a referendum to the British electors. (Laughter.) Tenth, that there will not be a referendum— (loud laughter),—but that we must accept the Colonial offer. Eleventh, that we do not want to accept the Colonial offer, and that we do not intend to accept the Colonial offer unless the Colonies in- sist. (Laughter.) And, twelfth, the most alarming of all, if food taxes are dropped Mr. Bonar Law will resign. (Laughter and cheers.)" I will not spoil that graphic and delightful picture by attempting to add another stroke of the brush.
A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

"The mysterious lady in red "has made her first appearance before a Warrington audience and her visit has occasioned no small amount of sensation, not merely because of the mystery which surrounds her identity but rather because the " turn " she provides at the Hippodrome is exceptionally good. The curtain rises and we see before us a lady of medium height clad from head to toe in red, and with her features hidden by a red velvet mask. It does not take long for her to justify the title which has been given her, "The lady with the phenomenal voice." Contrary to expectations she rendered some of the latest songs, her best number being undoubtedly that of " My Hero" from the." Chocolate Soldier." With little or no exertion r.he puts into the song the necessary spirit of love and pleading. Other numbers aro given with equal success. Quite a novelty to Warrington audiences is a diving and swimming act given by Serene Nord and her assistant. There is a real river on the stage, and the couple of dainty " mermaids " disport themselves in every way to delight the audience. High diving is an outstanding feature, as is also the accomplishment of the assistant in discarding a bathing suit whilst under water. Many capital " tricks " are also well executed. Tom E Hughes is one of the most elaborate and funny comedians we have seen for some time and in a way quite his own, he cannot fail to please all lovers of genuine comedy. Eiji skit "One of the Upper Ten" was exceedingly well done. Arthur Croxou is a clever entertainer, his mimicry of children being capital. A novel and pleasing acro- batic act is supplied by the Vigoranto Trio, to whom nothing in the way of acrobatics seems impossible. They are also clever teeth performers, one member holding the other two suspended in mid-air by means of a swivel and strap held in his teeth. The Lillie.s cause much fun in their novelty mirror illusion act and also please with their dancing, their facility in executing the most intricate steps being highly com- mendable. "Pastimes in Camp" is the title of a bounding cable act supplied in a pleasing manner by the Gilberts who are accomplished cable walkers and performers. Avis and Barre also appear as comedy conjurors and shadowists.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The leading " turn " next week will he provided by Three Alvarettas in the original comedy act "I can't shut my m uth." The Four Astors will present American rag-time songs and dances. Anna Dorothy "The Ginger Girl" foots an attractive and well varied Dill of fare.

div.head: LIQUOR CONTROLS
div.p: LIQUOR CONTROLS
Mr. H. Smith M.P. and the Temperance League.

We have received for publication the following copy of correspondence that has passed between Mr. B. T. Parkes, hon. secretary of the Warring- ton Citizens' Temperance League, and Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. :
Warrington Citizens' Temperance League, • December 14th, 1912

Dear Sir,—Two public meetings have been held, namely, November 28th, 1912, at Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, and December 11th, 1912, at, Independent Church, Brick-street, both in the County Borough of Warrington, at each of which the following resolution was unanimously passed : "That this meeting declares that delay in dealing effectively with the drink evil which strikes down to the very roots or our national life, is fraught with danger and disaster to the State, and in full reliance upon the Prime Minister's pledges calls upon the Government to introduce and pass the promised Licensing Bill (including the power of the local Veto) in the Parliamentary Session of 1913."—Yours faithfully,
BENJAMIN T. PARKE S , Hon. Sec
IhTernbet 16th, 1912

Dear Sir,—l have to acknowledge with thanks your letter of Saturday with copy of resolution adopted recently at two meetings held in War- rington. You will have seen the report of Mr. Asquith's speech to the deputation which he re- ceived on Wednesday last to the effect that the Government are unable to introduce licensing legislation next session. I shall be. glad to hear from you whether your League desire that Clubs should be dealt with in any Bill which way be introduced, or Whether it is proposed to ignore this uncontrolled source of supply which is reach- ing such enormous proportions.—Yours very truly. HAROLD SMITH. Mr. Benjamin T. Parkes.

• January 9th, 1913. Dear Sir,—l shall be glad to•receive your reply to the letter which I addressed to you in answer to yours of December 14th. lam very interested in temperance matters, and am most anxious to have the views of those who forward me such resolutions as you were good enough to send me.— Yours very truly, HAROLD SMITH. Mr. Benjamin T. Parkes.

Warrington Citizens' Temperance League, January 10th, 1913. Dear Sir,—At the Executive Meeting of the above League held on Wednesday, the Bth, your first letter (December 16th) was read, in which, after acknowledging receipt of copy of resolution, you ask for our desire in regard to clubs. We are in agreement with you that "this uncon- trolled source of supply is reaching such enormous proportions," and we desire that .it should be dealt with drastically, if it is at All possible to so deal with it. We desire that all clubs should be placed under magisterial control, and subject to inspection, also that the sale of intoxicating drink in clubs should be controlled, by the same laws that the public-houses are Subject unto, Thanking you for your inquiry, and trusting that, as you say you are interested in temperance mat- ters, we may hope for your support, as our Mem- ber, to help those of our fellow-citizens who, through intemperance, have become weak by bringing this "trade" under proper control and supervision,—Yours truly, BENJAMIN T. PARKES.

H. Smith, Esq., M.P. House of Commons, January 14th, 1913. My dear Sir,—l have to thank you for your letter of the 10th inst., and note with satisfaction that your League agree with the view that I ventured'to put forward, with respect to the prac- tically uncontrolled sale of liquor in clubs. It has always been a matter of amazement to me that so many who are devoted to the cause of temper- ance should remain satisfied with demands for further restricting the sale of liquor in premises licensed and controlled by the magistrates, and at the same time ignore the fact that the trade is increasing enormously in clubs under conditions which very often constitute a grave scandal. Until this state of affairs is remedied, temperance re- form, is in my view, impossible. If all those who are working for true temperance will make it clear that no Bill will be acceptable unless a proposal to deal with this evil is included, then I believe we shall be brought nearer to effective legislation. I respectfully invite your League to give to this aspect ,of the temperance question your very earnest consideration, and would be personally much gratified to hear that in my constituency there was a body of temperance reformers bold enough to take a strong line and to make it a condition precedent to their acceptance of any Bill that this serious matter should be dealt with. Only those who have given the matter close study can realise the evils which the drinking club is responsible for. As I imagine that this corre- spondence is of public interest, I venture to send copies to our local Press.—l am, yours very truly, HAROLD SMITH. Mr. Benjamin T. Parkes. P.S.—I enclose a copy of the "Clubs Bill" which I "backed."

div.head: WARRINGTON P.S.A. SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The 20th anniversary of this Society was celebrated in the Park Picture Palace, Sankey-street, on Sunday when there was a good attendance of members and friends. The President (Mr IZ. Nelson) presided and addressed a few words of encouragement to the mem- bers, urging them to greater diligence in all that was good so that 1913 might be a blessing to themselves and those about them. The speaker for the day was Mr E Wynne Jones, an ex-president of the Society who Broke of the advantages we possess to-day in having such institutions as the great brotherhood meetings in all our cities and towns. They were open to all, whether Cathac, Anglican, Nonconformist or of no religion at all. They held meetings where something could be learned of the religion of Jesus Christ. He asked the men to go onward and use the present, determined to do to-day what they ought. A band of such men consecrated to the Master was capable of doing great work. The orchestra, under the direction of Mr E J Hannon, gave selections in fine style. The cornet solo "The Lost Chord," by Mr Harding accom- panied by the band, was a vEry pleasing item. Mr William Clegg in thanking those who had sustained the programme, referred to the fact that these meetings were started as part of tha work of the Young Men's Christian Association, by Mr Thomas S Kent on the Bth January, 1893. They had been con- tinued every Sunday since that date. Mr William Hickman followed Mr Kent and successfully continued the work. He (the speaker) was the next president and the G.M.A.O. Committee having decided to close its doors, Mr Clegg with a vigorous committee and a large membership determined that the meetings should be continued and transferred them to the Co-operative Hall, where the society continued to prosper. Mr Wynne Jones succeeded Mr Clegg and successfully controlled the society until called by his own church for special work. Mr Robert Nelson then accepted the leader- ship. Circumstances made it necessary to transfer the meetings to the Picture Palace, where there is every reason to believe such a useful work may 13ng be continued.

div.head: INSURANCE BABIES.
div.p: INSURANCE BABIES.
FIRST LOCAL RECIPIENTS OF THE MATERNITY BENEFIT.

Those babies which were ushered into the world on Monday had a special claim to be known as "insurance babies," for with the dawn of January 13th, the maternity benefit of 30s. to the workers insured under the National Insurance Act became payable. Naturally there was a great deal of interest as to who would be the first workers in Warrington to become entitled to the State onus' especially in view of the fact that Mr, A, H. Crosfieid had made an offer of silver spoons and enlarged photographs to the insured parents of all children born in the borough between the hours of midnight on Sunday and midnight on Monday.
Photo Burrell. iT WARRINGTON BOUNTY BABY.
kindly offices of neighbours who locked in to attend to the wants of herself and the little one. _
Mrs. Rowland told our representative that her husband had already received the 30s. maternity benefit through the Prudential Approved Society.

"Yes," she added. "It has been a great help. I don't know what I should have done without it." Despite the grind of life on perpetually inadequate means—a maximum of 275. a week to keep a family of B—Mrs i,owland was not inclined to repine—in fact the receipt of the 30s. benefit seemed to have given her a brighter outlook on life and she repeatedly expressed her appreciation of it. "I could have done with the benefit too," observed a neighbour, "but I was a month too soon."
Mrs Rowland submitted to the ordeal of a flashlight photograph, while Warrington's first bounty baby yawned unconcernedly.

The following is a list of the parents whose babies have been born "with a silver spoon in their mouths." Mr and Mrs Arthur Henry Howland, 17, Hopwood- street (boy), born 1.30 am, Mr and Mrs Jonathan Barton, 27, Lord Nelson- street (girl), 1.50 a.m. Mr and Mrs William Jones, 20, Fonter-street (boy), 3.10 a.m.

GRIFFITHS proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfield. He remarked that they would be lacking in respect of their duty if they separated with- out showing their appreciation of his thoughtfuluess and generosity in recognising this memorable week. Councillor FIRTH LINDLEY k•econded and the vote was carried with acclamation.

A comprehensive vote of thanks to the Chairman, the committee of ladies who had prepared the tea, and the artistes, was proposed by Councillor J. WILKINSON. He remarked that they all recognised that their hopes had been realised by the passing of the Act, vvhich would bring sunshine to many thousands of homes in this happy land of ours. (Applause.) He hoped the benefits would be counted as blessings to go on for ever.
Mr. E. LLOYD JONE,4 seconded, and the resolution was unanimuusly carried. The singing f the National Anthem brought a very pleasaut evening to a close.

The number of births registered in War- rington during the year works out at about 2,200, giving a daily average of about six, On Monday, however, the normal rate was doubled, at least a dozen babies arriving in time to entitle their parents to the State bounty and Mr. Crosfield's gift. The distinction of being Warrington's first "insurance baby" belongs to a boy—the son of Mr. Arthur Henry and Elizabeth Rowland of 17, Hopwood-street. 1,20 a.m. was the time at which this youngster made his entry into the world. Exactly twenty minutes later, a daughter was born to Jonathan and Alice Ann Barton, of 27, Lord Nelson-street, Twins born in Warburton-street were just a little too early to be entitled as bounty babies. div.head: INSURANCE BENEFITS COMMEMORATED.
div.p: INSURANCE BENEFITS COMMEMORATED.
SUCCESSFUL LIBERAL GATHERING.
Telegram From Mr. Lloyd George.

It was a happy idea which prompted the Liberal Associations to commemorate the coming into operation of the benefits of the Insurance Act by the holding of a social in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. The proceedings took the form of a tea and concert and the evening's enjoyment for those who participated will long live in their memory. The keen interest with which the spirit of the occasion was entered into, was evidenced by the large party of ladies and gentlemen, numbering nearly 800, who sat down to tea. Every provision for the com- fort of the guests had been made by the committee of the Women's Liberal Associa- tion. Mrs. E. Osborne (secretary) and her band of energetic workers were most diligent in attending to the wants of the guests. It speaks volumes for the efficient organization of the Association that the arrangements for the catering and accom- modation of so huge a gathering were carried through to a successful conclusion without the slightest hitch. The ladies are to be complimented on the triumph of their powers of organization. Everyone was made to feel quite at home, and the happy, smiling faces testified to the general satisfaction. It was a matter for regret that Mr and Mrs Crosfield were unable to be present, but they sent a very warm message couched in the following terms : "Very hearty good wishes for health and happiness in 1913 to all friends at Parr Hall. May the Insurance Actgive added security, comfort and peace of mind, and the maternity grant be the only portion of its benificence required."

Mr. C. E. PARKER filled the breach and made a very admirable chairm4n, delighting the audience with several humorous stories. During the evening a congratulatory tele- gram was sent to Mr Lloyd George at West- minster in the following terms : "Magnificent public meeting in pro- gress celebrating the fruition of the Insurance Act benefits sends heartiest congratulations to the author." Before the party dispersed a reply was received as follows : House of Commons :—Parker Chair- man Parr Hall Warrington :—Sincerest thanks for kind congratulations. LLOYD GEORGE.

Enthusiasm ran high when the announce- ment of the names of the fortunate parents who were entitled to the gifts of Mr. Crosfield was made by the chairman.lt was impossible to make the formal presentation to the parents in view of the fact that the spoons ' for our latest citizens would have to be ' inscribed with their names, and the photo- graphs of the parents will be taken at an opportune time. The entertainment which followed was highly successful and greatly appreciated. An excellent programme had been arranged which included musical items by Mrs. E. A. Sanders, Madame Sara Silcock, Mr, E. Walker, Mr. J. Sephtor, . The soloists acquitted themselves in a very creditable manner. There were repeated calls for encores, but in view of the length of the pro- gramme the Chairman wisely ruled them out. The humorous element was supplied by Mr. W. W. Whittle, Mr. Kilduff and Mr. Martin Cain who proved themselves capital humorous entertainers. Mr. H. Val Vousden created much merriment with his repertoire of Irish stories. Miss A. Kilduff and Ernest Wilkes played the pianoforte accompani- ments with tact and judgment. Mr Parker wag supported on the platform by Alderman Burton, Councillors Peacock, Wilkinson, Lindley, Locker, Hawthorn, Gough, Skelland, Cunningon, Messrs E Griffiths, E Wynne Jones,E Lloyd Jones, P Delaney.

was born bears the impress of straightened circumstances and a stern struggle to make ends meet. No more fitting illustration of the blessings conferred by the National Insurance Act could be forthcoming than the case of Mr. and Mrs. Rowland. The little stranger who arrived on Monday makes their seventh child and all are living. The eldest—a girl of eighteen—is, however, a patient at the Sankey Sanatorium, having been sent there by the local Insurance Corn - mittee for treatment under the consumption clauses of the Act. An " Examiner "reporter who visited the house yesterday found Mrs. Rowlands full of gratitude for the 30s. bounty awarded under the maternity provisions of the health charter As is the case in many poorer working- class homes, during times of sickness, the bed had been transferred to the front room down- stairs and the invalid had to rely upon the

During an interval Councillor locKER read the telegram from Mr. Crosfleld, which evoked hearty cheers.—Mr. Locker expressed his delight in being able to participate in such a memorable occasion. To his mind the Itisurance Act was the finest Act that had ever been placed on the Statute Book of our country. It was the first genuine move in the direc- tion of social reform. (Applause.) The people had been remarkably patient, but the time had now arrived when they could participate in the benefits, and that evening they were to have some semblance of what had already been obtained. As an employer of labour who had bad some little to do with the payments of the workpeople, he was bound to say neither the workpeople nor the employers had felt the mite that came out of their pockets. As a rough estimate, a maternity benefit of from £:2,004) to £3,000 would be paid to the people of the town, which had never come from any other source. No other party had ever Riven such benefits, and as time went on, with such a leader as Mr. Asquith, they might look forward to more of those splendid Acts which were for the welfare of the people. The Liberal party wei e desirous that the conuitions of the working classes should be improved. (Applause).

, ['he CHAIRMAN, at the outset, said he wanted to con- gratulate the committee who had organised such a magnificent gathering. He thought it was a fit and happy thought that they should gather together on such an occasion. There had been going on in our history great social revolutions in connection with this Act. Most revolutions of the past had been accompanied with conflict, sometimes with hurt to health, life and property, but that revolution brought with it a safeguard of health, life and of the home. It t.‘ as a wonderful thing that that great revolution had come about so smoothly. He would like them just to think of the fact that there were thirteen million people who had been brought during the last six months into the National Insurance Scheme. Previously about six million were already insured in friendly societies, trade unions, and other organiza- tions. He thought they could conic atulate the friendly societies and rther organizations in having accom- plished such a wonderful work in bringing in so many people to combine for their own interests. But it was recognised that outside those societies there was a great number who were in greater need of insurance The Government through Mr. Lloyd-George (cheers)—had come to their help and brought an addition of seven millions of people who were not in any way insured, and who were obliged ii case of sickness coming into the home, to experience the bitter frost of want and poverty. Through that Act 13,000.000 of people bad been brought under supervision. (Applause.) The amount contributed by the people along with the emoloyers now in the hands of the State was over eight millions which had been paid in during the past six months. It was ready, at hand and at the call of those who were insured. He was informed that the local branch of the Ancient Order of Foresters had already received from the Government the sum of to be ready for the calls of their members upon that fund. (Applause.) They all knew how the Act had been received by many of their opponents. They would remember the agitation in the Press and the misrepresentation which had been carried on at recent by-elections. Mr Lloyd George was right when he described the agitation in respect of the servants' tax as the meanest which had ever been set on foot by the Press. They could now afford to smile at all this froth because the servants who were the least likely to understand the merits of the question. now completely understood it and came forward as its staunchest supporters. Our , goodly ship had now come in, Mr Lloyd George had been its pilot and Mr Ma• terman had been at the wheel. That night they gathered together to wel- come the ship home with all its goodly cargo and its message of benefit to the whole nation. He thought they ought to definitely congratulate in the first place Mr Lloyd George—(applause)—whose wonderful energy, patience, tact and perseverance had carried the Bill forward and won all along the line. t Applause) They congratulated the Liberal party generally, and themselves as a part of the party, for the backing they had given to the Chancellor of the Exchequer in the matter. The Act was now a National asset. One of his Conservative friends told hint the other day that the Act was one of the finest things passed for many years. If there were others present that night who did not think entirely with them on their general policy he wanted them to rejoice that this great national benefit had through the wisdom of Parliament been brought forward and carried into effect. (Applause). There was another duty he had to perform, which had reference to the births which had occurred in Warringtou on Monday. They all knew that Mr CrosfieM very thoughtfully had given to each child born on that day a silver spoon with the name of the child engraved upon it, and a framed photograph of the parents and child. He had pleasure in announcing the fortunate parents. There were nine altogether. Seven boys arid two girls. As it was a woman's day' Mr Parker jocularly remarked in regard to sex that they ought to have played up better than they did. (Laughter.) He hoped they would grow up healthy men and women, and make good citizens. (Applause.)

div.head: INFIRRIARY AND INSURANCE
div.p: INFIRRIARY AND INSURANCE
Honorary Staff's Request for Payment.
IMPORTANT CONFERENCE OF EMPLOYERS. P. & K. SUBSCRIPTION REDUCED.

The authorities of the Warrington Infirmary have been experiencing some anxiety as to the probable effect of the National Insurance Act upon the emi- ti ibutions to the funds of the Institution. Some important points were raised at a conference of employers held at the Infirmary yesterday after- noon, under the presidency of Mr. J. H. Smethurst (Chait man of the Board of Management). The Pearson 8z Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd. had intimated their intention to reduce their annual subscription from £5O to £lO, in view of the fact that the Act had imposed upon the Company a burden to the extent of £6,500 per annum. Messrs. William Robertson Ltd. wrote regretting that, owing to the cost of the Insurance Act, they were reluc- tantly compelled to discontinue their subscription to the Institution.

The Board of Management was also favoured with a notification from the honorary surgeons that in future they could not attend insured patients free of charge. They asked for an allowance of 14s. per head per week. For three months, at any rate, the Board do not intend to make any depar- ture from the system already obtaining, and Dr. Law, the senior house surgeon, gave a denial to the suggestion that one or two insured patients had all eady been told that their treatment could not be continued and that they must go to a doctor on the panel. Such a course would have been contrary to the express, instructions of the Board of Management. Dr. 'Law stated, however, that some patients had been advised to go to doctors on the panel, but there had been no attempt et coercion.
Three alternative suggestions were laid before the local Insurance Committee by the Board of Manage- ment. They were:—
(1) The payment by the Comniittee of £2 2s. a week for each insured person While in hospital.
(2) Payment to the Infirmary of :Id. a week for each insured person in the town.
(3). An undertaking to subscribe such a sum to the Infirmary as shall be the equivalent to the amount suggested in No. 1. _ _

Councillor H. Roberts said the sooner the idea of receiving two guineas per week per patient was got out of the minds of the Board, the better. It was an absolutely impossible and impracticable suggestion.

Mr. F. W. Monks: A most unreasonable demand. Councillor Roberts said the contribution which the Board asked for aggregated 0,000 a year. The only answer the Insurance Committee could give was that they did not know where on earth the money was to come from. He believed the posi- tion of the hospitals at the end of the first year of the Act would be such as would compel some State assistance. Therefore, in order that those institutions might not be punished by the with- drawal of subscriptions, they ought to plead for a continuance of the present support until the .position of the Infirmaries under the Act was properly defined. Mr. Smethurst explained that the charge of two guineas per week was made up of the cost of maintenance and nursing of the patient, plus a proportion of the demand of the Medical Board. Councillor Roberts said people who were in a far better financial position than many insured per- sons had been treated in the Institution at a charge of one guinea per week. Why should the Board ask the Insurance Committee to base their contri- bution on two guineas per week? Dr. Law: It is to meet the reasonable demands of the men who do the work—the doctors.

Dr. Sutherland said medical men throughout the country had thought for a long time that they were being abused, as honorary surgeons. They took it that people who availed themselves of chari- table institutions were on the poverty line and they treated them free. Now the doctors had been forced into a system of treating insured persons who were no longer necessitous, and they considered they were entitled to some acknowledgment of their work for Infii rnaries.

Mr. F. \X'. Monks said the action of the Medical Board was going to strike at the whole position of honorary surgeons. If there was to be a demand for payment for services rendered, they would have to throw the work open to all the medical men in the toi,vn and give them an equal opportunity. It was stated that the employees of several works had intimated that they could not continue their usual contributions but, when appealed to by the secretary (Mr. Hampson), they had revoked' that decision.

Ultimately it was resolved, on the proposition of Councillor Roberts: That the employees be respect- fully and urgently requested to continue their present rate of subscriptions, pending the adjustment of the financial relations between the Infirmary and the InstitTnce Committee, aided by the National Insur- ance Commissioners.
The Board of Management has approached Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Masterman with a view to a solution ot their difficulties.

div.head: MAYOR'S "AT HOME."
div.p: MAYOR'S "AT HOME."

The Mayor and Mayoress (Councillor Dr Joseph and Mrs Arnold Nield) held an "At Home " at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon. The weather favoured the function and the attendance was well up to the average, about 500 ladies and g•iitlemen attending to pay their respects to the chief magistrate and his daughter. The visitors were received in the Council Chsmber. An orchestra, under the conductorship of Mr E Wilkes, was in attendance and played the following programme in very pleasing style : March, " Under the .double eagle," Wagner ; Gavotte, "Mignon," Thomas; entre' acte, "lii the shadows," Finck ; waltz, "Chocolate soldier," 0. Straus ,• overture, " Tancredi," Bossini ; intermezzo, "Rendez- vous," Alletter ; Atneiican sketch, "Down South," Middleton; Barcarolle," Tales of Hoffman," Offenbach; intermezzo, 'Hearts and Flowers," Czibulka ; selection." Faust," Gounod ; "Song Without Words," Mendelssobn ; march, "Per Aspera ad Astra," Urbach ; prelude, Bach; waltz, "Nights of Glad- ness," Ancliffe ; selection, "II Trovatore," Verdi ; march, "Franz Joseph," Gung'l ; waltz, " Pit- chounetta,"_Bose. -

The vestibule of the hall was tastefully decorated with plants which had been arranged by Mr R Whit- field, head gardener to the Corporation. After having been received by the Mayor and Mayoress, the visitors passed into the committee rooms where refreshments were served.

NATIONAL INSURANCE ACT, 1911. CHESHIRE INSURANCE COMMITTEE. ARRANGEMENT FOR MEDICAL BENEFIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN to Insured Persons that the Insurance Committee for the County Palatine of Chester have made arrangements with Medical Practitioners and Chemists and other persons for the administration of Medical Benefit. Only one Panel of Doctors has been formed for the whole of the Committee's Area and a printed list of Doctors, and Chemists etc., in book form, has been issued to all Post Offices and Sub-Post Offices and Officers of Customs and Excise in the County and , places adjacent thereto. For the purpose of convenient exhibition in Placard Form the list ba3 been split up into sections represent- ing Districts and these placards have been sent to the Post Offices, &c., in those Districts and to such other Post Offices, &c., in the immediate neighbourhood to which the insured persons resident in those Districts might reasonably be expected to go for information. Copies of the Booklet, above referred to, have been sent to Approved Societies having Insured Members in the Committee's Area. Every Insured Person has the right to choose any Doctor on the Panel whether his name is on the Placard for the District in which the Insured Person resides or whether his name is on the Placard for some other District, and subject to the consent of the practitioner an selected, of being attended and treated by him. An Insured Person should, after consulting the list, present his Medical Ticket to the Doctor selected. He is entitled to have any prescription given to him by a Doctor made up by any Chemist whose name appears on the list. Any further information can be obtained upon appli- cation to the local branch of the insured person's Approved Society, or to the nearest Officer of Customs and Excise, whose address will be given on enquiry at any Post Office, or by writing to the undersigned. FRANK T. WEST, Clerk to the Committee. 100, Northgate Street, Chester. 13th January, 1913.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that by an Instrument dated the 18th day of December, 1912, the Local Government Board have given authority to the Corporation of Warrington to prepare a Town Planning Scheme under tho provisions of part 2 of the above Act. A copy of the Instrument giving such authority may be inspected and any necessary explanation or informa- tion with regard thereto may be obtained, without payment of any fee, at my office during the hours of 10 a.m. end 5 p.m. on any week-day (Saturday 10 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.) pending the preparation or adoption of the scheme. The Corporation now propose to prepare a scheme and any person interested or affected desiring to be heard in reference to such proposal, including any persons representing architectural or archreological societies or otherwise interested in the amenity of the proposed soheme should give notice in writing to me within 21 days from the date thereof. COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.— The Warrington Insurance Committee invite Applications for the position of CLERK at a salary of 4150 per annum. Applicants must have had experience in book-keeping and general business administration, and preference will be given to candidates who have a knowledge of shorthand and typewriting. Applications stating age, experience and qualifications and also stating the earliest date the candidate will be prepared , to commence duties, to be in the candidate's own hand- writing, and to be accompanied by a copy of ONE RECENT TESTIMONIAL from the candidate's present or last employer, must be adddressed to the under- signed and received by him before Neon on Saturday, the 25th January, 1913. Envelopes must be sealed and marked "Clerkship." The person appointed will be required to devote the Whole of his time to the duties of the office ; office accommodation and necessary office expenses will be found by the Committee. Warrington.A .T.HALLAWAY, Acting Clerk. Town Hall,
